abandoned.text: banished, kept away “from” Shr. Ind. ii. 117 .

abase.text: to lower (the eyes) 2H6 i. ii. 15, R3 i. ii. 248 (Ff).

abate.text: 1 the usual sense ; the corresponding intr. sense ' decrease ' is rare ; 2 is common Eliz. ; 3-6 are rare) 1 to lessen, shorten MND. in. ii. 432 A. thy hours! 2 to blunt, fig. 2H4 I. i. 117 his metal . . . once in him abated, R3 v. iv. 48 [v. 35] Abate the edge of traitors. 3 to deprive o/Lr. n. iv.lQla-d me of half my train. 4 to bar, except LLL. v. ii. 545 A. throw at novum, and the whole icorld again Cannot pick out five such. 5 to depreciate (a person) Cym. i. iv. 78 I would abate her nothing. 6 to humble Cor. in. iii. 130 most Abated captives.

abatement.text: in sense 1 usu. legal metaphor) 1 reduction, diminution Ham. iv. vii. 120 abate- ments and delays, Lr. I. iv. 64, Cym. v. iv. 21. 2 depreciation of a person's character Tw.N. i. i. 13.

abhor.text: 2 term of canon law = Latin ' detestor ') 1 to horrify, disgust Ham, v. i. 205 (Ff) how abhorred my imagination is, Oth. rv. ii. 162 It does a. me. 2 to protest against H8 n. iv. 79 I utterly abhor, pea . . . Refuse you for my judge ; cf. Err. in. ii. 165.

abhorred.text: abominable (freq.j John iv. ii. 224. abhorring" (rare ; ' abhorrence ' is post-S.) 1 abhorrence, loathing Cor. i. i. Hi flatter Beneath a. 2 object of disgust Ant. v. ii. 60 let the water-flies Blow me into abhorring ; cf. ' an abhorring unto

abide.text: senses 'remain ' and 'endure' are common) 1 no more but a., make only a brief stay Wint. iv. ii. [iii.] 100. 2 to face or encounter in fight MND. in. ii. 422 A. me, if thou dar'st, 2H4 n. iii. 36, Cym. in. iv. 186. 3 esp. with ' dear' = aby MND. in. ii. 175 (Q2 Ff), Caes. in. i. 94, ii. 120.

ability.text: wealth, means Tw.N. in. iv. 380, 2H4 i. iii. 45 ; cf. Ado iv. i. 201 Ability in means.

abject.text: adj. his abject object, the object of his con- tempt H8 i. i. 127.— sb. the queen's abjects, the most servile of her subjects R3 i. i. 106.

abjectly.text: basely Tit. n. iii. 4 thinks of me so abjectly. able adj. (1 occurs six times, 2 once) 1 strong, vigorous, active All'sW. iv. v, 87, 2H4 i. i. 43, Ham. v. ii. 211. 2 talented, clever Sonn. lxxxv. 7 that able spirit. able vb. : to warrant, vouch for Lr. iv. vi. 173. abode sb. (1 and 2 now obs. ; 3 now chiefly in echoes of the Bible ; cf. ' We will . . . make our abode with him ' John xiv. 23) 1 waiting, delay Mer.V. n. vi. 21 my long abode. 2 temporary remaining, stay Cym. i. vi. 53. 3 make abode, to dwell, reside Gent. iv. iii. 23. Lr. i. i. 136. abode vb. : to bode, forebode 3H6 v. vi. 45, H8 1. i. 93.

abomination.text: sense of ' detestation ' not S.) 1 abominable thing or act Ant. in. vi. 94 most large In his abominations, Lucr. 921, 1832. 2 abominableness Lucr. 704 Ere he can see his own a.

abortive.text: adj. born prematurely ; (hence) un- timely, unnatural, monstrous, lit. and fig. LLL. i. i. 104 an a. birth, 2H6 iv. i. 60 this thy a. pride, E3 i. ii. 21, i. iii. 228.— sb. untimely or monstrous birth John in. iv. 158 Abortives, presages.

abound.text: to be rich H8 1. i. 83 ; cf. Philippians iv. 18.

about.text: used imperatively : get to work, bestir yourself ! Wiv. v. v. 61, 2H4 in. ii. 305, Cses. in. ii. 209, Ham. n. ii. 625. about prep. : follows its noun in Per. in. Gower 2 No din but snores the house about.

above.text: upstairs Wiv. iv. ii. 80, Err. n. ii. 211, 1H4 ii. iv. 558.

abram.text: corruption of ' abron ' = auburn Cor. n. iii.

abridgefrom.text: to deprive of, debar from Mer.V.i. i. 127 to be abridged From such a noble rate.

abridgement.text: means of shortening or whiling away the time, pastime MND. v. i. 39 what abridge- ment have you for this evening ?, Ham. n. ii. 448 look where my abridgement comes [i.e. the players],

abroach.text: set abroach, to set on foot 2H4 iv. ii. 14, R3 i. iii. 325, Rom. i. i. 110.

abroad.text: the following are the chief uses) 1 outside certain limits : (i) away or apart from one's own body or person 2H6 in. ii. 172 His hands abroad displayed, Cym. i. ii. 4, in. iv. 180, Compl. 137, 183 All my offences that abroad you see ; (ii) away from one's home, out of one's house, in foreign lands Tp. in. i. 52, C*es. v. iii. 95, Ham. i. i. 161 then . . . no spirit can walk abroad. 2 about in the world, in public Meas. in. ii. 90, LLL. i. i. 187 There's villany abroad, Rom.v. iii. 190, Oth. i. iii. 393.

abrook.text: to brook, endure, bear 2H6 ir. iv. 10.

abruption.text: breaking off in speech Troil. in. ii. 68.

absent.text: absent time, time of absence R2 n. iii. 79 ; so absent hours Oth. in. iv. 173. absey-book, i.e. ABC-book : primer, hornbook John t. i. 196 then comes answer like an absey-book.

absolute.text: sense 3 is common in 17th cent.) 1 free from imperfection, complete, finished, per- ABSTRACT 2 - ACTOR feet. Meas. v. i. 54, Ham. v. ii. 112 an absolute gentleman, Per. iv. Gower 81. 2 unrestricted, unconditional 2H4 iv. i. 186, Cor. in. i. 115 Though there the people had more a. power. 3 positive, perfectly certain, decided Meas. m. i. 5, Cor. in. i. 89 mark you His absolute ' shall ' 1, Cym. iv. ii. 106.

abstract.text: 3 and 4 are peculiar to S.) 1 epitome (of something greater), compendium (of many qualities) John n. i. 101, Ant. i. iv. 9 the abstract of all faults. 2 summary account R3 iv. iv. 28, Ham. n. ii. 555 abstracts and brief chronicles of the time. 3 summary proceeding All'sW. iv. iii. 100 an ab- stract of success, Ant. in. vi. 61 {obstruct f). 4 short catalogue or inventory Wiv. iv. ii. 65. abuse sb. (1 and 2 were common Eliz., now obs.) 1 ill-usage, injury, wrong, insult, offence, crime Wiv. v. iii. 9, Meas. v. i. 241, 3H6 in. iii. 188 the abuse done to my niece, Rom. in. i. 199, Sonn. exxxiv. 12 through my unkind abuse. 2 imposture, deception, delusion Ham. iv. vii. 50 Or is it some a. and no such thing ? (Cf. self- abuse.) 3 corrupt practice Meas. n. i. 43, Caes. n. i. 115 the time's abuse, Ven. 792. 4 injurious speaking, reviling 2H4 it. iv. 341 ; pi. (obs.) Meas. v. i. 342 his treasonable abuses. abuse vb. (precise meaning often doubtful ; in many examples two or more senses are blended) 1 to impose upon, cheat, deceive Ado v. ii. 104, Ham. n. ii. 640, Lr. iv. i. 22 thy abused father's wrath, iv. vii. 77, Cym. I. iv. 129. 2 to ill-use, maltreat, do violence to Wiv. i. i. 3, Err. v. i. 199, R3 i. iii. 52 his simple truth must be a-'d,Rom. iv. i. 29, Lr. iv. vii. 15, Sonn. xlii. 7. 3 to insult Ant. v. ii. 43, Cym. n. iii. 154. [v. 41. 4 to disgrace, dishonour Wiv. n. ii. 310, 1H6 iv. 5 to malign, revile Tim. n. ii. 48, Oth. v. i. 123.

abuser.text: corrupter Oth. i. ii. 18 abuser of the world.

aby.text: to pay the penalty for, atone for MND. in. ii. 175 (Q2 Ff abide), 335 (Ff abide).

abysm.text: orig. form 'abime'; rhymes with 'time' as late as 1616) 1 bottomless pit Ant. in. xi. [xiii.] 147 abysm of hell. 2 profound chasm or gulf (fig.) Tp. i. ii. 50 abysm of time, Sonn. cxii. 9.

academe.text: academy, philosophical school LLL. I. i. 13, iv. iii. 303.

accent.text: 1 first in S., as also the senses ' peculiar mode of utterance ' AYL. in. ii. 363, ' metrical stress ' LLL. iv. ii. 125) 1 word, speech, language John v. vi. 14 any accent breaking from thy tongue, 1H4 1. i. 3, Rom. n. iv. 31, Caes. in. i. 113 In. . . accents yet unknown, Lucr. 566. 2 second accent, echo H5 n. iv. 126.

accidence.text: rudiments of (Latin) grammar Wiv. iv. i. 18.

accident.text: occurrence, incident, event Tp. v. i. 305 the particular accidents gone by, Ado n. i. 190, Ham. in. ii. 211.

accite.text: 1 common 1500-1680 ; 2 used by Ben Jonson) 1 to summon, cite 2H4 v. ii. 141, Tit. i. i. 27. 2 used for « exeite ' 2H4 n. ii. 67 (Ff 3 4 excites).

accommodate.text: rare ; 1 first in S.) 1 to furnish, equip 2H4 in. ii. 73, Lr. rv. vi. 82. 2 pa. pple. favoured Cym. v. iii. 32 A-d by the place.

accommodation.forms: accommodation (Ben Jonson in his ‘Discoveries’ speaks of
accommodation.text: the perfumed terms of the time, as ‘accommodation’, ‘complement’, ‘spirit’, &c.) 1. provision, entertainment Oth. I. iii. 239 “such and besort As levels with her breeding.”

speaksof.text: the perfumed terms of the time, as 1 accommodation ', ' complement ', c spirit ', &c.) 1 provision, entertainment Oth. i. iii. 239 such a. and besort As levels with her breeding. 2 pi. conveniences, comforts Meas. in. i. 14 all th' accommodations that thou bear'st.

accomplish.text: (not very freq.; sense 2 only S.) 1. to equip perfectly Mer.V. III. iv. 61 , R2 II. i. 178 “Accomplish'd with the number of thy hours” (= of the same age as thou), H5 IV. Chor. 12 “The armourers, accomplishing the knights.”

accomplishdwiththenumberofthyhours.forms: Accomplish d with the number of thy hours
accomplishdwiththenumberofthyhours.text: = of the same age as thou), H5 iv. Chor. 12 The armourers, accomplishing the knights. 2 to gain, obtain 3H6 in. ii. 152 to accomplish twenty golden croivns. accord sb. : (' at a.' is Chaucerian ; 2 not post-S.) 1 harmony, concord Shr. in. i. 74, H5 v. ii. 381 : AYL. i. i. 69 at accord (—in agreement). 2 assent, consent Err. n. i. 25, H5 v. ii. 71, Ham. i. ii. 123 ; Troil. i. iii. 238 Jove's accord, with Jove, i. e. heaven, on their side. accord vb. : to agree, assent AYL. v. iv, 140, Rom. i. ii. 19 my consent and fair according voice.

accordant.text: agreeing, consenting Ado. i. ii. 16. accosting* t : see coasting.

accountant.text: liable to give an account, account- able Meas. ii. iv. 87, Oth. n. i. 305 accountant for as great a sin.

accuse.text: accusation 2H6 in. i. 160 By false accuse.

acerb.text: sour and bitter Oth. i. iii. 355 (Qi only). acne sb. : pronounced ' aitch ' like the letter H (cf. Ado in. iv. 55) ; hence pi. aches is of two

syllables.text: Tp. i. ii. 370). [edd. ache vb. : pronounced ' ake ' and so spelt in orig.

acheron.text: river of the infernal regions, app. supposed by S. to be a lake Tit. iv. iii. 44.

achieve.text: freq. in sense 1 ; rare in 2 and 3) 1 to gain, obtain AlFsAV. i. i. 53, Cor. i. ix. 33, Sonn. lxvii. 3. 2 to make an end of, kill (Fr. achever) H5 iv. iii. 91. 3 to accomplish one's purpose Cor. iv. vii. 23.

achievement.text: acquisition 2H4 iv. v. 188, Troil. i. ii. 317, iv. ii. 72.

achilles'spear.text: the rust from which cured the wounded Telephus 2H6 v. i. 100.

achitophel.text: Absalom's counsellor (2 Samuel xv.), 2H4 i. ii. 39. [iii. 320.

acknown.text: “be on,” confess knowledge of Oth. III. iii. 320 .

a-cold.text: cold Lr. in. iv. 57 Tom's a-cold.

aconitum.text: poisonous extract of the plant wolfs- bane or monk's-hood, Aconitum Napellus 2H4 iv. iv. 48.

acquit.text: the foil, are the rarer meanings in S.) 1 to atone for Lucr. 1071 Till life to death acquit my fore'd offence. 2 to repay, requite Mer.V. v. i. 138, H5 n. ii. 144. 3 pa. pple. acquit of, rid of Wiv. I. iii. 25. acquittance sb. (rare ; a doubtful instance occurs in Oth. iv. ii. 193; Qi only, the rest acquaintance) 1 writing in evidence of a discharge LLL. n. i. 160 acquittances For such a sum, Cym. v. iv. 174. 2 discharge, acquittal Ham. iv. vii. 1. acquittance vb.: to acquit, clear R3 in. vii. 231.

across.text: = cross adv. All'sW. ii. i. 70 (cf. note s.v. TRAVERSE adv.). along* : adv. at full length AYL. n. i. 30, Rom. v. iii. 3 ; cf. lie along below ; prep, throughout the length of AYL. n. i. 32.

action.text: gesture, gesticulation Shr. Ind. i. 132, Caes. in. ii. 226 A., nor utterance, nor the power of speech, Mac. v. i. 31, Ham. in. ii. 20, Lucr. 1403.

action-taking'.text: litigious, seeking satisfaction at law Lr. ii. ii. 18 action-taking knave.

actor.text: doer Meas. n. ii. 37 Condemn the fault, and not the actor of it ?, All'sW. n. iii. 29, Lucr. 608. ACTUAL - :* - AFFECT

actual.text: consisting in action, active Mac. v. i. 13 her /calking and other actual performances, Oth. iv. ii. 153 of thought or actual deed.

adam.text: 2 ' buff ' was used for ' the naked skin ') 1 the offending Adam, the Old Adam, H5 i. i. 29. 2 the picture of old Adam, (jocularly for) the bailiff's officer, who wore buff {like Adam) Err. iv. iii. 13. 3 =Adam Bell, a famous archer Ado i. i. 269 [261]. Hence Adamf Cupid i.e. Cupid the Archer, Rom. n. i. 13, for orig. Abraham Cupid (which has not been satisfactorily explained).

adamant.text: stone or mineral of excessive hardness 1H6 i. iv. 52 ; identified with the loadstone or magnet MND. n. i. 195, Troil. m. ii. 186 as turtle to her mate, As iron to adamant. a-days (mod. edd. o' days) : 2H4 n. iv. 250, Tim. iv. iii. 293.

addiction.text: inclination, bent H5 1. i. 54, Oth. n. ii. 6.

addition.text: the ordinary uses occur ; 1 is freq. ; 2 and 3 rare) 1 something added to a man's name to denote his rank, &c. ; title, style of address ; mark of dis- tinction ; Wiv. ii. ii. 316 devils' additions, All's W. ii. iii. 134, Cor. i. ix. 66, Mac. in. i. 106 (cf. sense 3), Ham. i. iv. 20, Lr. i. i. 138 The name and all tW addition to a king, ii. ii. 26, Oth. iv. i. 105. 2 something added to a coat of arms as a mark of honour Troil. iv. v. 140. [20. 3 particular a-s, distinctive attributes Troil. i. ii.

address.text: most freq. in sense 2 ; 3 and 4 are rare) 1 to direct LLL. v. ii. 92, MND. ii. ii. 143, Tw.N. I. iv. 15 address thy gait unto her. 2 to prepare, make ready MND. v. i. 106, Mer.V. ii. ix. 19, H5 in. iii. 58 To-morrow for the march are we addrest, Caes. in. i. 29, Ham.i. ii. 216 it. . . did address Itself to motion. 3 to get oneself ready Troil iv. iv. 146 Let us address to tend on Hector s heels. 4 to make one's speech Lr. i. i. 193.

adhere.text: to hang together, agree Wiv. n. i. 63, Mac. I. vii. 52 Nor time nor place Did then adhere.

adjunct.text: not pre-Eliz.) adj. connected, annexed John in. iii. 57, Sonn. xci. 5 every humour hath his adjunct pleasure. sb. something annexed LLL. iv. iii. 314 Learning is but an a. to ourself; person in attendance Sonn. cxxii. 13 To keep an a. to remember thee.

admirable.text: to be wondered at, wonderful MND. V. i. 27 strange and admirable. [x. 2].

admiral.text: flagship 1H4 in. iii. 28, Ant. in. viii. 12

admiration.text: the foil, are occasional uses) 1 quality of exciting wonder or approbation, ad- mirableness Tp. in. i. 38. 2 object of wonder, marvel All'sW. n. i. 91. 3 note of admiration, the sign ! Wint. v. ii. 12.

admire.text: rare use) : to wonder (at) Tp. v. i. 154, Tw.N. iii. iv. 167 nor admire not in thy mind, why I do call thee so.

admired.text: 1 cf. unavoided = inevitable) 1 admirable Tp. in. i. 37, Ant. n. ii. 125. 2 wonderful Mac. in. iv. 110 With most a. disorder.

admittance.text: acceptance, sanction; (hence) vogue, fashion Wiv. III. iii. 61 ; II. ii. 240 “of great admittance” (= in high favour).

adoptedly.text: by adoption Meas. i. iv. 47 Adoptedly ; as school-maids change their names.

adoptiouschristendoms.text: christenings of adopted children All'sW. i. i. 190*.

advance.text: to raise, lift up Tp. i. ii. 405, H5 v. Prol. 44, R3 1. ii. 40 A. thy halberd higher than my breast, Rom. ii. iii. 5. •fj The many passages in which flags and standards are said to be 'advanced' may bear this meaning. advantage sb. (sense ' profit, benefit ' is freq. with phr. make or take a. of, rarely on Ven. 405) ; also 4 advantageous or favourable position ') 1 favourable opportunity, chance Tp. in. iii. 13 The next a. Will we take, Oth. i. iii. 299, n. i. 249, Ven. 129 ; 3H6 in. ii. 192 for advantages ( = as it serves my convenience ; cf. Compl. 123) ; Oth. m. iii. 312

totheadvantage.text: = opportunely). 2 pecuniary profit, interest on money Mer.V. i. iii. 71 neither lend nor borrow Upon advantage; fig. John in. iii. 22. 3 with advantages Kb iv. iii. 50 ('his story will lose nothing in the telling '). advantage vb. (1 the trans, sense is more freq.) 1 to be of benefit Tp. i. i. 36 our own doth little a. 2 to augment K3 iv. iv. 324 Advantaging their loan with interest.

advantageable.text: profitable, advantageous H5 v, ii. 88 advantag cable for our dignity.

advantageouscare.text: anxiety to obtain a position of advantage Troil. v. iv. 23. adventure sb.: hazard, chance Wint. v. i. 156, John v. v. 22 ; at all adventures, at all hazards, whatever may be the consequences Err. n. ii. 220, H5 iv. i. 123. adventure vb.: to venture Wint. i. ii. 38, R3 i. iii. 116, Rom. n. ii. 84, v. iii. 11, Cym. in. iv. 156.

adversity.text: perverse one, quibbler Troil. v. i. 14.

adve'rtise.text: to inform, instruct Meas. i. i. 41* one that can my part in him advertise, 3H6 v. iii. 18, H8 ii. iv. 176 he might the king . . . advertise.

advertisement.text: stressed always on the second syllable) 1 information 1H4 in. ii. 172 this a. is five days old. 2 advice, counsel Ado v. i. 32, All'sW. iv. iii. 240 an advertisement . . . to take heed, 1H4 iv. i. 36. advertising" : attentive Meas. v. i. 384 Advertising and holy to your business.

advice.text: consideration, deliberation, consultation Gent. ii. iv. 208, Mer.V. iv. ii. 6, Shr. i. i. 116, John in. iv. 11, H5 n. ii. 43 on his more advice (= after maturer reflection).

advise.text: ' to counsel ' is the commonest sense ; cf. advised 2) 1 refl. and intr. to bethink oneself, consider Tw.N. iv. ii. 104, H5 in. vi. 171, Rom. in. v. 192, Lr. ii. i. 29 Advise yourself. 2 to inform, apprise Gent. in. i. 122, All'sW. in. v. 26, H5 ii. Chor. 12 advis'd by good intelligence, H8 i. ii. 107 I shall anon advise you Further.

advised.text: see also well-advised) 1 considerate, deliberate, cautious,well-considered Mer.V. i. i. 143 ivith more advised watch, John iv. ii. 214, R2 i. iii. 188, H5 i. ii. 179 The advised head defends itself. 2 be advised, take good advice, take care, be cautious LLL. iv. iii. 368, H8 i. i. 139, Oth. i. ii. 55. 3 art thou not advised, art thou unaware ? Shr. i. i. 190 ; so 2H4 i. i. 172, 2H6 n. i. 47 ; i" am advised, I know very well Err. v. i. 214. [122.

advocation.text: pleading of an advocate Oth. in. iv.

sedile.text: magistrate in ancient Rome who had the superintendence of public buildings, police, &c. Cor. in. i. 173, &c.

aerial.text: of the atmosphere Oth. n. i. 39 (Ff eriall).

aerie.text: nest, or (esp. in S.) brood of a bird of prey, and particularly of hawks John v. ii. 149, R3 i. iii. 264 ; Ham. n. ii. 362 aerie of children (with reference to the young choristers of the Chapel Royal and St. Paul's, who acted plays).

afaroff.text: remotely, indirectly Wiv. i. i. 215, Wint. ii. i. 103. affect sb. (both senses were in common Eliz. use) 1 kind feeling, affection R2 i. iv. 30. AFFECT— 2 disposition, tendency LLL i. i. 150, Oth. i. iii. 265

theyoungaffects.text: = youthful inclinations). affect vb.1 (2 by far the commonest sense ; 4 only once) 1 to aim at, aspire to Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 433, 2H6 iv. vii. 103, Cor. m. iii. 1 affects Tyrannical power, iv. vi. 32. 2 to be fond of, love Tw.N. n. v. 28, Lr. t. i. 1. 3 to be inclined Ant. i. iii. 71 making peace or war As thou affect'st. 4 to assume the character of, imitate John I. i. 86 The accent of his tongue affecteth him. affect vb.2 : to act upon contagiously, as a disease Troil. ii. ii. 59 what infectiously itself affects.

affected.text: the mod. sense ' full of affectation ' occurs once LLL. v. i. 15) 1 disposed, inclined Gent. i. iii. 60, Shr. i. i. 26 in all affected as yourself, Lr. n. i. 100 ill affected. 2 in love LLL. n. i. 230 that which ive lovers entitle affected, Ven. 157.

affectedly.text: lovingly Compl. 48. [145. affecting* : using affectation, affected Wiv. n. i. affection sb. (the usual S. sense is the ordinary one of ' love ' ; 4 is rare) 1 emotion, feeling, esp. pi. LLL. i. i. 9, Mer.Y. i. i. 16, Caes. n. i. 20 when his affections sway'd More than his reason. 2 mental tendency, natural disposition Mer.V. i. ii. 37, Mac. iv. iii. 77 my most ill-compos'd affection. 3 state of mind towards a thing, bent, inclination, wish Tp. i. ii. 478 My affections Are then most humble, Ado n. ii. 7 ivhatsoever comes athwart his affection, LLL. v. i. 95, Cor. i. i. 109. 4 affectation LLL. v. ii. 408, Ham. ii. ii. 473 (Qq). affection vb. : to have affection for Wiv. i. i. 234. affectioned * : (a) full of affectation ; (b) self- willed, obstinate Tw.N. n. iii. 162.

affeer.text: to confirm Mac. iv. iii. 34 The title is affeer'd.

affiance.text: confidence H5 n. ii. 127, Cym. i. vi. 163.

affianced.text: betrothed Meas. m. i. 221 affianced to her by oath.

affined.text: sense 2 is only S.) [all affined and kin. 1 related Troil. i. iii. 25 The ivise and fool . . . seem 2 bound Oth. i. i. 39 Whe'r I . . . am ajfirtd To love the Moor.

affirm.text: to maintain (a statement) H5 v. ii. 117, Lr. ii. ii. 83,

affray.text: to frighten away Rom. in. v. 33. [87. affront sb. : gave W o:., made the stand Cym. v. iii. affront vb. (the precise sense in passages under 2 and 3 is doubtful) 1 to meet, accost Ham. in. i. 31 That lie . . . may here Affront Ophelia. 2 to face, encounter Wint. v. i. 75, Cym. iv. iii. 29. 3 to confront ; meet, respond to Troil. in. ii. 173.

affy.text: both senses were in gen. use till 1650) 1 to trust in Tit. i. i. 47 I do affy In thy uprightness. 2 to betroth 2H6 iv. i. 80.

a-front.text: abreast 1H4 n. iv. 226 four came all a.

after.text: unusual applications of common meanings) 1 according to Tp. n. ii. 79 after the ivisest ( = in the wisest fashion). 2 at the rate of Meas. ii. i. 261. after- in comb. : = later, subsequent, future ; after- debts All'sW. iv. iii. 256, -hours R3 iv. iv. 294, -inquiry Cym. v, iv. 187, -loss Sonn. xc. 4, -love Gent. in. i. 95, -meeting Cor. n. ii. 44, -nourishment Per. i. ii. 13, -times 2H4 iv. ii. 51, -wrath Ant. v. ii. 289.

after-dinner.text: time following dinner, afternoon Meas. in. i. 33, Troil. n. iii. 122.

after-eye.text: to look after Cym. i. iii. 16 left To after-eye him. [i. 34.

again.text: sense 2 arose first with vbs. like ' ring ' : cf. Mac. v. iii. 54 the very echo, That should applaud a.) 1 back AYL. m. v. 132 why I answered not again, Shr. ii. i. 217 come again, Good Kate, Cym. iv. iii. 1, Sonn. lxxix. 8 pays it thee again. 2 used to indicate intensity of action Mer.V. in. ii. 204 ivooing here until I sweat again, 2H6 iv. i. 78 shall hiss at thee again.

against.text: see also the aphetic form 'gainst) 1 exposed to Sonn. lxxiii. 3 those boughs which shake against the cold. 2 in expectation of, in time for AYL. iv. i. 158, Troil. i. ii. 189, Rom. iv. ii. 47, Ham. n. ii. 513 as we often see, a. some storm, A silence in the heavens. 3 as conj.: in expectation of the time when, by the time that MND. in. ii 99 against she do appear, Shr. iv. iv. 104.

agate.text: used fig. in allusion to the small figures cut in agates for seals Ado in. i. 65, 2H4 1. ii. 18 I was never manned with an agate till now ; so agate- Stone Rom. i. iv. 56.

babeofclouts.text: rag doll John in. iv. 58. ^J ' Babe that children play with,' Palsgr.

babyofagirl.text: infant of a very young mother Mac. in. iv. 106*.

bacchanal.text: from Bacchus, the name of the Greek and Roman god of wine) [i. 48. 1 priest, priestess, or devotee of Bacchus MND. v. 2 dance in honour of Bacchus Ant. n. vii. 111. back sb. (1 said orig. of a sword which is all steel from edge to back and not merely edged with steel ; 3 was common 1560-1660) 1 metal . . . steel to the very back, sound all through Tit. iv. iii. 47. 2 rear of an armed force 2H4 i. iii. 79. 3 support, backing Ham. iv. vii. 153 this project Should have a back or second. back vb. (S. is earliest authority for both uses) 1 to mount 1H4 n. iii. 76, Cym. v. v. 428, Ven. 419. 2 is ivith a vineyard backd, has a vineyard at the back of it Meas. iv. i. 31. [i. 73.

backare.text: old edd. bac(c)are) : stand back ! Shr. n.

back-friend.text: pretended or false friend Err. iv. ii. 37 (with punning allusion to the sergeant approaching from behind or clapping the man on the back), ■jj In the Warwickshire dialect ' back- friend ' is a name for the troublesome agnail.

backsword-man.text: fencer at single-stick 2H4 in. ii. 71. [i. iii. 133.

back-trick.text: (?) some figure in the galliard Tw.N.

backward.text: what lies behind, the past Tp. i. ii. 50.

backwardly.text: perversely Tim. in. iii. 18 And does he think so backwardly of me now ?

back-wounding-.text: injuring treacherously from behind Meas. in. ii. 201 back-ivounding calumny.

badge.text: device, emblem, or mark on a piece of cloth or of silver used to identify a knight or distin- guish his followers 1H6 iv. i. 177 he ivears the badge of Somerset, Lucr. 1054 ; (hence) token, symbol Mer.V. i. iii. Ill, 2H4 iv. iii. 114 the badge of pusillanimity, Sonn. xliv. 14 ; so badged (fig.) Mac. ii. iii. 109 badg'd with blood (applied to Duncan's ' grooms ').

baffle.text: to subject (a perjured knight) to public in- BAO- BAB famy by exhibiting the picture of him hanging by the heels 1H4 i. ii. 113; (hence) to disgrace, treat with contumely Tw.N. II. v. 177, R2 i. i. 170 disgraced, impeach' d, and baffled, 2H4 v. iii. 106 And shall good news be baffled? bag" and baggage : (to retreat) with all belongings saved, without surrender of anything, and there- fore honourably AYL. in. ii. 171, Whit. I. ii. 206. bail sb. (2 not recorded before S.) 1 security given for the release of a prisoner Meas. in. ii. 44, All's W. v. iii. 290 Til put in bail. 2 person or persons who secure the release of a prisoner by becoming surety for his appearance in court All'sW. v. iii. 300, 2H6 v. i. Ill Sirrah, call in my sons to be my bail. bailvb.1 : to procure the liberation of (a person) from arrest or prison by becoming bail for him Tit. ii. iii. 299 ; fig. Lucr. 1725. bail vb.2: to confine, guard Sonn. cxxxiii. 10*.

bailiff.text: only once in S.) : officer of justice under a sheriff, who executes writs, distrains, and arrests Wint. iv. ii. [iii.] 103.

bait.text: 1 cf. baiting-place 2H6 v. i. 150 ; 3 first in S.) 1 to set on dogs to bite and worry (an animal, e.g. a bear, bull) 2H6 v. i. 148 ; (hence) to harass, worry Tw.N. in. i. 132, R2 iv. i. 238 my wretched- ness doth bait myself, Mac. v. vii. 58 [viii. 29J baited with the rabble's curse. 2 intr. bait at, harass R3 i. iii. 109 (Qq) so taunted, scorn d, and baited at (Ff so baited, scorn'd and storm'd at). 3 to entice with bait (lit. and fig.) Err. n. i. 94 Do their gay vestments his affections bait?, Mer.V. in. i. 57 To bait fish withal. baiting* of bombards : drinking deep H8 v. iv. 87.

baked-meats.text: meat pies Rom. iv. iv. 5, Ham. i. ii. 180 the funeral bak'd meats. ■J] Bake meate = [Fr.] ' viande en paste ', Palsgr.

baker.text: Ham. iv. v. 43 the owl was a baker's daugh- ter ; the allusion is to a local legend to the effect that our Lord, being churlishly refused bread by a baker's daughter, turned her into an owl.

balance.text: 1 cf. ' a pair of ballance ', Fuller 1655 ; 2 and 3 are not pre-S.) 1 used as pi. Mer.V. iv. i. 255 Are there b. here? 2 scale-pan of a balance (fig.) R2 in. iv. 87. 3 fig. counterpoise, something of equal value All'sW. n. iii. 183 to thy estate A b. more replete. balance vb.: to give due weight to 2H6 v. i. 9.

bald.text: 1 nonce-use peculiar to S.) 1 bare-headed Cor. iv. v. 206 stand bald before him. 2 meagre, trivial, paltry Err. n. ii. 112, 1H4 i. iii. 65 This bald un jointed chat of his. [i. 169.

bale.text: injury; “have bale,” get the worst of it Cor. I. i. 169 .

balk.text: 2 cf. ' in stryfful termes ... to balke,1 Spenser) 1 to let slip, fail to use, &c. Tw.N. in. ii. 27, Lucr. 696 altogether balk The prey. 2 balk logic, to chop logic, bandy words Slir. i. i. 34. balked* : (?) heaped up 1H4 i. i. 69 Balled in their own blood.

ball.text: also = ' round mass ', ■ eye-ball ', ' the globe ') 1 the golden orb borne together with the sceptre as an emblem of sovereignty H5 iv. i. 280. 2 = hand-ball or tennis-ball, esp. in fig. phrases All'sW. ii. iii. 314, H5 I. ii. 261 When we have match' d our rackets to these balls. 3 = cannon-ball H5 v. ii. 17. ballad sb. (2 used contemptuously in H5 v. ii. 166) 1 light, simple song MND. iv. i. 222 to write a ballad of this dream, AYL. II. vii. 148. 2 popular song, esp. one celebrating or scurrilously attacking some person or thing Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 186, 2H4 iv. iii. 52. ballad vb.: to make (a person) the subject of a popular song Ant. v. ii. 215 scald rimers Ballad us out o' tune.

ballad-monger.text: contemptuous term for ' ballad- maker' 1H4 in. i. 129. ballast pa. pple.: freighted, loaded Err. in. ii. 142. ballasting*: freight, weight (fig.) Cym. in. vi. 77.

ballow.text: north-midland word for ' cudgel ' Lr. iv. vi. 248 (Qq battero, bat).

balm.text: only thrice in S.) 1 to anoint with fragrant oil or liquid Shr. Ind. i. 48, Per. in. ii. 65. 2 to soothe, heal Lr. in. vi. 107 This rest might yet have balmed thy broken sinews.

balmy.text: only thrice in S.; 2 first in S.) 1 deliciously fragrant Oth. v. ii. 16 balmy breath. 2 deliciously soothing Oth. n. iii. 260 balmy slum- bers, Sonn. cvii. 9 this most b. time. [v. 112. balsam, balsamnm = balm Err. iv. i. 90, Tim. in.

banburycheese.text: kind of cheese which, when pared, was very thin Wiv. i. i. 133.

band.text: the loll, were all common uses in S.'s time) 1 pi. fetters, bonds Tp. Epil. 9, 3H6 i. i. 186. 2 obligation, bond, tie Ado in. i. 114 To bind our loves up in a holy band, All'sW. iv. ii. 56 in the band of truth, Ham. in. ii. 172. 3 agreement, promise Err. iv. ii. 49, R2 i. i. 2 according to thy oath and band* 4 deed by which a person binds himself 1H4 in. ii. 157 the end of life cancels all bands.

banditto.text: old edd. -etto) : outlaw, brigand 2H6 iv. i. 135 (either attrib. sb. or Italian pa. pple.)

bandy.text: (of obscure origin; 2 first in S.) 1. to strike or throw (a ball) to and fro as in the games of tennis and bandy; mostly fig. to give and take (blows, words) LLL. V. ii. 29 , Shr. V. ii. 173 , 3H6 I. iv. 49 “I will not bandy with thee word for word,” Rom. II. v. 14 , Lr. I. iv. 92 “Do you bandy looks with me?,” II. iv. 178 “To bandy hasty words.”

andtake.text: blows, words) LLL. v. ii. 29, Shr. v. ii. 173, 3H6 i. iv. 49 / will not bandy with thee word for word, Rom. n. v. 14, Lr. i. iv. 92 Do you bandy looks with me ?, n. iv. 178 To bandy hasty words. 2 to contend, strive, fight AYL. v. i. 62, 1H6 iv. i. 190, Tit. i. i. 312, Rom. in. i. 94 the prince ex- pressly hath Forbidden bandying in Verona streets. bane sb. (1 the orig. sense ; 2 cf. ' ratsbane ' ; 3 obs.) 1 cause of the death of another 2H6 v. i. 120, Tit. v. iii. 73 Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself. 2 poison Meas. i. ii. 138. 3 murder, destruction Mac. v. iii. 59 afraid of death and bane, Ven. 372. bane vb.: to poison Mer.V. iv. i. 46.

banished.text: banished man, outlaw, bandit Gent. v. iv. 152 ; b. years, years of banishment R2 1. iii. 210. bank sb. (1 not later than S.; 2 not earlier than S.) 1 sea-shore 1H4 in. i. 45, Troil. i. iii. 328 as barren as banks of Libya, Sonn. lvi. 11. 2 shelving elevation in the sea or bed of a river Mac. I. vii. 6* upon this bank and shoalf of time. bank vb.: to coast, skirt (S.) John v. ii. 104*.

banner.text: little fringed flag on a trumpet (S.) H5 iv. ii. 61.

banquet.text: in ordinary sense freq.; 1 and 2 are obs.) 1 running banquet, slight repast between meals ; fig. H8i. iv. 12, v. iv. 71 ( = whipping). 2 course or repast of sweetmeats, fruit, and wine, dessert Shr. v. ii. 9 My banquet is to close our stomachs up, Rom. i. v. 126, Tim. I. ii. 162. bar sb. (3 properly, the barrier marking off the precinct of the judge's seat, at which prisoners stand) 1 plea or objection of force sufficient to arrest entirely an action or claim at law Wiv. in. iv. 7, Shr. i. i. 138 this bar in law, H5 i. ii. 35, 42. 2 obstruction, obstacle, barrier Ado n. ii. 4, Mer.V. n. vii. 45, in. ii. 119, Caes. i. iii. 96. 1 3 tribunal, court H5 v. ii. 27, R3 v. iii. 200. BARB ARY -

barbary.text: country on the north coast of Africa) 1 short for ' Barbary horse ' R2 v. v. 78. 2 Barbary hen, Guinea hen 2H4 n. iv. 107.

barbed.text: having the breast and flanks armed R2 in. iii. 117, R3 i. i. 10.

barber-monger.text: constant frequenter of the barber's shop, fop Lr. n. ii. 36. bare sb.: naked surface Compl. 95. bare adj.: napless, threadbare Gent. n. iv. 47 ; fig. All'sW. iv. v. 105, H8 v. iii. 125. bare vb.: to shave (S.) Meas. iv. ii. 188, All'sW. iv. i. 54 the baring of my beard.

bare-bone.text: lean skinny person 1H4 n. iv. 363 ; so bare-boned Lucr. 1761. [119.

barely.text: in a state of nakedness All'sW. iv. ii. 19.

barful.text: hindering Tw.N. i. iv. 41 a barf id strife.

bargain.text: to sell (a person) a bar yam, to make a fool of him, to 'sell' him LLL. in. i.107. (Cf. boot sb?.)

barkabout.text: to cover as with bark Ham. i. v. 71 a. . . tetter barked (Ff baked) about ...All my smooth body.

barley-broth.text: ale H5 in. v. 19 sodden water . . . their barley-broth.

barn.text: to store as in a barn Lucr. 859. barn(e = child, bairn Ado in. iv. 48 (with pun), All'sW. i. iii. 28.

barnacle.text: species of goose formerly supposed to be hatched from the fruit of a tree or from sea- shells growing on it Tp. iv. i. 251.

baron.text: 2 first created under Richard III ; 3 is obs.) 1 noble, peer (orig. one who held from the king) 1H4 iv. iii. 66 the lords and barons of the realm. 2 one of the lowest rank of nobility 2H6 i. i. 8, Ven. Ded. Baron of Tichfield. 3 pi. the freemen of the Cinque Ports H8 iv. i. 48.

bartholomewtide.text: the feast of St. Bartholomew, 24th August, H5 v. ii. 335 ; Bartholomew boar-pig, one sold at Bartholomew fair in West Sniithfield 2H4 ii. iv. 249.

basan.text: Ant. iii. xi. [xiii.] 127 ; cf. Psalms xxii. 12 ('bulls of Basan '). base sb.1: reason Tw.N. v. i. 79 on base and ground enough. base 8b.2: boys' game, in which a player who leaves his ' base or ' home ' is chased by another, and, if caught, made prisoner Cym. v. iii. 20 to ran The country base ; phrase bid a or the base, to challenge as to a race Gent. i. ii. 94, Ven. 303.

base.text: 2 a 16th cent, use, e.g. ' colored high or base ') 1 low, low-lying R2 n. iv. 20 the b. earth, Lucr. 664. 2 (?) dark-coloured (with pun on fig. senses) Tit. iv. ii. 72 is black so base a hue ? base-court [Fr. 'basse-cour']: lower or outer court of a mansion R2 m. iii. 176.

bases.text: pleated skirt of cloth, velvet, or rich bro- cade, appended to the doublet and reaching from the waist to the knee Per. ii. i. 173. base string* : string of the lowest pitch in a musical instrument 1H4 ir. iv. 6 the very b. of humility.

base-viol.text: form of violoncello Err. iv. iii. 22. Basilisco-like John i. i. 244 : see Kyds ' Soliman and Perseda ' i. iii. 169 [310] Bas.— I, the aforesaid Basil isco— Knight, good fellow, Knight, Knight.

basilisk.text: 2 cf. 'serpentine ', ' culverin ') 1 fabulous reptile, also called cockatrice, supposed to be hatched by a serpent from a cock's egg and said to kill by its breath and look Wint. i. ii. 388. 2 Urge cannon, generally made of brass 1H4 n. iii. 58, H5 v. ii. 17 (with pun on sense 1).

basimecu.text: contemptuous term for a Frenchman 2H6 iv. vii. 31 Mounsieur Basimecu, the dauphin of France. ^] Still applied to Italian organ- 13 -BAVIN grinders, with the pronunciation ' bozzimacu ', in some parts of Warwickshire.

basis.text: S. is earliest for fig. sense of ' foundation ') 1 base, foot Tp. n. i. 127 o'er his wave-worn basis. 2 pedestal Ca?s. in. i. 115 on Pompey's b. lies along. bastard sb.: sweet Spanish wine, resembling mu's- cadelMeas. in. ii. 4 bro wn and white b., 1H4 n. iv. 30. bastard adj. : counterfeit, spurious Mer.V. in. v. 8 a kind of bastard hope, Sonn. lxviii. 3.

baste.text: to sew loosely Ado i. i. 297 [289].

bastinado.text: beating with a stick; AYL. V. i. 61 ; fig. John II. i. 463 “He gives the bastinado with his tongue: Our ears are cudgell'”

tongue.text: to speak, utter Cym. V. iv. 147 “such stuff as madmen ” ; to speak against, scold, abuse Meas. IV. iv. 28 “How might she tongue me.”

bat.text: stick, club Cor. i. i. 167, Lr. iv. vi. 248 (Qq). batch. : quantity of bread produced at one baking ; fig. Troil. v. i. 5 Thou crusty batch of nature. bate sb. : strife 2H4 n. iv. 271 • b. -breeding Ven. 655. bate vb.1: to beat the wings impatiently and flutter away from the fist or perch Shr. iv. i. 199 these kites That bate and beat, 1H4 iv. i. 99 (old edd. baited, bayted, Malone bated) ; fig. H5 in. vii. 127 (with pun on bate vb.2 3), Rom. in. ii. 14 Hood my unmanned blood, bating in my cheeks. bate vb.2 (for the meanings cf. the older abate) 1 to blunt LLL. i. i. 6 bate his scythe's keen edge. 2 to reduce, diminish, weaken Mer.V. in. iii. 32, iv. i. 72, Tim. in. iii. 26 ; bated Ireath : subdued or restrained breathing Mer.V. i. iii. 125. 3 to decrease, fall off 1H4 in. iii. 2 do I not bate ? do I not dwindle ? 4 to deduct Tp. i. ii. 250 To bate me a full year, 2H4 Epil. 16, Ham. v. ii. 23 no leisure bated ; absol. Cym. in. ii. 55 0 let me bate.

bateless.text: not to be blunted, keen Lucr. 9. bat-fowling* : catching of birds on dark nights by dazing them with lights and beatingthem down with poles Tp. ii. i. 193 [185].

batlet.text: so Ff 23i ; Fi batler) : bat or club for beating clothes in theprocess of washing AYL. n. iv. 48. % Current recently in Yorks. and Warwick.

battalion.text: so Ff ; Qq battalia) : R3 v. iii. 11, Ham. iv. v. 79 not in single spies, but in battalions. [67.

batten.text: to grow fat o*n Cor. iv. v. 35, Ham. in. iv.

battery.text: 2 not a common sense in or outside S.) 1 beating, assailing with blows, also fig. John n. i. 446, Cym. i. iv. 23 ; in law, unlawful attack on another by beating or wounding Tw.N. iv. i. 38 an action of battery, Ham. v. i. 110. 2 wound, bruise 3H6 in. i. 37, Ven. 426 where a heart is hard, they make no battery.

battle.text: all the foil, are now obs. or archaic) 1 single combat R2 l. i. 921 . . .ivillin battle prove. . . 2 body or line of troops in battle array 1H4 iv. i. 129 ; fig. Ven. 619 battle. . . of bristly pikes (on a boar's back). 3 main body of an armed force R3 v. iii. 300 the main battle, Mac. v. vi. 4 Lead our first battle.

battlement.text: used loosely for 'embattled roof John n. i. 374.

batty.text: bat-like MND. in. ii. 365 leaden legs and batty wings.

bauble.text: orig. ' babel ' ; the spelling 'bauble 'appears first in English in S. Fi ; 1 is the orig. sense ; 2 cf. ' bable for a foole,' Palsgr. ; 3 and 4 are obs.) 1 showy trinket of little worth Shr. iv. iii. 82. 2 stick carried by a court fool All'sW. iv. v. 32, Tit. v. i. 79. 3 foolish, childish person, trifler Oth. iv. i. 137 thither comes this bauble. 4 mere toy Cym. in. i. 27 his shipping — Poor ignorant baubles! 5 attrib. bauble boat, toy boat Troil. i. iii. 35.

bavin.text: brushwood, fagpots ; b. wits 1H4 in. ii. 61 (' soon ablaze '). ^J Still current in the midlands. BAWBLING 14 BED WORK. bawbling* : trifling Tw.N. v. i. 58 A bawbling vessel. ^j Only S. and echoed by mod. writers, bawcock [Fr. ' beau coq 'J : fine fellow H5 m. ii. 27.

bawd.text: north-midland word) : hare Rom. u. iv. 139. bay sb.1: division of a house included under one gable or between party-walls Meas. ir. i. 261. baysb.2(orig. 'abay' = OFr. 'abai',mod. Fr. 'aboi') 1 deep prolonged barking Tit. n. ii. 3 Uncouple here and let us make a bay. 2 in phrases relating to che position of a hunted animal when it turns and faces the hounds, also fig. R2 ii. iii. 128 To rouse his ivrongs and chase them to the bay, Ven. 877 the hounds are at a bay, Tit. iv. ii. 42, Pilgr. xi. 13 [155]. bay vb. (1 in mod. use an echo of S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1 to bark at Cses iv. iii. 27 bay the moon. 2 to pursue with barking, drive to bay MND. rv. i. 119 they bay d the bear With hounds of Sparta, 2 H4 i. iii. 80 Baying him at the heels. 3 to hold at bay (fig.) Cses. rv. i. 49 bay'd about with many enemies.

bead.text: 1 not known earlier than S.) 1 pi. drops (of liquid), tears John ii. i. 171, 1H4 n. iii. 63 beads of sweat (most old edd. beds), Cses. in. i. 284 beads of sorrow. 2 applied to a very small thing, e. g. a fairy Wiv. v. v. 55 (Ff, &c. Bede), MND. in. ii. 330. 3 set of beads, rosary R2 in. iii. 147.

beaded.text: in the form of beads Compl. 37 Of amber, crystal, and of beaded jet (Q bedded).

beadle.text: inferior parish officer who might punish petty offences 2H6 n. i. 135, &c, H8 v. iv. 72 ; fig. with reference to his punitive functions LLL. in. i. 185 [177J, H5 iv. i. 180 war is his b.

beadsman.text: man paid or endowed to pray for others, pensioner or almsman Gent. i. i. 18, R2 in. ii. 116.

beagle.text: small variety of hound, tracking by scent; fig. used contemptuously of a woman Tim. iv. iii. 176% but also approvingly(?) Tw.N. n. iii. 198*.

beak.text: pointed and ornamented projection at the prow of ancient vessels Tp. i. ii. 196.

beam.text: 1 cf. 'the staff of [Goliath's] spear was like a weaver's beam ', 1 Samuel xvii. 7) 1 wooden roller in a loom, on which the warp is wound Wiv. v. i. 24 ; lance Troil. v. v. 9. 2 with ref. to Matthew vii. 3 : LLL. iv. iii. 162 Me king your mote did see ; But la beam do find. bear sb. : the constellation Ursa major Oth. n. i. 14. bear vb. (besides the mod. senses we find the foil.) 1 to have as a member or part of itself Wint. i. ii. 309, 3H6 v. i. 69 the dearest blood your bodies beart Rom. i. iii. 29 I do bear a brain. 2 to contain (a meaning or the like) AYL. in. ii. 176 more feet than the verses ivould bear, 1H4 iv. i. 20 His letters bear his mind, Ant. i. ii. 130, Compl. 19 often reading what content it bears. 3 to carry as a consequence Tim. i. i. 132. 4 to sustain (a part), keep going (the burden of a song) Tp. i. ii. 380, Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 299 1 can bear my part, Lucr. 1132, &c. 5 to carry on, conduct, execute Ado n. iii. 240 [229], John in. iv. 149 This act so evilly borne, H5 i. ii. 212, Mac. in. vi. 3 Things have been strangely borne. 6 refl. (freq.) and intr. to behave Meas. i. iii. 47 (Ff beare ; mod. edd. bear me), H8 n. i. 30 ; also occas. passive Troil. n. iii. 252 surly borne ( = of surly behaviour). Dear back, to move or go back Cass. in. ii. 173 Stand back! room! bear back !, Lucr. 1417; bear down, to overwhelm, overthrow Mer.V. iv. i. 214 That malice bears down truth, 2H4 i. i. 11, Tit. ii. i. 30, Cym. n. i. 61 ; bear hard (1) to bear ill will to Cass. I. ii. 318 Casardolh bear me hard, ii. i. 215 ; (2) to take heavily or sadly 1H4i. iii. 270 iv ho bears hard His brother's death, R3 II. i. 57 (hardly) ; bear it, to carry the day 2H4 iv. i. 135 He ne'er had borne it out of Coventry, Troil. n. iii. 231, Oth. i. iii. 23 ; bear off, to keep off Tp. n. ii. 18 neither bush nor shrub to bear off any iveather; bear out, (1) to support, back up John iv. i. 6 / hope your warrant ivill bear out the deed, 2H4 v. i. 53 ; (2) with it, to have the upper hand, carry the day Tw.N. i. v. 22, Oth. n. i. 19, Sonn. cxvi. 12 Love . . . bears it out even to the edge of doom ; bear up, to put the helm up so as to bring the vessel into the direction of the wind, fig. Tp. in. ii. 3.

bearer.text: possessor, owner, holder 2H4 iv. v. 28 0 majesty ! When thou dost pinch thy bearer, H8 n. iii. 15, Troil. in. iii. 104. bear-herd (Ff, &c. bear(e)-heard, bearard, berard, berrord, mod. edd. bear- ward) : one who keeps and exhibits a bear Ado n. i. 43, Shr. Ind. ii. 21, 2H4 i. ii. 194, 2H6 v. i. 149, 210. bearing*: carriage, deportment, behaviour, de- meanour Ado n. i. 168, H5 iv. vii. 186 his blunt bearing, Cor. n. iii. 257. [in. iii. 119.

bearing-cloth.text: child's christening-robe Wint. beastly adv.: in a beastly manner, like a beast Shr. iv. ii. 34, Ant. i. v. 50, Cym. v. iii. 27.

beat.text: 1 intr. use peculiar to S. ; cf. bate vb.1) 1 to flap the wings with force Shr. iv. i. 199. 2 to think or ponder laboriously Tp. v. i. 246, Ham. in. i. 183 Whereon his brains still beating ; said of the thoughts Tp. i. ii. 176 still 'tis beating in my mind, Lr. in. iv. 14. beated* : usually taken to be a term of the south- west country and the Welsh border for slicing sod from the ground for burning Sonn. lxii. 10 Beated and chopp'd with tann'd antiquity.

beaver.text: face-guard of a helmet 2H4 iv. i. 120, H5 iv. ii. 44 through a rusty beaver peeps, Ham. I. ii. 229 ; sometimes, the whole helmet R3 v. iii. 50 is my beaver easier than it ivas ?

become.text: (pa. t. became, pa. pple. become and becomed) 1 to agree with, befit Mer.V. v. i. 57. 2 impers. to be fitting 1H6 v. iii. 169 as it becomes, Tit. i. i. 347 as becomes. 3 to adorn, grace Tp. in. ii. 115, Shr. n. i. 253, Cym. v. v. 407 He ivould have well becom'd this place.

becomed.text: S.) : becoming, befitting Rom. iv. ii. 27.

becoming-.text: grace (S.) Ant. i. iii. 96, Sonn. cl. 5.

bed.text: 1 still to be seen at Rye House, Herts.) 1 bed of Ware, enormous bed 11 ft. square Tw.N. in. ii. 53. 2 grave Tp. n. i. 292 [284], Cym. iv. iv. 52. 3 b. of down, delightful resting-place Oth. i. iii. 232. 4 went unto my beds, (?) arrived at the ' bed-time ' or close of life Tw.N. v. i. 413*. bed, bedded : old forms of bead, beaded.

bedded.text: laid in a smooth layer Ham. in. iv. 120. Bedlam (earlier * Bedlem ', ' Bethlem ', ' Bethle- hem ') 1 the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem in London used as an asylum for the mentally deranged 2H6 v. i. 131 To Bedlam with him ; Tom o' Bedlam, madman Lr. i. ii. 152. 2 lunatic, madman John n. i. 183 Bedlam, have done, Lr. in. vii. 103. 3 as adj. mad H5 v. i. 20 Art thou bedlam ?, 2H6 in. i. 51, v. i. 132 a bedlam and ambitious humour. bed-presser, lazy fellow 1H4 n. iv. 272 ; bed- swerver, one unfaithful to marriage Wint. n. i. 92 ; bed-vow, marriage vow Sonn. clii. 3 ; bed-work, easy work such as could be done in bed Troil. i. iii. 205. brownist.text: adherent of the sect founded in Eliza- beth's reign by Hubert Brown, an English Puri- tan Tw.N. m. ii. 36. [198. bruit sb.: rumour, report 3H6 iv. vii. 64, Tim. v. i. bruit vb. (1 the ordinary sense ; 2, 3 only in S.) 1 to noise abroad, report, rumour 1H6 n. iii. 68 / find thou art no less than fame hath bruited. 2 to herald with noise Mac. v. vii. 22 By this great clatter, one of greatest note Seems bruited. 3 bruit again, to echo Ham. i. ii. 127.

brush.text: forcible rush, hostile encounter Troil. v. iii. 34 the b-es of the war ; fig. Tim. iv. iii. 265 with one winter's b.* ; app. associated with 'bruise' 2H6 v. iii. 3 Aged contusions and all b. of time.

bubble.text: fig. empty, unsubstantial thing AYL. n. vii. 152 Seeking the bubble reputation, All'sW. in. vi. 5 (said of a person).

bubukle.text: mixture of ' bubo ' and ' carbuncle ' H5 in. xi. Ill (Fluellen's speech).

buck.text: quantity of clothes put through the ' buck ' or lye ; hence, quantity washed 2H6 iv. ii. 52 she washes bucks ; so buck-basket, dirty-linen basket Wiv. in. iii. 2, &c; bucking, washing Wiv. in. iii. 140.

bucket.text: come off and on swifter than he that gibbets on the brewer's bucket 2H4 in. ii. 286 : allusion of doubtful meaning.

buckle.text: lit. sense ' fasten with a buckle ' is freq.; also in fig. context Troil. n. ii. 30, Mac. v. ii. 15) 1 buckle in, to limit AYL. in. ii. 141 the stretching of a span Buckles in his sum of age. 2 to join in close combat with 1H6 1. ii. 95 In single combat thou shalt buckle with me, IV. iv. 5, v. iii. 28 ; also with bloivs as obj. 3H6 i. iv. 50 (Qq). 3 to bend under stress or pressure 2H4 i. i. 141 ivhose /ever -weaken' 'd joints . . . buckle under life. buckler sb.: shield; I give thee the bucklers ( = 1 own that you are the better man) Ado v. ii. 17. ^[ Similar phrases were 'to yield, lay down the bucklers ' ; the opposite was expressed by ' to carry away the bucklers '. buckler vb. (thrice in S., not otherwise common) 1 to shield, defend Shr. in. ii. 242 III buckler thee against a million, 2H6 in. ii. 216, 3H6 in. iii. 99 buckler falsehood with a pedigree. 2 to catch or ward off (blows) 3H6 i. iv. 50 (Ff).

bucklersbury.text: street of London off Cheapside, inhabited by herbalists Wiv. in. iii. 79 smell like Bucklersbury in simple-time.

buckram.text: coarse linen stiffened with gum or paste 1H4 n. iv. 217 two rogues in buckram suits ; attrib. prob. fig. = stiff, starched, stuck-up 2H6 iv. vii. 28 (with quibble : see say). buck-washing Wiv. in. iii. 165 : see buck. bud sb.: used for ingrafting under the bark of a different stock Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 95 make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race ; fig. John in. iv. 82 now will canker-sorrow eat my bud [i.e. Arthur]. bud vb.: ficr. to develop Shr. iv. v. 37 budding virgin, H8 i. i. 94 The sudden breach . . . is budded oiit.

budge.text: old ed 1. also bouge, boudge) : spec, to flinch Cor. i. vi. 44, Cses. iv. iii. 44; hence budger (S.) : one who flinches Cor. i. viii. 5 the first budger. BUDGET 25 -BUT

budget.text: pouch, wallet Wint. iv. ii. 20 (Fi Bowyet rhyming with avoiich-it). "buff: stout leather made of ox-hide, used for the attire of soldiers, and (in S.) sergeants and bum- bailiffs Err. iv. ii. 36, 1H4 i. ii. 48 is not a buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance ?

bug.text: hobgoblin, bogey, imaginary object of terror Shr. i. ii. 214 fear boys nut It bugs, Ham. v. ii. 22 such biif/s and goblins ; fig. 3H6 v. ii. 2, Cym. v. iii. 51 The mortal bugs o' the field ; so bugbear in lit. sense Troil. iv. ii. 34.

bugle.text: tube-shaped glass bead, commonly black, used to ornament wearing apparel ; only attrib. Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 224 Bugle-bracelet ; = black AYL. in. v. 47 bugle eyeballs.

building.text: 2 cf. Err. in. ii. 4 Shall love, in building, grow so ruinous?, Sonn. cxix. 11, cxxiv. 5 [my dear love] was builded far from accident) 1 This jewel holds his building ( = keeps its place) Per. II. i. 168 (Malone and Steevens bidingi). 2 edifice (fig.) Troil. iv. ii. 110 the strong base and b. of my love, Cor. n. i. 218 the b-s of my fancy. 3 build (of a ship) Sonn. lxxx. 12 / am a worthless boat, He of tall building.

bulk'.text: 1 in 'use 1460-1720 ; 3 cf. 'the bulke, bellie, or bodie of a ship ', Cotgr.) 1 trunk, body (of a person) R3i. iv. 40 my panting b., Ham. ii. i. 95, Lucr. 467 her heart . . . Beating her b. 2 huge body Troil. iv. iv. 128 the qreat bulk Achilles. 3 hull of a ship Tvv.N. v. i. 59, Troil. i. iii. 37 shallow bauble boats . . . making their way With those of nobler bulk, n. iii. 280 (Q and mod. edd. hulks). bulk 2 : framework projecting from the front of a shop Cor. it. i. 229, Oth. v. i. 1 stand behind this b.

bull.text: the sign Taurus of the zodiac Tit. iv. iii. 70.

bull-bearingmilo.text: a celebrated athlete of Crotona, Italy, said to have carried a four-year-old bullock on his shoulders for forty yards Troil. n. iii. 261.

bull-beef.text: flesh of bulls 1H6 i. ii. 9 their fat bull- beeves. ^1 In 16th-17th cent. ' bull-beef ' was an abusive term for a big blustering fellow.

bully.text: familiar endearing term = fine fellow ; often prefixed to a proper name or a designation = gal- lant Tp. v. i. 258 bully-monster, Wiv. i. iii. 6, &c, ii. iii. 18 bully doctor, MND. iv. ii. 20 0 sweet bully Bottom !, H5 iv. i. 48 the lovely bully ; so bully- rook Wiv. i. iii. 2, &c. (not pre-S.; a common 17th cent, form was 'bully-rock').

bum-baily.text: sheriff's officer Tw.N. m. iv. 197 (some mod. edd. bum-bailiff, but -baily is the regular midland form to this day).

bunch-back'd.text: hump-backed E3 i. iii. 246 this poisonous bunch-back'd toad.

bung.text: pickpocket 2H4 it. iv. 136 you filthy bung.

buoyup.text: not pre-Eliz.) : to rise up Lr. in. vii. 60. burden, burthen (old edd. chiefly burthen ; in several passages there is a play between the sense of ' load ' and sense 2 or 3, e.g. Gent. I. ii. 82, R3 iv. iv. 168) 1 freight, carrying capacity of a ship All'sW. n. iii. 215 a vessel of too great a burden ; freq. Troil. i. iii. 71 matter needless, of importless burden.

ith.text: abstract and concrete) Err. i. i. 55, v. i. 345 bore thee at a burden two fair sons, Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 266, John in. i. 90 Pray that their burdens may not fall this day, Sonn. lix. 4. 3 bass or undersong AYL. hi. ii. 263 I would sing my song without a b.; fig. Shr. I. ii. 68; refrain Tp. i. ii. 380 And, sweet sprites, the b. bear, Wint. iv. iii. [iv.] 195 such . . . b-s of dildos.

burden'd.text: burdensome R3 iv. iv. Ill my b. yoke.

burdenous.text: oppressive R2 it. i. 261 b. taxations.

burden-wise.text: as a burden or undersong Lucr. 1133.

burgher.text: citizen of a borough Meas. i. ii. 108.

burgomaster.text: magistrate corresponding to an alderman 1H4 n. i. 84 b-s and great oneyers.

burgonet.text: light casque or steel cap 2H6 v. i. 200 ; iig. Ant. r. v. 24 The derm-Atlas of this earth, the arm And b. of men (Fi burganet).

burgundy.text: old edd. also Burgonie, -ony, -uny (H5 v. ii. 68, Lr. i. i.250), Burgo{i)gne (H5v. ii. 7).

burial.text: has the orig. sense of ‘burying-place, grave’ (like the older ‘buriels’, Anglo-Saxon ‘byrgels’) in Mer.V. I. i. 29 (fig. of a ship).

grave'.text: like the older ' bunds', Anglo-Saxon ' byrgels ') in Mer.V. i. i. 29 (fig. of a ship).

burn.text: the ordinary physical senses are freq.) 1 burn daylight, burn candles in daytime, (hence) waste time AViv. it. i. 54, Rom. i. iv. 43 ; so Ant. iv. ii. 41 To burn this night with torches. 2 to make (drink) hot Wiv. n. i. 222 burnt sack, Tw.N. ii. iii. 209 Til go burn some sack. 3 intr. and refl. to be on fire, wax hot, glow, con- sume oneself with love, &c. Gent. n. v. 56 b. him- self in love, John iv. ii. 103 b. in indignation, 2H6 v.i. 160, 3H6 1. i. 60, Lr. iv. vi. 41 B. itself out,Ven. 49 He b-s with bashful shame, 50, 810, Compl. 304.

burnish'd.text: made bright as if by friction Ven. 858 burnished gold ; bright like polished metal Mer.V. it. i. 2 the burnish 'd sun.

burr.text: rough seed-vessel or flower-head of a plant, esp. the burdock ; (hence) something that clings like a burr and is difficult to get rid of Meas. iv. iii. 193 I am a kind of burr ; I shall slick, MND. in. ii. 260 Hang off, thou cat, thou burr ! burthen, fee.: see burden.

burton-heath.text: supposed to be Barton-on-the- heath, in Warwickshire, the home of one of S.'s aunts Shr. Ind. ii. 19.

bury.text: often in fig. use (not pre-S.), to consign to oblivion, put out of sight, conceal 3H6 iv. i. 55 in your bride you bury brotherhood, Ca?s. n. i. lb faces buried in their cloaks, iv. iii. 158 In this [bowl of wine] I bury rdl unkindness.

bush.text: bush of ivy hung out as a vintner's sign AYL. Epil. 4 good tvine needs no bush (cf. line 6).

buskin'd.text: first in S.) : shod with buskins or half- boots MND. ii. i. 71 Your buskin'd mistress.

busky.text: bosky, bushy 1H4 v. i. 2 yon husky hill. buss sb. and vb. : kiss John in. iv. 35, 2H4 n. iv. 291 ; fig. Trcil. iv. v. 219 Yond towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds, Cor. in. ii. 75 Thy knee bussing the stones.

busylesst.text: Theobald's emendation of Fi busie lest in Tp. in. i. 15 ; others read with Singer busiest^.

but.text: the foil, uses are now obs. or archaic) 1 after negative sentences containing a comparison : -than MND. i. ii. 84 they would have no more discretion but to hang us, Tw.N. i. iv. 13 Thou know'st no less but all. 2 =only Tp. i. ii. 169 Would I might But ever see that man !, Err. iv. i. 33 he . . . stays but for it, Oth. iv. i. 88 / say, but mark his gesture; used redun- dantly with only, 2H4 i. i'. 192, 3H6 iv. ii. 25, Mac. v. vii. 69 [viii. 40]. 3 but now, just now, only this moment Mer V. in. ii. 170 even now, but mow, Ven. 497 But now I liv'd ; so Tp. iii. ii. 130 but while-ere, Ven. 1026 but late. 4 = anything but, otherwise than Tp. i. ii. U9 I should sin To think but nobly of my grandmother ; so after cannot MND. III. ii. 56 It cannot be but thou hast murder'd him. 5 = if • . . not, unless, except MND. in. ii. 150 Can you not hate me, . . . But you must join in souls to mock me too?, Cym. v. v. 41 And, but she spoke it dying, I would not Believe her lips ; Tp. I. ii. 91 but by being so retird, Ant. iv. x. 10 [xi. 11

butbeingcharged.text: - if we are not charged); Gent. I. i. 86 It shall go hard but Til prove it, BUTCHER 26 -CALL Mer.V. ii. vi. 52 Beshrew me, but Hove her heartily ; similarly but that Tp. I. ii. 4. 6 = who, which, or that . . . not (freq.) 1H6 i. ii. 5 What towns of any moment but we have ?, R3 1. in. 186 No man but prophesied revenge for it. 7 = that . . . not, esp. after verbs of thinking, doubting, &c. Tp. in. i. 44, MND. in. ii. 298 {but that), 1H4 iv. iii. 38, Oth. in. iii. 225. 8 =that, after negatived verb of denying Ado i. iii. 33, All'sW. v. iii. 168.

butcher.text: man of blood, brutal murderer AYL. m. v. 14 tyrants, b-s, murderers, John iv. ii. 259 b. of an innocent child, R3v. iv. 39 [v. 26] b. to the sire.

butcherly.text: murderous 3H6 n. v. 89 how fell, how b.

buttl.text: cask for wine or ale containing two hogs- heads Tp. ii. ii. 130 ; fig. Troil. v. i. 32*. ^ In Tp. t. ii. 146 of doubtful meaning (mod. edd. boatf). butt 2 : mark for archery practice, properly a mound or other erection on which the target is set up H5 i. ii. 186 To which is fixed, as an aim or butt, Obedience, 3H6 i. iv. 29 / am your butt, and I abide your shot ; (hence) goal, object Oth. v. ii. 266 my journey's end . . . my butt. See also butt-shaft. butt3 : butting of a horned animal Shr. v. ii. 41.

butt-end.text: fig. the concluding part, fag-end R3 n. ii. 110 the butt-end of a mother's blessing.

butterfly.text: vain, gaudily attired person (e.g. one who flutters about a court) Lr. v. iii. 13 well . . . laugh At gilded butterflies.

buttery.text: orig. store-room for liquor, later for provisions generally Shr. Ind. i. 102 ; buttery- bar, ledge on the top of the buttery hatch or half- door, to rest tankards on Tw.N. i. iii. 75 bring your hand to the buttery-bar and let it drink.

button.text: 1 the origin of the phrases is doubtful) 1 'tis in his buttons, he has fortune at his command, is sure to succeed Wiv. ni. ii. 74 ; butcher of a silk button, expert fencer Rom. n. iv. 25. 2 knob on the top of a cap Ham. n. ii. 237 On For- tune's cap we are not the very button. 3 bud Ham i. iii. 40 before their buttons be disclosed.

button-hole.text: take (a person) a button-hole lower, humiliate, take down a peg LLL. v. ii. 705.

butt-shaft.text: unbarbed arrow used in shooting at the butts ; applied to Cupid's dart LLL. i. ii. 184, Rom. n. iv. 17 the blind bow-boy's butt-shaft.

buxom.text: twice in S.) : lively, brisk H5 in. vi. 27 of b. valour, Per. i. Grower 23 b., blithe, and full of face.

buy.text: sense 2 (i) is obs.) 1 buy and sell, barter, traffic with, in a bad sense H8 1. i. 192 Does b. and sell his honour ; so bought and sold, betrayed Err. in. i. 72, John v. iv. 10, R3 v. iii. 306 Dickon thy master is bought and sold. 2 buy out, (i) ransom, redeem Err. i. ii. 5 not being able to buy out his life ; (ii) get rid of by a money payment John in. i. 164 the curse that money may buy out, 1H4 iv. ii. 24 bought out their services {= paid money to be released from service in the army), Ham. in. iii. 60 Buys out the law. buzz sb.: baseless rumour Lr. i. iv. 350 Each b., each fancy ; so buzzing* H8 n. i. 148, and buzzer, one who whispers tales in the ear Ham. iv. v. 90 buzzers to infect his ear With pestilent speeches.

buzz.text: exclamation of impatience or contempt when a person tells a well-known piece of news Ham. ii. ii. 421 ; ? also in Shr. n. i. 207 (Ff should be,

should.text: 1 cf. shall 1 ; 3 common Eliz.) 1 used where the mod. idiom requires 'would' Mer.V. I. ii. 98 you s. refuse toperform your father's will, ?/..., "Wint. i. ii. 57 To be your prisoner s. import offending, Troil. i. iii. 116 Force s. be right, Ham. iii. ii. 321 Your wisdoms, show itself more richer to signify this to his doctor. 2 was likely to, (hence) = might (have), could (have) Tp.v. i. 279 where s. they Find this grand liquor ?, 1H6 ii. i. 71 how or whichivay should they first break in ?, Oth. in. iv. 24 Where s.llose that handkerchief?. 3 in narrative or reported speech, serving as the auxiliary of the past tense Gent. n. iii. 27-8, AYL. in. ii. 183 didst thou hear without wondering, how thy name should be hanged and carved upon these trees ?, Shr. in. ii. 162 ivhen the priest Should ask . . .

by'rlady.text: old edd. by'r Lady, birladie, byrlady, ber Lady, berlady) : by our Lady (freq.). cabin sb. (1 in use 1400-1650 ; 2 was common Eliz.) 1 temporary shelter of slight materials Tw.N. i. v. 289 a willow cabin, Pilgr. xiv. 3 [183]. 2 den of a wild beast Ven. 637 let him [i. e. the boar] keep his loathsome cabin ; cave, (hence) applied to the eye-socket Ven. 1038. cabin vb. (1 cf. 2 of prec; 2 echoed by mod. writers) 1 to lodge Tit. iv. ii. 181 And cabin in a cave. 2 to shut up within narrow bounds Mac. in. iv. 24 cabin'd, cribb'd, confin'd.

cabinet.text: 1 common term in military writers of the 16th cent.; 2 cf. cabin sb. 2) 1 tent Lucr. 442 They, mustering to the quiet cabinet [i. e. the heart]. 2 bird's nest Ven. 854 From his [i. e. the lark's] moist cabinet.

cable.text: give him cable, allow him scope Oth. i. ii. 17.

caddis.text: short for ' caddis ribbon ', worsted tape or binding used for garters, &c. Wint. IV. iii. [iv.] 208 ; so caddis-g-arter 1H4 n. iv. 80.

cadent.text: falling Lr. i. iv. 309 cadent tears.

cadmus.text: founder of Thebes MND. iv. i. 118.

caduceus.text: wand, having two serpents twined round it, fabled to have been carried by Hermes (Mercury), the messenger of the gods Troil. n. iii. 13 the serpentine craft of thy caduceus.

caesar.text: absolute ruler, emperor (first in S.) 3H6 in. i. 18 No bending knee will call thee Casar now, R3 iv. iv. 337 sole victress, Caisar's Casar. [ii. 59.

cage.text: prison for petty malefactors, lock-up 2H6 iv.

cain-coloured.text: of the reputed colour of Cain's hair, i.e. 'red' Wiv. i. iv. 23* a C. beard (Ff Q3 Cain(e, Qqi2 kane, some mod. edd. cane-). caitiff = wretch (2 thrice as freq. as 1) 1 expressing pity Oth. iv. i. 109 Alas ! poor caitiff! 2 expressing contempt Meas. n. i. 187 0 thou c! 0 thou varletl ; also attrib. R2 i. ii. 53 A c. recreant.

cake.text: (one's) cake is dough, one's project has failed Shr. i. i. 109, v. i. 146.

calendar.text: (1 not post-S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. guide, directory Ham. V. ii. 115 “he is the card or calendar of gentry” (‘the general preceptor of elegance’, Johnson).

calendarofgentry.text: ' the general preceptor of ele- gance ', Johnson). 2 record All'sW. i. iii. 5 the c. of my past endeavours.

calf.text: term of endearment Wint. i. ii. 128 Art thou my calf? ; stupid fellow, dolt Ham. in. ii. 112.

caliver.text: light kind of musket or harquebus, in- troduced during the 16th cent., which seems to have been the lightest portable fire-arm, except- ing the pistol, and to have been fired without a « rest ' 1H4 iv. ii. 21, 2H4 in. ii. 292, 295. call sb.: decoy-bird John in. iv. 174 they would be as a call To train ten thousand English to their side. call vb. (1 only S. ; 2 a few uses only are given here) 1 ='call upon,' to visit (a person) at his house CALLET Meas. iv. iv. 18 Til call you at your house, Tw.N. in. ii. 58 We'll call thee at the cubiculo. 2 with preps, and advs.: callback, (i) to summon to return Gent. i. ii. 49 ; (ii) to revoke H8 n. iv. 232 to call back her appeal ; (iii) to recall to memory Sonn. iii. 10 she in thee Calls back the lovely April of her prime ; call in, to withdraw from action 2H4 iv. iii. 28 Call in the powers ; call on or upon, (i) to make a claim upon (a person) for payment 1H4 v. i. 130, Tim. n. ii. 22 My master is awak'd by great occasion To call upon his own ; (ii) to impeach, challenge Ant. i. iv. 28* ; or ? = (i). callet, -at, -ot : lewd woman, trull Oth. iv. ii. 121 ; ? = scold Wint. n. iii. 90 A callet Of boundless tongue. calling* (late instance of the sense) : name, appel- lation AYL. i. ii. 250 I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son, . . . and would not change that c. calm sb.: confused with qualm 2H4 n. iv. 39-41. calm vb. (rare outside S.): to becalm (a ship) 2H6 iv. ix. 33 (F4 calm'd, Fi calme, F2 claimd, F3 claim'd) ; Oth. i. i. 30 be-lee'd and calm'd (? for ' becalm'd ').

galydon.text: the prince of Calydon (2H6 i. i. 236) =

meleager.text: son of (Eneus of Calydon and Alth?ea), whom the Fates decreed to die when a certain log on the hearth was burnt.

cambyses.text: 1H4 ii. iv. 430 in King Cambyses' vein, in the ranting style of ' King Cambyses, a lament- able Tragedy, mixed ful of pleasant mirth ' by Thomas Preston, 1569-70.

camel.text: great awkward hulking fellow Troil. I. ii. 269, ir. i. 59 do, rudeness ; do, camel ; do, do.

camelot.text: Lr. II. ii. 89 “Goose . . . I'd drive ye cackling home to Camelot” * ; not yet satisfactorily explained: see the commentators.

camlet.text: a fabric which has varied considerably in material ; in 16th and 17th cent, made of the hair of the Angora goat H8 v. iv. 95 (Fi chamblet). camp vb.: to serve as a lodging for Ant. iv. viii. 33 Had our great palace the capacity To camp this host. can vb.1 (1 instances with apparent pronominal object, as all I can, such as I can, I can no more, are probably to be regarded as due to ellipsis of the infinitive 'do') 1 trans, to know, be skilled in Phoen. 14 the priest in surplice white That defunct/ re music can. 2 intr. to be skilled Ham. iv. vii. 84 they can well on

horseback.text: FT ran). can vb.2 : altered form of ' gan ', past tense of ' gin ' = to begin, used for 'did' LLL. iv. iii. 106 the wind one with claps can sound.

canakin.text: small can or drinking-vessel Oth. it. iii. 72 let me the canakin clink, clink. canary sb. (1 the idea of the dance is said to have been borrowed from the Canary Islands) 1 lively Spanish dance All'sW. n. i. 77. 2 light sweet wine from the Canary Islands Wiv. in. ii. 92, Tw.N. i. iii. 88, 2H4 n. iv. 29. canary vb.: to dance a 'canary' LLL. in. i. 13 canary to it with your feet.

cancel.text: c. off (Ff), strike off, annul Per. i. i. 113 We might proceed to c. off your days (Qq counsel of M alone cancel off, taking c. as sb.; but the sb. io not recorded in this sense till the 19th cent.).

cancer.text: the fourth of the signs of the zodiac, which the sun enters at the summer solstice, June 21 Troil. ii. iii. 208 add more coals to Cancer.

candidatus.text: candidate for office in Rome (proper- ly = one clothed in white) Tit. i. i. 185 Be candi- datus then, and put it on [viz. This palliament of white and spotless hue, line 182].

candied.text: 2 not common outside S.) i crystallized with frost Tim. iv. iii. 227 the cold brookt C. with tee ; (hence) congealed Tp. n. i. 287\ 27 -CAP 2 sugared, honied Ham. in. ii. 65 the candied tongue.

candle.text: 3 cf. candle-holder) 1 applied to the heavenly luminaries Rom. in. v. 9 Night's candles are burnt out, Mac. n. i. 5. 2 applied to the 'light' of life 3H6 n. vi. 1 Here burns my c. out, Mac V. v. 23 Out, out, brief c. ! 3 hold a candle to, assist at Mcr.V. n. vi. 41.

candle-case.text: case to keep candles in Shr. in. ii. 47.

candle-holder.text: one who lights others at their work ; (hence) a mere looker-on Rom. i. iv. 38 I'll be a candle-holder, and look on.

candle-waster.text: one who wastes candles by late study, bookworm Ado v. i. 18. candy t s used as adj. = sugared 1H4 1. iii. 251 candy

canker.text: 1 fig. ? sometimes to be referred to 2) 1 eating, spreading sore or uloer, usu. fig. John v. ii. 14 the inveterate canker of one wound, 2H6 i. ii. 18 the canker of ambitious thoughts, Tim. iv. iii. 49. 2 ' worm ' that destroys buds and leaves, also fig. (freq.) Gent. i. i. 43, MND. n. ii. 3, Rom. n. iii. 30, Ham. i. iii. 39 The canker galls the infants of the spring, v. ii. 69 this canker of our nature, &onn. xxxv. 4 ; hence canker-bit, worm-eaten Lr. v. iii. 124, canker-sorrow John in. iv. 82. 3 dog-rose Ado I. iii. 28 I had rather be a canker in a hedge than a rose in his grace, 1H4 1. iii. 176 ; hence canker-bloom Sonn. liv. 5.

canker-blossom.text: worm that ' cankers ' the blos- som [of love] MND. in. ii. 282.

cankered.text: 2 and 3 very freq. in the 16th cent.) 1 rusted, corroded, tarnished 2H4 iv. v. 70 The canker'd heaps of strange-achieved gold. 2 infected with evil, corrupt Cor. iv. v. 97 I'll fight against my canker'd country. 3 malignant John n. i. 194, 1H4 i. iii. 137, Rom. I. i. 101 your canker'd hale.

canon.text: properly, law or decree of the Church ; the canon = canon law All'sW. i. i. 160 self-love, which is the most inhibited sin in the canon ; (hence) law or rule in general LLL. i. i. 260, Ham. i. ii. 132 fix'd His canon 'gainst self-slaughter.

cano'nize.text: to place in the canon of saints John in. i. 177, 2H6 i. iii. 63 ; fig. to enrol among famous persons Troil. n. ii. 202 And fame in time to come canonize us.

canoniz'd.text: buried according to the Church's rule Ham. i. iv. 47 thy canoniz'd bones, hearsed in death.

canopy.text: S. is earliest for the application of the sb. to 'the firmament ' Cor. iv. v. 41, Ham. rr. ii. 318, and for the use of canopy vb. Sonn. xii. 6, and canopied Cym. n. ii. 21, Lucr. 398.

canstick.text: candlestick 1H4 in. i. 130 a brazen c. cantherizing* : see cauterizing.

cantle.text: part, lit. corner-piece 1H4 in. i. 101 (Qq scantle) ; segment of a sphere Ant. in. viii. 16 [x. 6] The greater cantle of the world.

canton.text: song Tw.N. I. v. 291 Write loyal cantons.

Venelia, Venetia, Chi non ti vede non ti pretia [It.] : Venice, Venice, who sees thee not esteems thee not LLL. iv. ii. 100, 101. veni, vidi, vici [L.] : I came, I saw, I conquered LLL. iv. i. 68. ver [L.] : spring LLL. v. ii. 901. verbatim [L.] : word for word 1H6 m. i. 13. via [It.] : on, go on, say on Wiv. n. ii. 161, LLL. v. i. 160, v. ii. 112, Mer.V. n. ii. 11, H5 iv. ii. 4, 3H6 ii. i. 182. videlicet [L.] : namely Wiv. i.iMZifidelicet), LLL. iv. i. 70, MND. v. i. 331, AYL. iv. i. 100, Ham. ii. i. 61. Videsne quis venit ?— Video et g-audeo [L.] : Do you see who comes ?— I see and am glad LLL. v. i. 33, 34. Vilia miretur vulgus ; mihi fiavus Apollo Focula Castalia plena ministret aqua [L. ; Ovid, Amores i. xv. 35] : Let the base vulgar ad- mire trash ; to me golden-haired Apollo shall serve goblets filled from the Castalian spring; motto of Venus and Adonis. Vir sapit qui pauca loquitur [L.] : The man is wise who says little LLL. iv. ii. 82. viva voce [L.] : so that their voices can be heard H8 ii. i. 18. vocativo [L.] : in the vocative case Wiv. iv. i. 55. vocatur [L.] : is called LLL. v. i. 25. vox [L.] : lit. voice ; appropriate, i.e. loud, frantic, tone Tw.N. v. i. 307. printed in great Britain at the university press, oxford by john johnson, printer to the university I Onions* C. A Shakespeare Glossary I 7E 5 -M'S PARK Toronto 5, Canada 2892

bedlam.text: (earlier ‘Bedlem’, ‘Bethlem’, ‘Bethlehem’) 1. the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem in London used as an asylum for the mentally deranged 2H6 V. I. 131 “To Bedlam with him; Tom o' Bedlam,” madman Lr. I. ii. 152 .

bergomask.text: dance after the manner of the people of Bergamo (a province in the state of Venice), who were noted for the rusticity of their manners and speech MND. V. i. 361 , 370

bermoothes.text: Bermudas Tp. I. ii. 229 “the stillvex'd Bermoothes.”

bevis.text: of Hampton (i.e. Earl of Southampton), the hero of a mediaeval romance, of whom incredible stories were told H8 I. i. 38 .

calydon.text: “the prince of Calydon” ( 2H6 I. i. 236 ) = Meleager (son of Œneus of Calydon and Althæa), whom the Fates decreed to die when a certain log on the hearth was burnt.

capet.text: = Hugh Capet, the first French king of the Capetian dynasty (A.D. 987-996) H5 I. ii. 78 .

greek.text: “merry ,” Troil. I. ii. 116 , IV. iv. 56 ; a common phr. in 16-17th cent. for ‘merry fellow, roysterer, boon companion’; so “foolish Greek” addressed to the clown in Tw.N. IV. i. 19 .

grizel.text: later form of the proper name ‘Grisilde’ borne by the heroine of Chaucer's Clerk's Tale (adapted from a story of Petrarch's), who is the proverbial type of a meek, patient wife Shr. II. i. 289 [ 297 ].

h.text: Ado III. iv. 55 , quibble on ACHE sb. (q.v.).

harry.text: ten-shilling pieces coined in the reign of Henry VIII, 2H4 III. ii. 239 .

i.text: used, as freq. in the late 16th c. and in the 17th c., for ‘me’ Mer.V. III. ii. 320 “all debts are cleared between you and I,” AYL. I. ii. 19 “my father hath no child but I,” Sonn. lxxii. 7 “And hang more praise upon deceased ”

ides.text: fifteenth day of March according to the reckoning of the ancient Roman calendar Cæs. I. ii. 18 , &c.

jug.text: pet-form of, or familiar substitute for, the feminine name Joan, applied to a homely woman, a maidservant, or a mistress Lr. I. iv. 247 “Whoop, Jug! I love thee.”

lucina.text: goddess of childbirth Cym. V. iv. 43 , Per. I. i. 8 .

martlemas.text: old form of ‘Martinmas’; in 2H4 II. ii. 112 “how doth the , your master?” used derisively of Falstaff; perhaps short for ‘Martlemas beef’=meat of an ox slaughtered and salted at Martinmas; cf. 1H4 III. iii. 198 “O! my sweet beef.”

o.text: sb. (plural written “Oes,” in mod. edd. “O's”) 1. cipher, mere nothing Lr. I. iv. 214 “thou art an O without a figure.”

phebe.text: to treat cruelly, like Phebe AYL. IV. iii. 40 .

philippan.text: “sword ,” the sword that triumphed over Brutus and Cassius at Philippi, Ant. II. v. 23 ; taken by some as a noun, the proper name of the sword.

polack.text: Pole, Ham. II. ii. 63 , &c.;—adj. Polish V. ii. 390 . ∥ In Ham. I. i. 63 mod. edd. “Polacks”†, Qq Ff1 2 “pollax, Pollax,” F3 “Polax,” F4 “Pole-axe.”

sagittary.text: (2 cf. “Centaur” as the sign of an inn at Ephesus in Err. I. ii. 9 ) 1. the centaur who, according to mediaeval romance, fought in the Trojan army against the Greeks, Troil, V. v. 14 ,

salique.text: “ law,” the alleged fundamental law of the French monarchy, by which females were excluded from the succession to the crown H5 I. ii. 91 ; “ land,” = Latin ‘terra Salica’ (a term of which the meaning is disputed), alleged to mean France, H5 I. ii. 40 “Which Salique land the French unjustly gloze To be the realm of France” (cf. Hall's Chronicle, ‘They say that Pharamond made the law for the land Salicque, which the glose calleth Fraunce’).

a.text: for ‘ha’ = he, in mod. edd. usually “a',” or replaced by “he” Ham. II. i. 58 “There was a' gaming.”

abhorring.text: (rare; ‘abhorrence’ is post-S.) 1. abhorrence, loathing Cor. I. i. 174 “flatter Beneath ”

able.text: adj. (1 occurs six times, 2 once) 1. strong, vigorous, active All'sW. IV. v, 87 , 2H4 I. i. 43 , Ham. V. ii. 211 .

abode.text: sb. (1 and 2 now obs.; 3 now chiefly in echoes of the Bible; cf. ‘We will . . . make our abode with him’ John xiv. 23 ) 1. waiting, delay Mer.V. II. vi. 21 “my long abode.”

abridge.text: to deprive of, debar from Mer.V. I. i. 127 “to be abridg'd From such a noble rate.”

abuse.text: sb. (1 and 2 were common Eliz., now obs.) 1. ill-usage, injury, wrong, insult, offence, crime Wiv. V. iii. 9 , Meas. V. i. 241 , 3H6 III. iii. 188 “the abuse done to my niece,” Rom. III. i. 199 , Sonn. cxxxiv. 12 “through my unkind abuse.”

accord.text: (‘at a.’ is Chaucerian; 2 not post-S.) 1. harmony, concord Shr. III. i. 74 , H5 V. ii. 381 ; AYL. I. i. 69 “at accord” (=in agreement).

ache.text: pronounced ‘aitch’ like the letter H (cf. Ado III. iv. 55 ); hence pl. “aches” is of two syllables ( Tp. I. ii. 370 ).

acquittance.text: sb. (rare; a doubtful instance occurs in Oth. IV. ii. 193 ; Q1 only, the rest “acquaintance”) 1. writing in evidence of a discharge LLL. II. i. 160 “acquittances For such a sum,” Cym. V. iv. 174 .

act.text: sb. (S. has several ordinary uses; earliest known example of ‘act’ of a play H8 Epil. 3 ). 1. performance, action, operation, execution Mer.V. I. iii. 84 , All'sW. I. ii. 30 , John III. i. 274 , H8 III. ii. 183 “the honour of it Does pay the act of it.”

adoptious.text: christenings of adopted children All'sW. I. i. 190 * .

advantageous.text: anxiety to obtain a position of advantage Troil. V. iv. 23 .

adventure.text: hazard, chance Wint. V. i. 156 , John V. v. 22 ; “at all adventures,” at all hazards, whatever may be the consequences Err. II. ii. 220 , H5 IV. i. 123 .

affect.text: vb. 1 (2 by far the commonest sense; 4 only once) 1. to aim at, aspire to Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 433, 2H6 IV. vii. 103 , Cor. III. iii. 1 “affects Tyrannical power,” IV. vi. 32 .

affecting.text: using affectation, affected Wiv. II. i. 145 .

affection.text: sb. (the usual S. sense is the ordinary one of ‘love’; 4 is rare) 1. emotion, feeling, esp. pl. LLL. I. i. 9 , Mer.V. I. i. 16 , Cæs. II. i. 20 “when his affections sway'd More than his reason.”

affront.text: vb. (the precise sense in passages under 2 and 3 is doubtful) 1. to meet, accost Ham. III. i. 31 “That he . . . may here Affront Ophelia.”

aim.text: sb. (3 meaning doubtful; some interpret ‘let me have space or scope’） 1. mark, butt Meas. I. iii. 5 , R3 IV. iv. 90 “To be the aim of every dangerous shot,” H8 V. iii. 118 ; “gave aim to,” was the object of Gent. V. iv. 101 “her that gave aim to all thy oaths.”

air.text: sb. (senses 2, 3, and 4 become common after S., as also the sense of ‘tune’ MND. I. i. 183 ) 1. breath Wint. V. iii. 78 “There is an air comes from her,” 2H6 III. ii. 371 * “catch the air.”

alarum.text: to call to arms (fig.), rouse to action Mac. II. i. 53 , Lr. II. i. 55 .

allay.text: means of abatement Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 9 “to whose feeling sorrows I might be some allay”; so allayment Troil. IV. iv. 8 , Cym. I. v. 22 .

allaying.text: diluting Cor. II. i. 53 “not a drop of allaying Tiber.”

amaze.text: to bewilder, perplex John IV. iii. 140 “I am amaz'd . . . and lose my way,” Ven. 684 .

among.text: “ever among,” all the while 2H4 V. iii. 22 “And ever among so merrily.”

an.text: 1 (in old edd. often “and,” of which it is only a clipped form) 1. if (freq.); even if, though ( Mer.V. I. ii. 95 ); also “an if” Tp. II. ii. 125 , Mer.V. IV. i. 446 ; “what an if,” though Tit. IV. iv. 9 .

anchor.text: vb. (literal phrases are used in 2H6 IV. i. 9 , Lr. IV. vi. 19 ) 1. to fix firmly R3 IV. iv. 232 , Ant. I. v. 33 “There would he anchor his aspect.”

angle.text: to fish with a rod; fig. to use artful means to catch a person All'sW. V. iii. 214 “She . . . did angle for me,” Ant. II. v. 16 .

annothanize.text: to explain, interpret LLL. IV. i. 70 .

answer.text: sb. (the foll. uses are somewhat technical) 1. reply made to a charge, defence, account 2H6 II. i. 201 “call these foul offenders to their answers,” Cor. III. i. 176 , Cæs. I. iii. 114 .

antic.text: to make like buffoons Ant. II. vii. 132 .

antre.text: cavern Oth. I. iii. 140 “antres vast and desarts idle.”

apparent.text: adj. (most freq. in sense 1) 1. evident, plain Gent. III. i. 116 “Without apparent hazard of his life,” Cæs. II. i. 198 .

appeal.text: impeachment, accusation R2 I. i. 4 “to make good the . . . late appeal,” Ant. III. v. 12 .

appeared.text: made evident Cor. IV. iii. 9 “your favour is well (approved†) by your tongue.”

appellant.text: adj. accusing or impeaching another of treason R2 I. i. 34 “Come I appellant to this princely presence,” IV. i. 104 “Lords Appellants” (Fr. pl. of adj.).—sb. one who challenged another to single combat to prove upon his body the treason or felony of which he ‘appealed’ him R2 I. iii. 4 “the summons of the appellant's trumpet,” 2H6 II. iii. 49 .

apple.text: the pupil of the eye, so called because it was supposed to be a solid globular body MND. III. ii. 104 ; LLL. V. ii. 476 * “laugh upon the apple of her eye” (‘laugh upon her in a very affectionate manner’).

argosy.forms: argosy [orig. form ‘ragusy’=a vessel of Ragusa in Sicily]
argosy.text: merchant vessel of the largest size and burden Mer.V. I. i. 9 , &c.

arm.text: to take in one's arms Cym. iv. ii. 400 .

aroint.text: avaunt, begone Mac. I. iii. 6 , Lr. III. iv. 127 . ∥ Cf. the north-country ‘roint’ or ‘rynt thee’=get out of the way.

arrest.text: sb. (always with legal or judicial reference) 1. “under (an) arrest,” under legal restraint, arrested Meas. I. ii. 141 , R2 IV. i. 158 .
