articulate.text: set forth in articles, specified 1H4 V. i. 72 “These things . . . you have articulate.”

aslant.text: across, athwart Ham. IV. vii. 167 “aslant a brook.”

assay.text: vb. (now almost superseded by ‘essay’ except in the sense of testing metals) 1. to try, attempt Meas. I. iv. 76 “Assay the power you have,” Ham. IV. vii. 152 , Oth. II. iii. 209 “passion . . . Assays to lead the way.”

athwart.text: from an unexpected quarter, perversely, awry Meas. I. iii. 30 “quite athwart Goes all decorum,” 1H4 I. i. 36 .

atomy.text: 1 (common Eliz.; used archaically by Tennyson and Kingsley) 1. atom, mote AYL. III. ii. 246 “to count atomies.”

attaint.text: sb. (1 the orig. legal sense was ‘conviction of a jury for giving a false verdict’; 2 cf. ‘taint’) 1. impeachment Lr. V. iii. 83 (Ff “arrest”).

attempt.text: vb. (ordinary sense of ‘endeavour’ freq.; 2 is 16th-17th c.) 1. to try to win, obtain, or subdue Wiv. IV. ii. 230 , Tim. I. i. 127 , Lr. II. ii. 129 “him attempting who was self-subdu'”

attest.text: vb. (recorded first from S., who, however, does not use 1 with personal subject) 1. to certify, vouch for Tw.N. V. i. 162 “attested by the holy close of lips,” H5 Prol. 16

attorney.text: appointment of a legal representative, legal commission; hence “by attorney” = by proxy AYL. IV. i. 97 , R3 V. iii. 84 “I, by attorney, bless thee from thy mother.”

augur.text: prophet Sonn. cvii. 6 , Phœn. 7 “Augur of the fever's end.” ∥ In the technical sense S. uses AUGURER, q.v.

avail.text: vb. (2 intr. use (=refl.) is peculiar to S.) 1. to be of use to 1H6 III. i. 178 , Lucr. 1273 “it small avails my mood.”

ay.text: adv. (all old edd. have the spelling “I”) 1. yes Tp. I. ii. 268 ; introducing a more forcible statement than the preceding one Wint. II. i. 137 .

babe.text: rag doll John III. iv. 58 . ∥ ‘Babe that children play with,’ Palsgr.

baby.text: infant of a very young mother Mac. III. iv. 106 * .

back.text: sb. (1 said orig. of a sword which is all steel from edge to back and not merely edged with steel; 3 was common 1560-1660) 1. “metal . . . steel to the very back,” sound all through Tit. IV. iii. 47 .

bag.text: (to retreat) with all belongings saved, without surrender of anything, and therefore honourably AYL. III. ii. 171 , Wint. I. ii. 206 .

bail.text: sb. (2 not recorded before S.) 1. security given for the release of a prisoner Meas. III. ii. 44 , All'sW. V. iii. 290 “I'll put in bail.”

ballad.text: sb. (2 used contemptuously in H5 V. ii. 166 ) 1. light, simple song MND. IV. i. 222 “to write a ballad of this dream,” AYL. II. vii. 148 .

bane.text: sb. (1 the orig. sense; 2 cf. ‘ratsbane’; 3 obs.) 1. cause of the death of another 2H6 V. i. 120 , Tit. V. iii. 73 “Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself.”

bank.text: sb. (1 not later than S.; 2 not earlier than S.) 1. sea-shore 1H4 III. i. 45 , Troil. I. iii. 328 “as barren as banks of Libya,” Sonn. lvi. 11 .

bar.text: sb. (3 properly, the barrier marking off the precinct of the judge's seat, at which prisoners stand) 1. plea or objection of force sufficient to arrest entirely an action or claim at law Wiv. III. iv. 7 , Shr. I. i. 138 “this bar in law,” H5 I. ii. 35 , 42

bare.text: napless, threadbare Gent. II. iv. 47 ; fig. All'sW. IV. v. 105 , H8 V. iii. 125 .

bastard.text: sweet Spanish wine, resembling muscadel Meas. III. ii. 4 “brown and white ,” 1H4 II. iv. 30 .

batch.text: quantity of bread produced at one baking; fig. Troil. V. i. 5 “Thou crusty batch of nature.”

bate.text: to beat the wings impatiently and flutter away from the fist or perch Shr. IV. i. 199 “these kites That bate and beat,” 1H4 IV. i. 99 (old edd. “baited, bayted,” Malone “bated”); fig. H5 III. vii. 127 (with pun on BATE vb. 2 3), Rom. III. ii. 14 “Hood my unmann'd blood, bating in my cheeks.”

bawbling.text: trifling Tw.N. V. i. 58 “A bawbling vessel.” ∥ Only S. and echoed by mod. writers.

bay.text: sb. 2 (orig. ‘abay’=O Fr. ‘abai’, mod. Fr. ‘aboi’） 1. deep prolonged barking Tit. II. ii. 3 “Uncouple here and let us make a bay.”

bear.text: vb. (besides the mod. senses we find the foll.) 1. to have as a member or part of itself Wint. I. ii. 309 , 3H6 V. i. 69 “the dearest blood your bodies bear,” Rom. I. iii. 29 “I do bear a brain.”

bearing.text: carriage, deportment, behaviour, demeanour Ado II. i. 168 , H5 IV. vii. 186 “his blunt bearing,” Cor. II. iii. 257 .

beastly.text: in a beastly manner, like a beast Shr. IV. ii. 34 , Ant. I. v. 50 , Cym. V. iii. 27 .

becoming.text: grace (S.) Ant. I. iii. 96 , Sonn. cl. 5 .

beetle.text: “three-man beetle,” mallet requiring three men to lift it, used in ramming paving stones 2H4 I. ii. 259 ; beetle-headed, thick-headed, stupid Shr. IV. i. 160 “beetle-headed, flap-ear'd knave!”

before.text: prep. (follows its sb. LLL. IV. i. 93 ) “before me!,” on my soul! Tw.N. II. iii. 197 , Oth. IV. i. 147 . (∥ Modelled on “before (my) God!”)

beg.text: to petition the Court of Wards, established by Henry VIII and suppressed under Charles II, for the custody of (a minor, an heiress, or an idiot), as feudal superior or as having interest in the matter LLL. V. ii. 491 (‘You cannot prove us idiots’).

beggar.text: vb. (3 freq. echoed by later writers) 1. to reduce to beggary Mer.V. II. vi. 19 , R3 I. iv. 145 [“Conscience”] “beggars any man that keeps it.”

beholding.text: 1. sight Cor. I. iii. 10 , Lr. III. vii. 9 “not fit for your ”

behowl.text: to bay (the moon) MND. V. ii. 2 [ i. 379 ] (F1 &c. “beholds”).

being.text: (2 is an application peculiar to S.) 1. life, existence Shr. I. i. 11 “Pisa . . . Gave me my being,” Mac. III. i. 55 , Ham. II. i. 96 “end his being,” Oth. I. ii. 21 “my life and ,” Cym. I. i. 38 “he quit ”

belonging.text: (recorded first from S.) 1. (?) caparison (of a horse) Cor. I. ix. 62 .

beloving.text: loving Ant. I. ii. 24 “more than belov'”

bemoil.text: to befoul with mire Shr. IV. i. 77 .

bench.text: vb. (the foll. senses are rare outside S.) 1. to raise to authority Wint. I. ii. 314 “whom I from meaner form Have bench'd and rear'd to worship.”

bend.text: look, glance Cæs. I. ii. 123 , Ant. II. ii. 216 * (‘their adoring looks or obeisances added grace and beauty to her’).

bending.text: submissive, courteous R3 IV. iv. 95 , Troil. I. iii. 236 ; H5 V. ii. 404 * [Chor. 2] (a) bending under the weight of the task, (b) stooping to the hearers' clemency.

beneath.text: “this beneath world,” this world below Tim. I. i. 45 . Cf. “this under globe” Lr. II. ii. 170 .

bent.text: inclined (to), intent (upon) MND. III. ii. 145 , 2H6 II. i. 165 , Mac. III. iv. 134 “I am bent to know . . . the worst,” Per. II. Gower 23 * “full bent with sin” (=intent upon sin), Ven. 618 “bent to kill.”

besort.text: to befit Lr. I. iv. 274 “such men as may besort our age.”

bias.text: sb. (all the uses are derived from bowls) 1. one-sided form of the bowl which gives an oblique motion to it; in fig. phrase “against the bias” Shr. IV. v. 25 , R2 III. iv. 5 ; “assays of bias,” indirect attempts Ham. II. i. 65 .

biding.text: abode, dwelling Lr. IV. vi. 229 , Lucr. 550 .

big.text: (1 orig. sense; the S. exx. are late instances) 1. strong, stout, mighty H5 IV. ii. 43 “Big Mars” ; fig. Oth. III. iii. 350 “big wars.”

bile.text: spellings in the old edd. of BOIL sb.

bill.text: obsolete military weapon consisting of a long wooden handle having at one end a blade or axe-shaped head R2 III. ii. 118 ; in the 16th and 17th centuries painted or varnished in different colours, hence “brown bill” 2H6 IV. x. 14 , Lr. IV. vi. 93 ; a similar weapon used by constables (with play on BILL sb. 2 ) Ado III. iii. 189 “being taken up of these men's bills,” 2H6 IV. vii. 134 .

billet.text: vb. (twice only in S.) 1. to enroll Cor. IV. iii. 48 “distinctly billeted.”

bite.text: “bite the” (or “one's) lip” for the purpose of restraining anger or agitation Shr. II. i. 243 , H8 III. ii. 114 , Troil. III. iii. 256 ; “bite the thumb at,” to defy ‘by putting the thumbe naile into the mouth, and with a ierke from the upper teeth make it to knack’ (Cotgr.) Rom. I. i. 56 ; “bite one's tongue,” to be silent or speechless 2H6 I. i. 231 , 3H6 I. iv. 47 , Tit. III. i. 132 ; “bite by the ear” as a sign of fondness Rom. II. iv. 84 ; “bite by the nose,” to treat with contempt Meas. III. i. 107 .

blank.text: sb. (etymol. meaning is ‘something white’) 1. white spot in the centre of a target; fig. anything aimed at, range of such aim Wint. II. iii. 5 “out of the blank And level of my brain,” Troil. III. iii. 232 , Ham. IV. i. 42 “As level as the cannon to his blank” . . ., Lr. I. i. 161 , Oth. III. iv. 127 “stood within the blank of his displeasure.”

blazon.text: vb. (used partly with heraldic metaphor) 1. to describe fitly, set forth honourably in words, publish the praises of Rom. II. vi. 26 , Oth. II. i. 63 “the quirks of blazoning pens,” Compl. 217 “With wit well blazon'”

blear.text: to hoodwink, deceive Shr. V. i. 120 .

bleeding.text: running or suffused with blood, bloody John II. i. 304 “the ground,” Cæs. III. i. 168 , Mac. V. ii. 4 ; fig. unstanched, unhealed Cor. II. i. 87 “dismiss the controversy ” ; as adv. Tim. I. ii. 81 “-new.”

blench.text: to start aside, ‘shy’ “at,” flinch “from” Meas. IV. v. 5 “blench from this to that,” Troil. I. i. 30 “ at sufferance,” Ham. II. ii. 634 [ 626 ] “if he but ”

bloat.text: soft-bodied, puffed, bloated Ham. III. iv. 182 (Ff “blunt”). ∥ The proper form is “blowt” (Qq), for which Warburton substituted “bloat.” ‘Blowty’ in the same sense is used in Lincolnshire.

blood.text: （“flesh and , let” (a person) “ ” are freq.; “man of blood” Mac. III. iv. 126 , 4 a hunting expression) 1. vital fluid, (hence) life Rom. III. i. 189 “the price of his dear blood.”

blow.text: (?) mixture of senses (a) stroke, (b) blasting noise Shr. I. ii. 212 . ∥ S. is the earliest authority for “fall to blows” 2H6 II. iii. 82 , “at a ” 3H6 V. i. 50 .

blown.text: ppl. a. 1 (1 a very rare use) 1. whispered, hinted Oth. III. iii. 182 (Ff “blowed”).

bob.text: vb. 1 (of different origin from BOB vb. 2 and vb. 3 ) 1. to cheat “out of” Troil. III. i. 76 “You shall not bob us out of our melody.”

body.text: to give mental shape to MND. V. i. 14 . ∥ Imitated by modern writers.

boggler.text: waverer Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 110 “You have been a boggler ever.”

boil.text: Cor. I. iv. 31 “Boils and plagues Plaster you o'er!”

bolt.text: sb. (the senses ‘door-fastening’ and ‘thunderbolt’ occur; 2 was common from 1480 to 1690) 1. arrow, esp. one of the stouter and shorter kind with blunt or thickened head MND. II. i. 165 “the bolt of Cupid,” Cym. IV. ii. 300 ; “A fool's bolt is soon shot” (proverb common from the 13th to 18th c.) H5 III. vii. 137 ; “I'll make a shaft or a bolt on't,” I'll risk making something or other out of it, I'll make the venture Wiv. III. iv. 24 .

bombast.text: cotton wool used for padding or stuffing 1H4 II. iv. 364 “my sweet creature of ” ; fig. LLL. V. ii. 789 “As and as lining to the time.”

boot.text: sb. 1 (3 influenced by the word ‘booty’) 1. something given in addition or into the bargain Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 654, R3 IV. iv. 65 “Young York he is but boot,” Troil. IV. v. 40 “I'll give you boot; I'll give you three for one” ; esp. in phr. “to ” (freq.).

bore.text: sb. (2 metaphor from a gun) 1. small hole Cor. IV. vi. 88 (see AUGER), Cym. III. ii. 58 “the bores of hearing” (=the ears).

borrow.text: vb. (extensions of the common sense are) 1. to derive, receive Troil. IV. v. 132 “any drop” [of blood] “thou borrow'dst from thy mother,” Sonn. cliii. 5 “Which borrow'd from this holy fire of Love A dateless lively heat.”

bosom.text: sb. (“bosom multiplied” Cor. III. i. 130 prob. =the bosom of the many-headed monster, i.e. the people; “bisson multitude”†） 1. “Abraham's ” ( Luke xvi. 22 )=Paradise R3 IV. iii. 38 .

botch.text: flaw resulting from unskilful workmanship Mac. III. i. 134 ; so botch vb. to patch, esp. unskilfully (chiefly fig. with “up”) Tw.N. IV. i. 60 “how many fruitless pranks This ruffian hath b-'d up” (=clumsily contrived), H5 II. ii. 115 , Ham. IV. v. 10 “ the words up to fit their own thoughts” ; botcher All'sW. IV. iii. 211 , Cor. II. i. 99 .

botchy.text: “core,” central hard mass of a boil or tumour Troil. II. i. 6 (? some pun on BOTCH vb.).

bottled.text: bottle-shaped, big-bellied R3 I. iii. 242 “that bottled spider,” IV. iv. 81 .

bottom.text: sb. (freq. in the ordinary sense, and fig. = ‘depths’) 1. low-lying land, valley AYL. IV. iii. 80 “down in the neighbour bottom,” 1H4 III. i. 106 “so rich a ”

bounce.text: bang John II. i. 462 “cannon fire, and smoke and bounce,” 2H4 III. ii. 307 “‘bounce,’ would a' say.”

bound.text: sb. (‘bound’=leap is a different word) 1. boundary, limit, barrier (lit. and fig.) Tp. I. ii. 97 “A confidence sans bound,” MND. III. ii. 65 , John III. i. 23 “Like a proud river peering o'er his bounds” ; Ham. IV. vii. 128 “Revenge should have no bounds.”

bourn.text: boundary, confine, limit Wint. I. ii. 135 “No 'twixt his and mine,” Ant. I. i. 16 “I'll set a how far to be belov'd,” Lr. IV. vi. 58 “this chalky ” (=Dover cliffs). ∥ The meaning in Ham. III. i. 79 “country from whose No traveller returns” has been variously taken by modern writers to be ‘goal’ and ‘realm, domain’.

bow.text: to cause to bend, make crooked Shr. II. i. 151 “bow'd her hand to teach her fingering,” H8 II. iii. 36 “a three-pence bow'd,” Per. IV. ii. 94 “you are a young foolish sapling, and must be bowed” ; fig. H5 I. ii. 14 “wrest, or bow your reading,” Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 25 “He bow'd his nature.”

boy.text: Ant. V. ii. 219 ; allusion to the fact that boys or youths played female parts on the stage in S.'s time.

brace.text: sb. (etym. meaning ‘the two arms’, (hence) ‘armour covering the arms’; 3 orig. of dogs, perhaps because the leash was called a brace) 1. (?) coat of armour Per. II. i. 137 .

brag.text: vb. (the foll. are rare uses; 2 peculiar to S.) 1. to boast of, vaunt Cor. I. viii. 13 , Cym. V. iii. 93 .

bragless.text: without vain boasting Troil. V. ix. 4 .

braid.text: to plait Ven. 271 “braided . . . mane,” Compl. 35 “slackly braided. ”

brain.text: “bear a brain,” to have remembrance Rom I. iii. 29 ; “beaten with brains,” satirized, mocked Ado V. iv. 104 ; for other phrases see BOILED, DRY, HOT, &c.

brave.text: vb. (1 freq. in S.; 2 in common Eliz. use) 1. to challenge, defy (lit. and fig.) John IV. iii. 87 “dar'st thou brave a nobleman?,” R3 IV. iii. 57 “when traitors brave the field,” Lucr. 40 “so rich a thing, Braving compare” ; also intr. in pres. pple. All'sW. I. ii. 3 “A braving war,” R2 II. iii. 112 “braving arms.”

brawl.text: vb. (1 freq. in lit. sense; 2, 3 not pre-S.) 1. to quarrel noisily; (hence) to be clamorous, or noisy, or discordant Meas. IV. i. 11 “my brawling discontent,” Shr. IV. i. 209 “I'll rail and brawl,” 2H4 I. iii. 70 “as the times do ,” Rom. I. i. 181 “O b-ing love!”

brazed.text: hardened Ham. III. iv. 37 (Ff Q6 “braz'd,” Qq2-5 “brasd,” mod. edd. “brass'd”†), Lr. I. i. 11 “I am brazed to it.”

bread.text: “God's bread,” the sacramental bread, the Host (used in oaths) Rom. III. v. 177 ; “bread and cheese,” typical of simple fare Wiv. II. i. 139 “I love not the humour of bread and cheese.”

breathing.text: (1 cf. ‘Hide not thy ear at my breathing, at my cry’ Lamentations iii. 55 ) 1. utterance Ant. I. iii. 14 “to give to my purpose.”

breed.text: sb. (not pre-Eliz.; 2 now replaced by ‘brood’) 1. race, strain R2 II. i. 45 “This happy breed of men,” H8 II. ii. 4 , Cym. IV. ii. 25 “breed of greatness!” ; family Mac. IV. iii. 108 ; kind, species LLL. V. ii. 267 “the breed of wits so wonder'd at,” Ham. III. ii. 333 [ 327 ] “this courtesy is not of the right breed.”

breeding.text: parentage, descent Wint. IV. iii. 744 [ iv. 741 ], 2H4 V. iii. 109 .

bride.text: to play the bride Shr. III. ii. 254 .

bring.text: (the foll. are obs. or special uses; 1 is freq.; 2 peculiar to S.; 6 common in Eliz. dramatists) 1. to escort or accompany (a person) on his way Gent. I. i. 55 “thither will I bring thee,” H5 II. iii. 2 “let me bring thee to Staines,” Cæs. III. ii. 58 .

brock.text: badger; used contemptuously as if ‘a stinking fellow’ Tw.N. II. v. 115 .

brogue.text: rude kind of shoe, generally made of untanned hide, worn by the inhabitants of the wilder parts of Ireland and the Scotch Highlands Cym. IV. ii. 214 “My clouted brogues.”

broken.text: 1 cf. southmidland dial. ‘broken-mouthed’ = having lost teeth; R3 II. ii. 117 * “The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts” (so Qq; Ff “hates”), ‘your quarrels (or spirits) which had risen high and broken out into rancour’) 1. fragmentary, incomplete; “broken meats,” remains of food, as eaten by servants Lr. II. ii. 15 “A knave, a rascal, an eater of broken meats” ; All'sW. II. iii. 66 “My mouth no more were broken” (=having gaps in the teeth), H5 V. ii. 264 “broken English.”

brook.text: “flying at the brook,” hawking at the river with a goshawk for waterfowl (contrast BIRDING), the royal sport of falconry 2H6 II. i. 1 .

bruit.text: vb. (1 the ordinary sense; 2, 3 only in S.) 1. to noise abroad, report, rumour 1H6 II. iii. 68 “I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited.”

buckler.text: vb. (thrice in S., not otherwise common) 1. to shield, defend Shr. III. ii. 242 “I'll buckler thee against a million,” 2H6 III. ii. 216 , 3H6 III. iii. 99 “buckler falsehood with a pedigree.”

bud.text: used for ingrafting under the bark of a different stock Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 95 “make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race”; fig. John III. iv. 82 “now will canker-sorrow eat my bud” [i.e. Arthur].

buff.text: stout leather made of ox-hide, used for the attire of soldiers, and (in S.) sergeants and bumbailiffs Err. IV. ii. 36 , 1H4 I. ii. 48 “is not a buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance?”

bulk.text: 1 (1 in use 1460-1720; 3 cf. ‘the bulke, bellie, or bodie of a ship’, Cotgr.) 1. trunk, body (of a person) R3 I. iv. 40 “my panting ,” Ham. II. i. 95 , Lucr. 467 “her heart . . . Beating her ”

buoy.text: to rise up Lr. III. vii. 60 .

buss.text: kiss John III. iv. 35 , 2H4 II. iv. 291 ; fig. Troil. IV. v. 219 “Yond towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds,” Cor. III. ii. 75 “Thy knee bussing the stones.”

busyless.text: Theobald's emendation of F1 “busie lest” in Tp. III. i. 15 ; others read with Singer “busiest”†.

butt.text: mark for archery practice, properly a mound or other erection on which the target is set up H5 I. ii. 186 “To which is fixed, as an aim or butt, Obedience,” 3H6 I. iv. 29 “I am your butt, and I abide your shot” ; (hence) goal, object Oth. V. ii. 266 “my journey's end . . . my butt.” See also BUTT-SHAFT.

by.text: prep. (the following uses are now obs.) 1. about, concerning Ado V. i. 316 “virtuous In anything that I do know by her,” 2H6 II. i. 16 , Oth. I. iii. 17 “How say you by this change?”

cabin.text: sb. (1 in use 1400-1650; 2 was common Eliz.) 1. temporary shelter of slight materials Tw.N. I. v. 289 “a willow cabin,” Pilgr. xiv. 3 [ 183 ].

caitiff.text: =wretch (2 thrice as freq. as 1) 1. expressing pity Oth. IV. i. 109 “Alas! poor caitiff!”

call.text: vb. (1 only S.; 2 a few uses only are given here) 1. =‘call upon,’ to visit (a person) at his house Meas. IV. iv. 18 “I'll call you at your house,” Tw.N. III. ii. 58 “We'll call thee at the cubiculo.”

calling.text: name, appellation AYL. I. ii. 250 “I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son, . . . and would not change that ”

calm.text: to becalm (a ship) 2H6 IV. ix. 33 (F4 “calm'd,” F1 “calme,” F2 “claimd,” F3 “claim'd”); Oth. I. i. 30 “be-lee'd and calm'd” (? for ‘becalm'd’).

camp.text: to serve as a lodging for Ant. IV. viii. 33 “Had our great palace the capacity To camp this host.”

can.text: vb. 1 (1 instances with apparent pronominal object, as “all I can, such as I can, I can no more,” are probably to be regarded as due to ellipsis of the infinitive ‘do’) 1. trans. to know, be skilled in Phœn. 14 “the priest in surplice white That defunctive music can.”

canary.text: sb. (1 the idea of the dance is said to have been borrowed from the Canary Islands) 1. lively Spanish dance All'sW. II. i. 77 .

candy.text: used as adj.=sugared 1H4 I. iii. 251 “candy deal of courtesy” : see CAUDIE.

captain.text: sb. (the ordinary military senses are freq.; three syllables in 3H6 IV. vii. 30 , Mac. I. ii. 34 ） 1. chief, head (fig. from military senses) R2 IV. i. 99 “his Christ,” Lucr. 271 “Affection is my , and he leadeth” ; Rom. II. iv. 21 “the . . . of compliments” ; used of women 3H6 II. vi. 75 , Oth. II. i. 74 .

captivate.text: to take prisoner, make captive LLL. III. i. 131 ; fig. to subjugate, subdue 3H6 I. iv. 115 ; to fascinate, charm Ven. 281 .

captive.text: often used in the sense of ‘(one) vanquished’ LLL. IV. i. 76 , Troil. V. iii. 40 .

carbonado.text: to make a carbonado of Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 267 “toads carbonadoed”; (hence) to cut, hack, slash All'sW. IV. v. 108 “your carbonadoed face,” Lr. II. ii. 42 “I'll so carbonado your shanks.”

card.text: sb. (1 always in fig. phrases; 2 cf. ‘That law . . . is the card to guide the world by’, Hooker) 1. playing-card John V. ii. 105 “the best cards for the game,” Tit. V. i. 100 “As sure a card as ever won the set;—card of ten,” card with ten pips, hence phr. “fac'd it with a card of ten,” put on a bold front Shr. II. i. 399 (cf. the use of ‘facing-card’ in the 17th cent.=imposing allegation or argument); —“cooling card,” app. term or some lost card-game, used fig.=something that cools one's ardour 1H6 V. iii. 84 ;—“Pack'd cards with,” made a fraudulent arrangement with Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 19

cardinal.text: the four ‘natural’ virtues, justice, prudence, temperance, fortitude, to which some add the three ‘theological’ virtues, faith, hope, and charity, making in all seven H8 III. i. 103 “I thought ye . . . two reverend virtues; But sins . . . I fear ye” (with pun on the title of ‘cardinal’).

care.forms: care occurs in various proverbs and phrases
care.text: “care killed a cat” Ado V. i. 136 ; “past cure . . . past care” LLL. V. ii. 28 , Sonn. cxlvii. 9 ;—“have (a) care,” be attentive, pay attention, take care Tp. I. i. 10 , Wiv. IV. v. 77 , Ado I. ii. 30 , III. iii. 43 , MND. IV. i. 15 ; Tw.N. III. iv. 70 , Per. IV. i. 49 ;—“keep” or “make a care of,” care for Tp. II. i. 311 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 367

carnation.text: flesh-colour H5 II. iii. 35 “A' could never abide carnation” ; attrib. LLL. III. i. 153 “carnation riband.” ∥ By association with the next word the meaning has passed into ‘carnation-coloured’.

carouse.text: cupful of liquor drunk ‘all out’ [German ‘gar aus’], full bumper, toast Shr. I. ii. 280 , Ant. IV. viii. 34 ; so carouse vb. (freq.).

cart.text: sb. (1 cf. CART vb.; 2 cf. CAR) 1. cart used for conveying criminals to the gallows, and for the public exposure and chastisement of offenders 1H4 II. iv. 554 .

case.text: sb. 2 (2 perhaps ‘a pair’, like ‘a case of pistols’) 1. applied to (i) a mask LLL. V. ii. 388 “that superfluous case,” Rom. I. iv. 29 ; cf. Ado II. i. 99 , and CASE vb. 1; (ii) the body, as enclosing the soul Tw.N. V. i. 169 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 41, xiii. [ xv. ] 89 “This case of that huge spirit”; (iii) the sockets of the eyes Wint. V. ii. 14 , Lr. IV. vi. 148 “with the case of eyes,” Per. III. ii. 99 ; (iv) the skin Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 849; (v) clothes Meas. II. iv. 13 , 1H4 I. ii. 200 “cases of buckram,” Compl. 116 “Accomplish'd in himself, not in his case.”

cast.text: vb. (the more unusual senses are) 1. to throw in wrestling Mac. II. iii. 47 “though he took up my legs sometime, yet I made a shift to him.”

catch.text: vb. (“caught” occurs 31 times, “catched” 4 times; the senses ‘overtake, come up with’ ( Tp. V. i. 315 , MND. II. i. 233 , R3 II. ii. 44 ), ‘apprehend by the senses or intellect’ ( LLL. II. i. 70 , Ant. I. ii. 149 , Sonn. cxiii. 8 ), ‘apprehend so as to adopt or appropriate’ ( Mac. I. v. 19 ), and ‘catch a cold’ ( Gent. I. ii. 133 ) are recorded first from S.; there are many other uses; the foll. are occas.) 1. to attain, get possession of 3H6 III. ii. 179 “I . . . Torment myself to catch the English crown,” Mac. I. vii. 3 “if the assassination Could . . . catch With his surcease success,” Sonn. cxliii. 11 ; absol. John I. i. 173 “have is have, however men do catch.”

catling.text: catgut Troil. III. iii. 309 “unless the fiddler Apollo get his sinews to make catlings on. ∥ Catling” is the name of a musician in Rom. IV. v. 133 .

cause.text: sb. (the foll. are obs. or archaic uses; 1 is a general application of the legal sense ‘subject of litigation’; 4 taken over from late Latin ‘causa’) 1. matter in dispute, affair to be decided Shr. IV. iv. 26 “a weighty cause Of love,” 2H6 III. i. 289 “What counsel give you in this weighty cause?”

cease.text: cessation Ham. III. iii. 15 “The cease of majesty” (Ff “cease,” Qq “cesse”), Lr. V. iii. 266 “Fall and cease?.” ∥ Partly an aphetic form of ‘decease’.

cement.forms: cement sb. and vb. (old edd. also “ciment, cyment, symant”)
cement.text: always stressed on the first syllable Cor. IV. vi. 86 , Ant. II. i. 48 , III. ii. 29 .

censure.text: sb. (2 the prevailing S. use; 3 not pre-S.) 1. judicial sentence, esp. a condemnatory one Cor. III. iii. 45 , V. v. [ vi. ] 143 “Your heaviest censure,” Oth. V. ii. 367 “the censure of this hellish villain.”

center.text: girdle John IV. iii. 155 (Ff “center,” mod. edd. “cincture, ceinture”); by some taken = CENTRE 3

cerements.text: waxed wrapping for the dead, (hence) graveclothes Ham. I. iv. 48 . ∥ A purely S. word, which has been caught up by modern writers.

cess.text: “out of all cess,” beyond all calculation 1H4 II. i. 8 .

cesse.forms: cesse [variant of ‘cease’ not generally current in S.'s time]
cesse.text: to cease All'sW. V. iii. 72 (F1): rhymes with “bless.”

chafe.text: not pre-S. in the intr. sense ‘to fret, rage’ of the sea or a river against its banks Wint. III. iii. 89 , Cæs. I. ii. 101 “The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores,” Lr. IV. vi. 22 ,

chafed.text: John III. i. 259 ; see CASE vb. 2

challenge.text: vb. (1 the orig. sense, the ultimate etym. of the word being Latin ‘calumniari’=to accuse falsely; 2, 3 the chief Eliz. uses) 1. to accuse, bring a charge against Tit. I. i. 340 “c-d of wrongs,” Mac. III. iv. 42 “ for unkindness.”

champion.text: sb. (3 Wyclif has ‘strong schampions and pileris of holy chirche’) 1. fighting man, man of valour 1H6 III. iv. 19 “A stouter champion never handled sword,” Tit. I. i. 65 “Rome's best champion.”

change.text: vb. (in Cor. V. iii. 152 * , Ant. I. ii. 5 * Ff read “change,” mod. edd. “charge”†: see commentators) 1. to exchange Tp. I. ii. 438 , LLL. V. ii. 134 , AYL. I. iii. 94 “Wilt thou change fathers?” ; to exchange (a thing) “with” (a person) Sonn. xxix. 14 “I scorn to change my state with kings,” Oth. I. iii. 318 “change my humanity with a baboon” ; intr. with “for” before the thing taken in exchange Oth. I. iii. 356 “She must change for youth,” Per. IV. vi. 179 .

changeling.text: (1 now obsolete or archaic) 1. fickle or inconstant person 1H4 V. i. 76 “fickle c-s,” Cor. IV. vii. 11 “his nature In that's no changeling.”

channel.text: street gutter=KENNEL 2H4 II. i. 54 -5, 3H6 II. ii. 141 . ∥ Still in use locally in northern counties.

chaps.text: jaws Tp. II. ii. 93 , Mac. I. ii. 22 (Ff “chops”).

character.text: sb. (in R3 III. i. 81 “chara'cter,” as often in 16th-17th cent.; the foll. uses are not pre-S.) 1. in collective sing. used=writing, printing Tim. V. iii. 6 “the character I'll take with wax,” Sonn. lix. 8 “Since mine at first in character was done.”

charge.text: sb. (the senses ‘accusation’ and ‘person or thing entrusted to one's care’ are also freq.) 1. load, burden (lit. and fig.) Wiv. I. iv. 103 , Ado I. i. 106 , Wint. I. ii. 26 “my stay To you a charge and trouble” ; (with quibble) Ham. V. ii. 43 “‘As’es of great charge.”

charm.text: the orig. sense ‘incantation, enchantment, magic spell’ ( Tp. I. ii. 231 ) runs through the fig. applications Wiv. II. ii. 108 * “surely, I think you have charms, la,” Rom. II. Prol. 6 “bewitched by the charm of looks,” Lr. V. iii. 49 , Pilgr. xi. 8 [ 150 ]; occas. the sense approaches to ‘person or thing that charms’ Oth. V. i. 35 “those charms, thine eyes,” Ant. IV. x. 29 [ xii. 16 ], 38 [ 25 ] “this false soul of Egypt! this grave charm.”

chase.text: vb. (in Tim. I. i. 25 Ff “chases,” mod. edd. “chafes,” Ven. 325 earlier Qq “chafing,” later “chasing”) 1. “chas'd your blood Out of appearance” (Ff1 2 “apparance”), driven the colour out of your face (i.e. rendered it invisible) H5 II. ii. 75 .

chat.text: sb. and vb. are both used in the obs. sense of (1) frivolous talking, and the current one of (2) familiar conversation; in Cor. II. i. 227 “chats him” =gossips about him.

check.text: reproof, rebuke, censure Wiv. III. iv. 84 “against all checks, rebukes and manners,” Shr. I. i. 32 * “Aristotle's checks” (? restraints), 2H4 IV. iii. 34 , Oth. III. iii. 67 , Ant. IV. iv. 31 “Rebukeable And worthy shameful check.”

cheek.text: side by side MND. III. ii. 338 .

cheer.text: sb. (5 whence the sense ‘fare, provisions’ Wiv. III. ii. 55 ; Ham. III. ii. 231 where some read “chair,” comparing Hall's Satires ‘Sit seven yeres pining in an anchor's cheyre’) 1. face, complexion MND. III. ii. 96 “pale of cheer.”

chiding.text: brawling or angry noise MND. IV. i. 121 “never did I hear Such gallant chiding” [of hounds], AYL. II. i. 7 “chiding of the winter's wind.”

childing.text: fertile, fruitful MND. II. i. 112 “ autumn.”

chirurgeonly.text: like a skilled surgeon Tp. II. i. 147 .

choice.text: sb. (1, 2, 3 not pre-S.; 4 only S.) 1. abundant and well-chosen supply John II. i. 72 , 1H6 V. v. 17 “So full replete with of all delights.”

chops.text: jaws Mac I. ii. 22 (Ff); person with fat or bloated cheeks 1H4 I. ii. 150 , 2H4 II. iv. 234 .

cipher.text: zero, usu. in fig. application=nonentity, a mere nothing Meas. II. ii. 39 , LLL. I. ii. 60 , AYL. III. ii. 310 ; with ref. to its increasing the value of figures preceding it Wint. I. ii. 6 “like a , Yet standing in rich place,” H5 Chor. 17 “let us, ciphers to this great accompt, On your imaginary forces work.”

cleanly.text: adv. (obsolete uses) 1. completely, quite Ven. 694 “till they have singled . . . the cold fault cleanly out.”

clear.text: vb. (the less common senses are the foll.) 1. to get (any one) clear of a place Wint. I. ii. 439 “I will . . . Clear them o' the city.”

clerkly.text: in a scholarly manner Gent. II. i. 119 , 2H6 III. i. 179 “ignominious words, though couch'”

climate.text: formerly used = region, country, ‘clime’, without ref. to climatic conditions R2 IV. i. 130 “in a Christian climate,” Cæs. I. iii. 32 .

cling.text: to pinch with hunger Mac. V. v. 40 .

clock.text: “twixt and ,” between the striking of one hour and another; “tell the ,” count the strokes of the clock Tp. II. i. 297 , R3 V. iii. 277 .

cloud.text: recorded first from S. in senses ‘to overspread with gloom or sorrow’ 3H6 IV. i. 74 , ‘cast a slur upon, asperse’ Wint. I. ii. 280 , ‘to become gloomy’ LLL. V. ii. 729 .

cock.text: perversion of ‘God’ in oaths Shr. IV. i. 121 “Cock's passion,” Ham. IV. v. 62 “By Cock” ; also cock and pie Wiv. I. i. 319 , in which ‘pie’ is commonly taken to be the word meaning ‘directory of divine service’.

cockle.text: applied to any bivalve shell, esp. that of the scallop Shr. IV. iii. 66 , Per. IV. iv. 2 “Sail seas in c-s; cockle hat,” hat with a scallop-shell stuck in it, worn by pilgrims as a sign of their having been to the shrine of St. James of Compostella in Spain Ham. IV. v. 25 (quoting an old ballad).

codling.text: immature or half-grown apple Tw.N. I. v. 168 “a when 'tis almost an apple.”

cog.text: (1, 2 common Eliz.; 3 not pre-S.) 1. to employ fraud or deceit, cheat Ado V. i. 95 , LLL. V. ii. 236 , R3 I. iii. 48 , Tim. V. i. 100 , Oth. IV. ii. 132 .

coil.text: （“kept a coil” * , in F2 “acoyle,” bustled about, pestered All'sW. II. i. 27 : see A 3 3) 1. noise, disturbance Err. III. i. 48 .

cold.text: adj. (5 the meaning is somewhat doubtful) 1. deliberate, cool 2H4 III. ii. 136 “a soldier,” V. ii. 98 “ considerance,” Cym. II. iii. 2 “the most coldest” [man] “that ever turned up ace.”

coloquintida.text: the colocynth or bitter-apple, Citrullus Colocynthis, which furnishes a purgative drug Oth. I. iii. 356 .

colour.text: sb. (after the literal sense and sense 1, 4 is the most freq. in S.; the word easily lends itself to quibbling; of doubtful place is All'sW. II. v. 65 “holds not colour with” =is not in keeping with) 1. pl. military ensigns (freq.); phr. “fear no c-s,” fear no enemy, have no fear Tw.N. I. v. 6 , 2H4 V. v. 94 ; “under her colours,” in her party, led by her Cym. I. iv. 21 .

colt.text: to befool 1H4 II. ii. 43 . ∥ In use 1580- 1620

command.text: “upon command,” (1) at a given order R3 I. iv. 202 “;” (2) at pleasure AYL. II. vii. 125 .

commanded.text: entrusted with command Cor. I. i. 268 “to be Under Cominius.”

commence.text: 2H4 IV. iii. 126 “learning, a mere hoard of gold kept by a devil till sack c-s it and sets it in act and use” ; allusion probably to the commencement at Cambridge University, i.e. proceeding to the degree of Master or Doctor and so qualifying to teach.

commend.text: vb. (senses 2, 3, and the sense ‘to praise’ are the most freq.) 1. to deliver, commit, entrust LLL. III. i. 177 “to her white hand see thou do This seal'd-up counsel,” R2 III. iii. 116 , H8 V. i. 17 , Mac. I. vii. 11 , Lr. II. iv. 28 , Lucr. 436 .

comment.text: mental observation, pondering John V. vii. 4 ; Ham. III. ii. 84 * “the very comment of thy soul,” thy most intense observation (Ff “my”).

common.text: adj. (all the foll. are common uses) 1. belonging equally to more than one, or to all mankind 1H4 II. i. 104 “homo is a name to all men” (cf. the grammatical term ‘common noun’), Mac. III. i. 69 “the common enemy of man.”

compact.text: ppl. a. 1 [Latin ‘compact-’ from ‘compingere’ to fasten together] 1. knit together Lr. I. ii. 7 .

companion.text: used as term of contempt=fellow Err. IV. iv. 63 , All'sW. V. iii. 252 , 2H4 II. iv. 130 “scurvy companion,” 2H6 IV. x. 33 , Cæs. IV. iii. 137 , Oth. IV. ii. 141 .

company.text: sb. (S. is earliest for the application to a ship's crew) 1. “from company,” alone, in solitude 1H6 V. v. 100 ; “for company,” by way of sociableness Shr. IV. i. 180 .

compare.text: vb. (2 cf. ‘Art stryving to compayre With Nature’, Spenser) 1. to draw comparisons R2 II. i. 186 .

daff.text: (2 “daff'd the world aside” 1H4 IV. i. 96 has been much imitated by modern writers) 1. to put off (clothes, armour) Ant. IV. iv. 13 “till we do please To daff't for our repose,” Compl. 297 “my white stole . . . I daff'”

dainty.text: “ of,” scrupulous or particular about Troil. I. iii. 145 , Mac. II. iii. 151 “let us not be of leave-taking.”

damask.text: the colour of the “ rose” ( Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 222), = (1) blush-red colour Cor. II. i. 235 “the war of white and in Their . . . cheeks” ; (2) striped red and white AYL. III. v. 123 “mingled ” ;—adj. of such colour (in both applications) LLL. V. ii. 297 “their sweet commixture,” Tw.N. II. iv. 114 “her cheek,” Pilgr. vii. 5 [ 89 ] “A lily pale, with dye to grace her.”

dare.forms: dare vb. 2 (of different origin from vb. 1 )
dare.text: to daze, dazzle, or fascinate (larks) and so entrap them, e.g. by means of a piece of scarlet cloth and a looking-glass H8 III. ii. 283 “And us with his cap like larks” (ref. to the cardinal's biretta); so H5 IV. ii. 36 “dare the field” (=make the prey crouch).

dark.text: S. is the earliest authority (in the mod. period) for the senses ‘iniquitous, evil’ ( R2 I. i. 169 ), ‘gloomy, dismal’ ( Mer.V. V. i. 87 , Rom. III. v. 36 ), ‘frowning, clouded’ ( Ven. 182 ), ‘indistinct, indiscernible’ ( Tp. I. ii. 50 , Ven. 760 ), ‘concealed, secret’ ( Lr. I. i. 38 ); also for “ house, room,” formerly considered a proper place of confinement for madmen Err. IV. iv. 96 , AYL. III. ii. 427 ; similarly “keep him ,” keep him confined in a dark room All'sW. IV. i. 101 .

dash.text: vb. (physical senses also occur) 1. to destroy, frustrate LLL. V. ii. 463 , 3H6 II. i. 118 .

dead.text: （“a dead man” = ‘a man marked out for death’ occurs once Wiv. IV. ii. 45 ） 1. “is dead” = has died Ado V. i. 254 , H5 V. i. 86 , Rom. V. iii. 210 “my wife is dead to-night,” Lr. V. iii. 294 .

deadly.text: = mortally (in various uses) Ado V. i. 182 “hate him ,” R3 III. vii. 26 “ pale,” Troil. V. v. 12 “deadly hurt,” Cor. II. i. 68 “they lie deadly.”

deal.text: to act (freq.) John V. ii. 22 ; phr. “ upon,” Pilgr. set to work upon, proceed against R3 IV. ii. 73 ; “ in,” (1) proceed or act in (a matter) Ado IV. i. 249 , V. i. 101 ; (2) have to do with Tp. V. i. 271 , 1H6 V. v. 56 , 3H6 III. ii. 154 ; “dealt on lieutenantry,” fought by proxy Ant. III. ix. [ xi. ] 39

dealing.text: “in plain ,” putting it plainly Meas. II. i. 270 .

dear.text: adj. 2 (of different origin from DEAR adj. 1 , but undoubtedly associated with it in use): hard, grievous, dire Tp. II. i. 142 , LLL. V. ii. 872 , All'sW. IV. v. 11 , Tw.N. V. i. 75 , John I. i. 257 “my offence,” R2 I. iii. 151 “thy exile,” R3 I. iv. 219 , Tim. IV. iii. 384 , V. i. 233 “In our peril,” Oth. I. iii. 261 , Sonn. xxxvii. 3 “fortune's d-est spite.” ∥ Cf. ‘turnd to disadvantage deare,’ Spenser.

debate.text: to fight Lucr. 1421 “ with angry swords,” Sonn. xv. 11 ; with “it” All'sW. I. ii. 75 * “nature and sickness Debate it at their leisure.” ∥ The sense of ‘discuss’ occurs.

debitor.text: statement of account, accountbook Oth. I. i. 31 , Cym. V. iv. 171 .

decay.text: sb. (1 a common 16th c. use) 1. downfall, destruction, ruin John IV. iii. 154 “The imminent of wrested pomp,” 2H6 III. i. 194 , R3 IV. iv. 410 , Lucr. 516 “thy life's ” ; also, cause of ruin Sonn. lxxx. 14 “my love was my decay.”

deceptious.text: delusive Troil. V. ii. 120 “As if those organs had deceptious functions.”

deck.text: pack of cards 3H6 V. i. 44 . ∥ Since 17th c. dial. (chiefly midland).

dedicate.text: dedicated Meas. II. ii. 154 “whose minds are To nothing temporal,” 2H6 V. ii. 37 “dedicate to war.”

deep.text: adj. (besides the sense of ‘intense’ the following are the chief fig. uses) 1. grave, serious, weighty 1H4 I. iii. 190 “matter and dangerous,” R3 III. VII. 66 “ designs,” IV. ii. 118 “my service” (Qq “true”), Mac. I. iii. 126 “In d-est consequence,” Cym. II. iii. 96 ; grievous, heinous R3 II. ii. 28 “ vice,” Tim. III. iv. 31 , Mac. I. vii. 20 , Lucr. 701 .

defeat.text: vb. (1 common 1435-1635; 2 rare sense) 1. to undo, destroy, ruin Tim. IV. iii. 164 , Ham. I. ii. 10 “a d-ed joy,” Oth. IV. ii. 160 “may my life.”

deign.text: to condescend to take, accept without grudging Gent. I. i. 162 , Ant. I. iv. 63 .

deject.text: downcast, dejected Troil. II. ii. 50 “Make . . . lustihood ,” Ham. III. i. 164 “ and wretched.”

demand.text: sb. and vb. are often used simply = question, without any idea of authoritative or peremptory asking.

demure.text: (?) to look demurely Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 29

denay.text: old form of DENY, 2H6 I. iii. 107 .

depart.text: vb. (2 this sense is now only used in ‘depart this life’) 1. to take leave of one another Tim. I. i. 263 “Ere we depart,” Cym. I. i. 108 “The loathness to depart.”

departing.text: separation 3H6 II. vi. 43 “life and death's departing.”

deplore.text: to tell with grief Tw.N. III. i. 176 .

deputed.text: sword delivered as an emblem of office or dignity Meas. II. ii. 60 .

derogate.text: to act in a way derogatory to one's position Cym. II. i. 50 ; in line 59 (quibblingly) degenerate.

descant.text: melody sung extempore upon a plainsong, ground, or bass, to which it forms the air Gent. I. ii. 91 “you . . . mar the concord with too harsh a ” ; (hence) fig. comment R3 III. vii. 48 “on that ground I'll make a holy descant.”

descending.text: descent, lineage Per. V. i. 130 (Qq1 2 3 “discending,” Qq4 5 6 “discent,” Ff3 4 “descent”).

descry.text: to reconnoitre R3 V. iii. 9 , Lr. IV. v. 13 .

design.text: the sense of ‘plan, scheme’ is weakened to that of ‘purpose, aim, intention’; whence ‘thing in view, project, enterprise’ LLL. IV. i. 89 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 515 “not prepar'd For this ,” R2 I. i. 81 , Troil. II. ii. 194 , Mac. II. i. 55 “murder . . . toward his Moves like a ghost,” Ant. V. i. 43 .

despite.text: sb. (3 the prepositional use is not pre-S.) 1. contempt, scorn, disdain Ado I. i. 245 “an obstinate heretic in the despite of beauty,” Oth. IV. ii. 116 .

determinate.text: pple. (1 legal metaphor; cf. next) 1. ended, expired Sonn. lxxxvii. 4 .

dialogue.text: vb. (not found before S.) 1. to hold a conversation Tim. II. ii. 51 .

die.text: phr. “to die the death,” to be put to death, suffer the penalty of capital punishment MND. I. i. 65 , Cym. IV. ii. 96 ; S. is earliest for “die (with laughing)” Shr. III. ii. 244 , Troil. I. iii. 176 “at this sport Sir Valour dies.”

diet.text: vb. (2 exact meaning not always clear) 1. to feed (lit. and fig.) 1H6 I. ii. 10 “d-ed like mules,” Cor. I. ix. 52 , Oth. II. i. 306 “to my revenge,” Cym. III. iv. 183 “all the comfort The gods will me with.”

disaster.text: unfavourable aspect of a star Ham. I. i. 118 “D-s in the sun” ; (hence) ill-luck Mac. III. i. 112 “So weary with d-s, tugg'd with fortune.”

disbench.text: to cause (a person) to leave his seat (S.) Cor. II. ii. 76 “I hope My words d-'d you not.”

discase.text: to undress Tp. V. i. 85 “I will me” ; to unmask Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 651 ∥ Cf. CASE sb. 2 1 (i) and 1 (v).

discharge.text: occurs 7 times in S., who is the earliest authority for the senses ‘letting off a firearm’ ( 1H4 I. i. 57 ), ‘emission’ ( AYL. II. i. 37 , Troil. IV. iv. 41 ), ‘payment’ ( Cym. V. iv. 173 ), ‘performance, execution’ ( Tp. II. i. 262 ).

discipline.text: sb. (the earliest sense in English, ‘chastisement, correction,’ is not S.) 1. instruction, teaching Gent. III. ii. 88 , Shr. I. i. 30 “this moral ,” Troil. II. iii. 33 “heaven bless thee from a tutor, and discipline come not near thee.”

disclose.text: vb. (the sense ‘reveal’ is the common one) 1. to unfold Ham. I. iii. 40 “before their buttons be d-'d,” Sonn. liv. 8 “their masked buds discloses.”

discomfort.text: sb. (sense ‘uneasiness’ is late) 1. discouragement R2 III. ii. 65 , Mac. I. ii. 28 . ∥ ‘Discourage’ and its compounds are not S.

discourse.text: sb. (“ of reason” dates from the 15th c.) 1. reasoning, thought, reflection Meas. I. ii. 196 “reason and ,” Tw.N. IV. iii. 12 , Troil. V. ii. 139 , Ham. IV. iv. 36 “with such large , Looking before and after; of reason,” process or faculty of reasoning Troil. II. ii. 116 , Ham. I. ii. 150 ; cf. “ of thought” Oth. IV. ii. 153 .

disjoint.text: ‘out of joint,’ distracted Ham. I. ii. 20 “thinking . . . Our state to be disjoint.”

dislike.text: vb. (the current trans. use is commonest) 1. to displease Rom. II. ii. 61 “if either thee ” (Q1 “displease”), Oth. II. iii. 50 “I'll do 't; but it d-s me.”

disorder.text: sb. (not earlier than the 16th c.; the verb occurs in S. only in the pa. pple.) 1. disorderly act or practice, misdemeanour Tw.N. II. iii. 107 , Lr. I. ii. 127 “machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders,” II. iv. 202 .

dispatch.text: vb. (the most freq. meaning in S. is ‘to make haste’) 1. to make away with, kill R2 III. i. 35 ; absol. John IV. i. 27 , R3 I. ii. 182 , Lr. II. i. 60 ; also “to dispatch” a person's “life” Lr. IV. v. 12 .

displanting.text: deposition from office Oth. II. i. 286 .

disport.text: refl. to amuse oneself 3H6 IV. v. 8 “Comes hunting this way to himself,” Tim. I. ii. 143 .

dispose.text: vb. (“dispose of” is common in sense 2) 1. to place or distribute, to manage, do with H5 IV. Chor. 51 , H8 I. ii. 116 “these so noble benefits . . . Not well d-'d,” Troil. IV. v. 115 “His blows are well d-'d: there, Ajax!.”

disproportion.text: to make out of proportion 3H6 III. ii. 160 “To me in every part, Like to a chaos.”

disseat.text: to unseat Mac. V. iii. 21 (F1 “dis-eate,” Ff2 3 4 “dis-ease”; many conj.).

dissembling.text: falseness, hypocrisy 3H6 III. iii. 119 ; so the ppl. adj.=false, hypocritical Err. IV. iv. 102 “ villain,” Troil. V. iv. 2 “That . . . varlet” ; fig. MND. II. ii. 98 “What . . . glass of mine.”

distemper.text: sb. (2 and 3 not pre-S.; 3 cf. DISTEMPERING) 1. ill humour, ill temper Wiv. III. iii. 230 , III. v. 80 “instigated by his ,” Wint. I. ii. 385 , Ham. III. ii. 358 “what is your cause of ?,” III. iv. 122 .

distinct.text: stressed “disti'nct” Troil. IV. v. 244 ; “di'stinct” Mer.V. II. ix. 61 , Troil. IV. iv. 45 .

distract.text: 1. to separate, divide, scatter All'sW. V. iii. 35 “to the brightest beams D-ed clouds give way,” Oth. I. iii. 328 , Ant. III. vii. 43 “Distract your army.”

divine.text: applied to a priest of a heathen religion Wint. III. i. 19 “Apollo's great divine.”

dog.text: occurs in various proverbs and comparisons, e.g. Wiv. I. iv. 118 , Mer.V. I. i. 94 , Tw.N. II. iii. 156 , 1H4 II. i. 10 , Tit. V. i. 122 ; “dogs of war” Cæs. III. i. 273 (cf. H5 I. Chor. 7 ) is a S. expression much echoed by mod. writers;—“(a) dog at,” an adept at Gent. IV. iv. 14 , Tw.N. II. iii. 66 “I am dog at a catch;—the dog's name,” applied to the letter R, which Ben Jonson says ‘is the dog's letter, and burreth in the sound’ Rom. II. iv. 225 .

dole.text: 1 (in 2H4 I. i. 169 =distribution) 1. share, portion All'sW. II. iii. 176 “what of honour Flies where you bid it.”

doom.text: sb. (1 the usual S. sense) 1. judgement, sentence R2 I. iii. 148 .

double.text: doubly, twice All'sW. II. iii. 252 , Wint. V. iii. 107 , Mac. IV. i. 83 “make assurance sure; double-fatal yew” R2 III. ii. 117 so called because it has poisonous leaves, and was used for instruments of death; with duplicity, deceitfully Rom. II. iv. 180 “deal double with her.”

dout.text: to put out, extinguish (fig.) H5 IV. ii. 11 , Ham. IV. vii. 192 (Qq Ff2 3 4 “drown(e)s”).

downright.text: adv. (in Ven. 645 ?=‘straight down,’ or ‘straightway, forthwith’) 1. positively, absolutely, out and out LLL. V. ii. 390 , Rom. III. v. 129 “It rains downright.”

dread.text: dreadful, terrible Tp. I. ii. 206 “his dread trident” ; held in awe, revered 2H6 V. i. 17 “our dread liege,” Ham. III. iv. 108 “your dread command.”

drink.text: “to ” (a person) “dead drunk, to bed,” said of the seasoned toper who sees his companions succumb to the effects of their potations Oth. II. iii. 85 , Ant. II. v. 21 .

ear.text: “about” (a person's) “e-s,” in expressions denoting severe treatment or hard measure H5 III. vii. 96 , 3H6 V. i. 108 , Rom. III. i. 87 ;—“by the ,” by hearsay All'sW. III. v. 50 ;—“by the e-s,” quarrelling, at variance (said orig. of animals) All'sW. I. ii. 1 , Cor. I. i. 239 ;—“in and ,” in everybody's ears Ham. IV. v. 94 ;—“in the ,” within hearing Ham. III. i. 193 ;—“o'er e-s,” drowned Tp. IV. i. 215 ;—“shake” (one's) “e-s,” to make the best of things (? like a dog when wet) Tw.N. II. iii. 135 , Cæs. IV. i. 26 .

earn.text: to gain deservedly or as recompense, deserve Ado III. i. 99 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 175, IV. i. 16 .

easy.text: adj. (the sense ‘not difficult, requiring little effort’ is the most freq., often with some ellipsis or condensation of expression, e.g. Cor. V. ii. 45 “the groans of old women,” Ant. III. viii. [ x. ] 41 “'Tis to 't” (= It is not a difficult journey thither), Cym. I. iv. 23 “which . . . an battery might lay flat” ; S. is earliest for sense 1 and the sense ‘loosely fitting’ All'sW. V. iii. 282 , R3 V. iii. 50 ) 1. moved without difficulty to action or belief, yielding, compliant Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 518, H5 II. ii. 125 * , H8 III. ii. 357 “good man,” Cym. II. iv. 47 “Your lady being so easy.”

ebb.text: fig. to decline, decay Tp. II. i. 230 “to , Hereditary sloth instructs me,” 234, AYL. II. vii. 73 “the . . . means do ,” Wint. V. i. 102 , Oth. III. iii. 459 ; “ebb and flow” 1H4 I. ii. 36 , Lr. V. iii. 19 .

effect.text: sb. (meaning ‘result, consequence’ is freq. and colours many exx. given below; quibbles are freq.) 1. contemplated result, purpose, end Gent. II. vii. 73 , 1H6 V. iv. 102 , Oth. I. iii. 105 ; “to ,” to the purpose Tit. IV. iii. 59 , Lr. III. i. 52 .

egal.text: equal Mer.V. III. iv. 13 , Tit. IV. iv. 4 ; so egally R3 III. vii. 212 .

eke.text: to increase, add to Mer.V. III. ii. 23 (cf. ECHE); “eke out,” to supplement AYL. I. ii. 211 , All'sW. II. v. 80 .

elbow.text: “rub the ,” show oneself pleased, chuckle LLL. V. ii. 109 , 1H4 V. i. 77 .

elder.text: older (freq.) Mer.V. IV. i. 251 “How much more art thou than thy looks!” ; more advanced, belonging to a later period R2 II. iii. 43 “ days,” Cym. V. i. 14 ;—sb. aged person 2H4 II. iv. 281 , Cæs. I. ii. 7 ; senator Cor. I. i. 232 , II. ii. 47 .

elf.text: to twist, tangle Lr. II. iii. 10 .

emballing.text: probably used in an indelicate sense; explained by comm. as ‘investing with the ball as the emblem of royalty’ H8 II. iii. 47 .

embossed.text: foaming at the mouth from exhaustion Shr. Ind. i. 17 “the poor cur is e-'d,” Ant. IV. xi. [ xiii. ] 3 “the boar of Thessaly Was never so e-'d”; cf. Tim. V. i. 222 “his embossed froth.”

enact.text: vb. (2 echoed in mod. use from S.; 3 Crowley, 1616 , has ‘enact a murder’) 1. to ordain, decree Mer.V. IV. i. 349 , 1H6 V. iv. 123 , Lucr. 529 .

enacture.text: performance, fulfilment Ham. III. ii. 209 “Their own enactures” (Qq; Ff “en(n)actors”).

encounter.text: sb. (the sense of ‘meeting, friendly or hostile’ is the common one; 1, 2, and 3 are only S.) 1. amatory meeting Wiv. III. v. 76 , Meas. III. i. 263 , Ado III. iii. 160 “this amiable ,” IV. i. 94 , All'sW. III. vii. 32 , Troil. III. ii. 217 .

end.text: sb. (some obs. or unusual phrases are given below; see also AN-END, LATTER END) 1. extremity, extreme part; “at the arm's end,” at arm's length AYL. II. vi. 10 ; “at the stave's end” Tw.N. V. i. 295 .

ending.text: vbl. sb. death John V. vii. 5 , H5 IV. i. 166 , Lucr. 1612 ; ppl. adj. dying 2H4 IV. v. 78 .

enew.text: to drive (a fowl) into the water Meas. III. i. 89 “Whose . . . deliberate word . . . follies doth As falcon doth the fowl” (Ff misprinted “emmew,” some mod. edd. “enmew”). ∥ An old hawking term.

engirt.text: surrounded, beset (lit. and fig.) 2H6 III. i. 200 “My body round with misery,” Lucr. 221 , 1173 “Grossly engirt with daring infamy.”

engraffed.text: implanted, firmly fixed Lr. I. i. 301 (Ff1 2 “ingraffed,” Qq1 2 “ingrafted”), Oth. II. iii. 146 (F1 “ingraft”); closely attached “to” 2H4 II. ii. 69 .

entail.text: to bestow as an inalienable possession 3H6 I. i. 194 “I here The crown to thee” ; to appoint (a person) heir 3H6 I. i. 235 “To him and his heirs unto the crown.”

enter.text: vb. (the ordinary physical senses occur) 1. intr. and pass. to bind oneself by a bond, &c. Err. IV. iv. 127 “I am here e-ed in bond for you,” R2 V. ii. 65 “some bond he's e-ed into” : to engage “in” Ado II. iii. 214 [ 203 ] “ into a quarrel,” Oth. III. iii. 412 “enter'd in this cause.”

entertain.text: vb. (4 the current mod. meaning of ‘amuse’ does not emerge) 1. to keep up, maintain (a state of things) Meas. III. i. 73 , Mer.V. I. i. 90 , Lucr. 1514 .

entitled.text: having a claim to or upon LLL. V. ii. 820 “Neither in the other's heart,” Sonn. xxxvii. 7 “Entitled in thy parts.” See also INTITULED.

entreat.text: vb. (the sense ‘ask earnestly’ is the usual one, and occurs with various constructions) 1. to treat R2 III. i. 37 , 2H6 II. iv. 82 , 3H6 I. i. 271 , R3 IV. iv. 152 , Troil. IV. iv. 113 .

epitheton.text: adjective indicating some characteristic quality or attribute LLL. I. ii. 15 (Q1 “apethaton,” F1 Q2 “apathaton”).

equal.text: 1. forming a perfect balance or counterpoise Meas. II. iv. 69 “ poise” (=equipoise), Mer.V. I. iii. 150 “an pound” (=an exact pound), 2H4 IV. i. 67 “ balance,” 2H6 II. i. 202 “justice' scales,” Ham. I. ii. 13 ; fig. equally balanced AYL. I. ii. 190 “a more enterprise,” Lucr. 1791 .

eringo.text: candied root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly used as a sweetmeat and regarded as an aphrodisiac Wiv. V. v. 23 .

estate.text: sb. (1 and 4 are the commonest uses) 1. state or condition Mer.V. III. ii. 317 “my is very low,” R2 III. iv. 42 , H5 IV. i. 100 “what thinks he of our ?,” Cor. II. i. 127 , Lr. V. iii. 211 “seen me in my worst ” ; Tw.N. V. i. 405 “man's ” (= manhood); spec. good or settled condition Mac. V. v. 50 .

esteem.text: to estimate the value of, value Cym. I. iv. 90 “What do you it at?”

even.text: adv. (employed in the foll. obs. or archaic uses; often contracted “e'en”) 1. in exact agreement Tw.N. V. i. 249 “as the rest goes ,” Cym. I. iv. 50 “to go with what I heard.”

evil.text: sb. 1 (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. sin, crime Meas. II. ii. 91 “to do that ,” R3 I. ii. 76 “Of these supposed e-s” (Ff “Crimes) . . . to acquit myself,” Lucr. 972 “the dire thought of his committed evil.”

example.text: vb. (2 a late 16th cent. sense) 1. to give an example of LLL. III. i. 89 , Sonn. lxxxiv. 4 .

excellent.text: surpassing, exceptionally great, exceeding (used in a bad sense) R3 IV. iv. 52 “That grand tyrant” Tit. II. iii. 7 , Lr. I. ii. 132 , Ant. I. i. 40 “ falsehood!” ;—adv. eminently, extremely Ado III. i. 98 “an good name,” Ham. II. ii. 174 .

exclaim.text: “ against,” protest against, rail at Ham. II. ii. 375 , Oth. II. iii. 316 , Lucr. 757 , Compl. 313 ; “ on,” accuse loudly, blame Mer.V. III. ii. 175 , R3 III. iii. 15 , Ven. 930 “e-s on Death,” Lucr. 741 .

excuse.text: vb. (the foll. are uses now obs.) 1. to seek to extenuate (a fault); used with a clause Err. III. i. 92 “she will well Why at this time the doors are made against you” ; absol. MND. V. i. 364 “Never excuse.”

exempt.text: cut off, debarred, excluded Err. II. ii. 175 “from me ,” AYL. II. i. 15 “ from public haunt,” 1H6 II. iv. 93 , Tim. IV. ii. 31 “from wealth ”

exempted.text: “ be from me,” far be it from me All'sW. II. i. 198 .

exile.text: stressed “exi'le”; but in attrib. use the pa. pple. is “e'xiled” Mac. V. vii. 95 [ viii. 66 ], Lucr. 640 : cf. EXHALED.

expect.forms: expect vb. (not pre-Eliz. in any sense)
expect.text: to wait for, await Gent. I. i. 54 , Mer.V. V. i. 49 , 1H6 V. iii. 144 “here I will thy coming,” Ant. IV. iv. 23 , Per. I. iv. 94 .

expiate.text: (of an appointed time) fully come R3 III. iii. 23 “the hour of death is ” (Ff2 3 4 “now expir'd,” Qq “the limit of your liues is out”).

express.text: to manifest, reveal, betoken Shr. II. i. 77 , 2H6 I. i. 18 “I can no kinder sign of love Than this kind kiss,” Cor. I. iii. 1 , Tit. I. i. 422 “hath e-'d himself . . . A father and a friend to thee,” Ham. I. iii. 71 “Costly thy habit . . . But not e-'d in fancy,” Lr. IV. iii. 19 .

exsufflicate.text: (?) puffed up, inflated, ‘windy’ Oth. III. iii. 182 .

extinct.text: extinguished, quenched R2 I. iii. 222 , Ham. I. iii. 118 “these blazes . . . in both.”

extreme.text: one third of the instances are in the superlative form “e-st”; for the stress cf. ENTIRE, LLL. V. ii. 748 “The e'xtreme part of time,” Sonn. cxxix. 4 “Savage, extre'me, rude, cruel” ;—sb. not preS. in the phrases “in the ” ( Oth. V. ii. 345 ), “in e-s” ( 3H6 III. ii. 115 ), “break into . . . e-s” ( Tit. III. i. 215 ).

eye.text: sb. (archaic pl. “eyne” 11 times for rhyme, but not rhyming in Per. III. Gower 5 , Lucr. 1229 ) 1. the organ of sight; phr. “put the finger in the eye” (like a child weeping) Err. II. ii. 208 ; phr. referring to drunkenness Tp. III. ii. 10 “thy eyes are almost set in thy head” ; fig. MND. III. ii. 435 “sorrow's eye,” Tim. V. i. 26 “opens the eyes of expectation,” Lr. IV. iv. 15 “close the eye of anguish.”

face.text: there are various transf. and fig. uses; of the heavens Mer.V. II. vii. 45 , Rom. IV. v. 41 “to see this morning's ,” Sonn. xxxiii. 6 ; of the earth R2 III. iii. 97 “the flower of England's ,” R3 V. iii. 267 “the earth's cold ” ; of immaterial things (=appearance) John V. ii. 88 “to know the face of right,” Cæs. V. i. 10 , Lr. III. i. 20 ;—phr. “from to foot” Cor. II. ii. 113 , “full of ,” (? beautiful, or florid) Per. I. Gower 23 , John V. ii. 159 “turn thy ” (=depart).

fadge.text: to fit, be suitable LLL. V. i. 158 , Tw.N. II. ii. 34 .

fading.text: ‘with a fading’ was the refrain of an indelicate song Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 195 “burthens of dildos and fadings.”

fail.text: sb. (2 and 3 only S.) 1. failure, omission Wint. II. iii. 169 “the Of any point,” V. i. 27 “fail of issue,” H8 II. iv. 196 .

fain.text: glad, pleased 1H6 III. ii. 114 “ by flight to save themselves,” 2H6 II. i. 8 “man and birds are of climbing high” ; glad under the circumstances Gent. I. i. 128 , AYL. IV. i. 61 , 2H4 II. i. 157 “I must be to pawn . . . my plate” ; (hence) necessitated, obliged Lr. IV. vii. 38 ;—adv. gladly, willingly, always with “would” (freq.).

faint.text: to lose heart John V. vii. 78 , Ven. 569 “f-s not like a pale-fac'd coward” ; also impers. “it f-s me,” I am depressed H8 II. iii. 103 ; to become feeble MND. II. ii. 35 , AYL. II. iv. 76 “f-s for succour,” Lucr. 1543 ; so 1H6 II. v. 40 “f-ing kiss,” 95 “my f-ing words.”

fair.text: that which is fair, a beautiful thing Rom. I. i. 237 “they hide the ,” I. iii. 90 , Cym. I. vi. 38 , Lucr. 780 “the supreme ” (viz. the sun); one of the fair sex, a woman, esp. a beloved woman LLL. V. ii. 37 , H5 V. ii. 176 “speak, my ,” Rom. II. Chor. 3 ; applied to a man Ven. 208 ; beauty Err. II. i. 98 “My decayed ,” LLL. IV. i. 17 , MND. I. i. 182 , Sonn. xviii. 7 “every fair from fair sometime declines.”

fall.text: sb. (of the following less frequent S. uses, 1 and 2 are only S., 3 and 4 are obs.) 1. shedding (of blood) H5 I. ii. 25 .

fame.text: common talk or report, rumour 1H6 II. iii. 68 “thou art no less than hath bruited,” H8 I. iv. 66 , Ant. II. ii. 169 ; personified Ado II. i. 223 “I have played the part of Lady Fame.”

fan.text: motion of the air such as is made by a fan Troil. V. iii. 41 “the and wind of your fair sword.”

fancy.text: to love, fall in love with Gent. III. i. 67 , Shr. II. i. 12 , 2H6 I. iii. 97 ; with a thing as object Shr. II. i. 16 ; intr. Tw.N. II. v. 30 “should she , it should be one of my complexion,” Troil. V. ii. 162 .

fang.text: canine tooth, tusk; also fig. AYL. II. i. 6 “the icy fang . . . of the winter's wind,” Tw.N. I. v. 197 “the very fangs of malice.”

fanged.text: having fangs Ham. III. iv. 203 “adders fang'”

fangled.text: fond of finery or foppery Cym. V. iv. 134 “our fangled world.”

farm.text: to rent (land) Ham. IV. iv. 20 ; to let or lease (land) R2 I. iv. 45 .

fashions.text: disease of horses closely allied to glanders Shr. III. ii. 54 .

fasten.text: to induce to accept Oth. II. iii. 51 “ but one cup upon him.”

fate.text: to destine All'sW. IV. iv. 20 ; so fated, (1) destined “to” Tp. I. ii. 129 , Lr. III. iv. 67 , Oth. III. iii. 276 ; (2) invested with the power of destiny All'sW. I. i. 236 .

father.text: the friend or relative that ‘gives away’ a bride at the altar Ado V. iv. 15 . ∥ Till recently termed ‘father-in-church’ in Warwickshire and Oxfordshire.

favoured.text: featured Cæs. I. iii. 129 ; see FAVOUR 4

fawn.text: to wag the tail with delight or fondness R3 I. iii. 290 , Cæs. V. i. 41 , Lucr. 421 “As the grim lion f-eth o'er his prey” ; fig. to wheedle, cringe (freq.).

fear.text: sb. (3 in some exx. ?=ground of alarm, as in Psalm liii. 6 (Prayer-book) ‘They were afraid where no fear was’) 1. dread, alarm, apprehension; phr. “give” or “put to,” make timid, intimidate Meas. I. iv. 62 , Ven. 1158 ; “for of trust” (= fearing to trust myself) Sonn. xxiii. 5 ; “Upon the foot of ,” in flight 1H4 V. v. 20 ; “out of ,” (i) for fear 1H4 IV. iii. 7 , (ii) without fear 1H4 IV. i. 135 “I am out of fear Of death” (cf. MND. III. i. 23 “this will put them out of fear” ).

fee.text: sb. (1 phrases derived from the sense of inheritance in land) 1. “in fee,” (to be held) in absolute possession Ham. IV. iv. 22 “should it be sold in fee; — at a pin's fee,” at a pin's value Ham. I. iv. 65 .

feed.text: feeding-ground, pasture-land AYL. II. iv. 84 “bounds of feed” ; food-fodder Tit. IV. iv. 92 [sheep] “rotted with delicious feed.”

feeding.text: food 2H4 I. i. 10 “a horse Full of high ,” Cor. V. i. 56 “wine and ,” Sonn. cxviii. 6 “To bitter sauces did I frame my ” ; pasture Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 169 ∥ Cf. FEED sb.

feeling.text: vbl. sb. (the sense ‘sensibility, susceptibility’, e.g. LLL. IV. ii. 30 , is not pre-S.; the foll. are obs. or rare) 1. experience Meas. III. ii. 129 , LLL. III. i. 120 .

fell.text: skin Lr. V. iii. 24 “flesh and ” (used quasiadv.=entirely); covering of hair or wool, fleece AYL. III. ii. 56 , Mac. V. v. 11 .

fellow.text: sb. (5 in 14th cent. implied polite condescension=‘comrade’, ‘my friend’; in S.'s time this notion had disappeared, but the word when addressed to a servant does not seem to have necessarily implied haughtiness or contempt, though its application to one not greatly inferior was a gross insult) 1. companion, associate (freq.) Tp. III. iii. 60 ; also attrib. AYL. III. ii. 378 , Ham. I. ii. 177 .

fetch.text: vb. (3 trans. from the phrase ‘fetch a blow’) 1. “ and carry,” said orig. of dogs, hence fig. to run backwards and forwards with news, tales, &c. Gent. III. i. 276 “her master's maid . . . hath more qualities than a water-spaniel . . . She can and carry.”

fever.text: to throw into a fever Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 138 “The white hand of a lady thee.”

fig.text: contemptuous gesture consisting in thrusting the thumb between two of the closed fingers or into the mouth H5 III. vi. 62 ; hence fig vb., to insult (a person) by giving him the ‘fig’ 2H4 V. iii. 121 .

fight.text: to fight one after another Tp. III. iii. 103 “I'll fight their legions o'er.”

figure.text: sb. (3 referred by some to the sense ‘horoscope, diagram of the aspects of astrological houses’) 1. distinctive shape or appearance Ado I. i. 15 “doing in the figure of a lamb the feats of a lion.”

file.text: to rub smooth with a file Tw.N. III. iii. 5 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 626; (hence) to polish, refine neatly LLL. V. i. 12 “his tongue [is] f-d,” Tit. II. i. 123 “she shall our engines with advice,” Sonn. lxxxv. 4 “precious phrase by all the Muses f-d” (Q “fil'd”); in Sonn. lxxxvi. 13 some, after Malone, read “fil'd,” but Q has “fild=filled.”

fill.text: to satiate, satisfy H5 IV. i. 289 , Tim. I. i. 271 “to see meat fill knaves,” Sonn. lvi. 5 “fill Thy hungry eyes” ; also intr. to be satiated Ven. 548 “glutton-like she feeds, yet never filleth” ; fill up, (1) to come up to the measure of, equal LLL. V. ii. 194 “How many inches do fill up one mile” ; (2) to fulfil, satisfy Mer.V. IV. i. 160 “comes . . . to fill up your Grace's request in my stead.”

film.text: fine thread, as of gossamer Rom. I. iv. 64 (F1 Qq “Philome,” others “filme”).

fine.text: sb. (3 extension of the sense ‘pecuniary mulct’) 1. end Ado I. i. 255 [ 247 ] “the is, . . . I will live a bachelor,” All'sW. IV. iv. 35 , Ham. V. i. 113 “is this the of his f-s” ; esp. in the phrase “in ,” in the end, finally All'sW. III. vii. 19 , 1H6 I. iv. 34 , Ham. II. ii. 69 , Lr. II. i. 50 ;— All'sW. IV. iv. 35 “the f-'s the crown,” probably a translation of the Latin ‘Finis coronat opus’.

finger.text: to pilfer, filch 3H6 V. i. 44 , Ham. V. ii. 15 “Finger'd their pocket.”

firstlings.text: first-fruits Troil. Prol. 27, Mac. IV. i. 147 .

fit.text: adj. (2 now only dial. exc. with ‘for’ or ‘to’) 1. of the right measure or size, well fitting Gent. IV. iv. 169 , LLL. IV. i. 50 “One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should be fit,” All'sW. I. i. 114 , Cym. IV. i. 2 “How fit his garments serve me!” ; fig. All'sW. II. ii. 21 “Will your answer serve fit to all questions?,” Ham. IV. v. 10 , Lr. I. ii. 206 “All with me's meet that I can fashion fit.”

flat.text: adj. (not very freq.; chiefly in fig. uses) 1. absolute, downright Meas. II. ii. 131 “ blasphemy,” Ado II. i. 231 “the transgression of a schoolboy,” IV. ii. 45 , John III. i. 298 ; “that's ” (not pre-S. =that's the absolute, undeniable truth LLL. III. i. 107 , 1H4 I. iii. 218 , IV. ii. 43 .

flatter.text: 1. to try to please by obsequious speech or conduct AYL. IV. i. 194 “that f-ing tongue of yours,” R2 II. i. 87 “I mock my name, great king, to thee” ; also intr. “ with” R2 II. i. 88 “Should dying men with those that live?.”

flaw.text: to make a flaw in, damage, mar H8 I. i. 95 “France hath f-'d the league,” I. ii. 21 , Lr. V. iii. 198 “his f-'d heart . . . 'Twixt two extremes of passion . . . Burst smilingly.”

fleer.text: to smile or grin contemptuously, gibe or sneer “at” Ado V. i. 58 , LLL. V. ii. 109 , Rom. I. v. 61 , Cæs. I. iii. 117 “no fleering tell-tale.”

flesh.text: vb. (the orig. meaning was ‘to reward a hawk or a hound with a piece of the flesh of the game killed to excite its eagerness in the chase’) 1. to initiate in or inure to bloodshed John V. i. 71 “ his spirit in a war-like soil,” Lr. II. ii. 50 “come, I'll flesh ye.”

flickering.text: shining with unsteady light Lr. II. ii. 114 “ Phoebus' front” (Qq1 2 printed “flitkering,” Q3 “fletkering,” Ff “flicking”).

flight.text: sb. (1 cf. ‘You must haue diuerse shaftes of one flight, fethered with diuerse winges, for diuerse windes,’ Ascham ‘Toxophilus’, 1545 ) 1. “of the self-same ,” having the same power of flight, applied to arrows of equal size and weight Mer.V. I. i. 142 .

fling.text: (2 used of animals from the 14th cent.) 1. to dash, rush Tim. IV. ii. 45 “He's flung in rage from this ingrateful sent Of monstrous friends.”

flourish.text: ostentatious embellishment, gloss, varnish LLL. II. i. 14 , IV. iii. 238 “Lend me the of all gentle tongues,” R3 I. iii. 241 , IV. iv. 82 , Ham. II. ii. 91 “since brevity is the soul of wit, And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,” V. ii. 187 .

flout.text: to quote with sarcastic purpose Ado I. i. 298 “ere you flout old ends any further.”

flow.text: vb. (pa. pple. once “flown” All'sW. II. i. 142 ) 1. to circulate Meas. I. iii. 52 “Lord Angelo . . . scarce confesses That his blood f-s,” Cym. III. iii. 93 “The princely blood flows in his cheek.”

fob.text: to cheat, deceive, delude 1H4 I. ii. 68 , Oth. IV. ii. 197 (see FOP); “ off,” (1) put off deceitfully 2H4 II. i. 39 (old edd. “fub”); (2) set aside by a trick Cor. I. i. 99 “to fob off our disgrace with a tale.”

foil.text: setting of a jewel, (hence fig.) that which sets something off to advantage R2 I. iii. 266 “as wherein thou art to set The precious jewel of thy home return,” 1H4 I. ii. 237 , R3 V. iii. 251 , Ham. V. ii. 269 “I'll be your , Laertes; in mine ignorance Your skill shall . . . Stick fiery off indeed,” Compl. 153 “the Of this false jewel” ; in Ant. I. iv. 24 Ff “foyl(e)s” is by some referred to this word, but see FOIL sb. 2 2

foin.text: thrust in fencing Lr. IV. vi. 252 ; so foin vb. Wiv. II. iii. 24 , 2H4 II. i. 19 .

fond.text: adj. (the mod. sense ‘having a strong affection or liking for’ is first recorded from S., who construes it with “of” Wint. I. ii. 164 , John III. iv. 92 , 98 , Oth. V. ii. 155 , and “on” MND. II. i. 266 , Sonn. lxxxiv. 14 ; a contemporary sense, ‘foolishly affectionate, doting’, is doubtfully represented) 1. infatuated, foolish, silly (the commonest sense in S. and in the Eliz. period, since when the literary use has been narrowed to that of ‘foolishly credulous or sanguine’).

fool.text: sb. 1 (the phrase “a to” = in every way inferior to Shr. III. ii. 160 is not pre-S.) 1. (with an adj. as “good, poor”） used as a term of endearment or pity Gent. IV. iv. 100 , Ado II. i. 328 , Tw.N. V. i. 381 , Wint. II. i. 117 , 3H6 II. v. 36 , Rom. I. iii. 31 , Lr. V. iii. 307 .

fooling.text: humour for jesting Tw.N. I. v. 35 .

foot.text: phr. “at ,” close behind Ham. IV. iii. 57 , Ant. I. v. 44 ;—“on ” (i) standing Troil. I. iii. 135 “keeps Troy on ” ; (ii) moving, astir Cor. IV. iii. 49 , Ven. 679 “when thou hast on the purblind hare” ; (iii) in active employment or operation LLL. V. ii. 755 “since love's argument was first on ;— to ,” with one's foot against one's opponent's, in close combat Ant. III. vii. 66 ;—“ and hand,” putting the foot forward and dealing a blow at the same time 1H4 II. iv. 245 ;—“set on” (one's) “,” start on one's way Cæs. II. i. 331 ;—“Upon the of fear,” in flight 1H4 V. v. 20 (cf. Mac. II. iii. 132 “Upon the of motion” ).

footing.text: (2 only S.) 1. step, tread Mer.V. V. i. 24 , Troil. I. iii. 156 , Ven. 722 ; “set ” (i) set foot, enter 2H6 III. ii. 87 , H8 III. i. 182 ; (ii) gain a footing or firm position R2 II. ii. 48 , 1H6 III. iii. 64 , Troil. II. ii. 155 .

fop.text: to fool, dupe Oth. IV. ii. 197 “to find myself fopt in it” (mod. edd. “fobbed”†).

forage.text: to range abroad for food John V. i. 59 ; to glut oneself as a wild beast, raven H5 I. ii. 110 , fig. Ven. 554 .

forbid.text: with personal object and negative clause Pilgr. ix. 8 [ 24] “She . . . Forbade the boy he should not pass those grounds.”

force.text: phrases:—“of force,” (1) of weight, weighty 1H6 III. i. 156 “those occasions . . . were of ,” 2H6 I. iii. 166 , 3H6 II. ii. 44 “arguments of mighty ” ; (2) necessarily LLL. I. i. 146 , MND. III. ii. 40 “That, when he wak'd, of force she must be eyed,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 436, 1H4 II. iii. 122 , Cæs. IV. iii. 202 “Good reasons must, of , give place to better;— perforce,” (1) by violent constraint, against one's will John III. i. 142 , 2H4 IV. i. 116 , 2H6 I. i. 259 ; (2) of necessity 2H4 IV. iv. 46 .

fore.text: prep. (in mod. edd. usually “'fore”; 1 and 2 late exx. of the senses) 1. in the presence of Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 403 “Contract us these witnesses”; in asseverations All'sW. II. iii. 51 “ God, I think so,” Cor. I. i. 126 “Fore me.”

forehand.text: “ shaft,” arrow used for shooting straight before one 2H4 III. ii. 52 ; done at an earlier time Ado IV. i. 50 “extenuate the sin;” —sb. “the ,” the upper hand or advantage H5 IV. i. 300 ; vanguard, mainstay (S.) Troil. I. iii. 143 “The sinew and the forehand of our host.”

forfeit.text: lost by reason of breach of an obligation or the like, to be given up as a penalty Meas. II. ii. 73 , LLL. V. ii. 426 , Mer.V. IV. i. 366 ; “ to,” liable to All'sW. IV. iii. 216 , Sonn. cvii. 4 .

forlorn.text: 2 adj. (“fo'rlorn” or “forlo'rn”; cf. ENTIRE) 1. (?) the same sense as in ‘forlorn hope’ Cym. V. v. 406 “The soldier, that so nobly fought.” ∥ ‘Forlorne boies,’ ‘forlorne sentinels,’ ‘forlorne fellowes’ are expressions found in the Eliz. period.

forted.text: fortified Meas. V. i. 12 “A forted residence.”

forth.text: adv. (used with “far” redundantly, in “thus far ” Tp. I. ii. 177 , “so far ” Wiv. IV. vi. 11 , “how far ” 2H4 IV. ii. 53 ) 1. forward (in movement or direction) Shr. IV. i. 149 “As he walked on his way,” H5 II. ii. 189 * “Then , dear countrymen,” Tim. I. i. 50 “flies an eagle flight, bold and on,” Cym. IV. ii. 149 “Did make my way long ” (=made it seem long).

forthcoming.text: ready to appear or to be produced when required, e.g. in court Shr. V. i. 95 , 2H6 I. iv. 56 , II. i. 177 .

forthright.text: straight path Tp. III. iii. 3 , Troil. III. iii. 158 .

fox.text: kind of sword H5 IV. iv. 9 . ∥ The wolf on some makes of sword-blade is supposed to have been mistaken for a fox.

frame.text: sb. (the sense of ‘picture frame’ is not preS., used fig. in Sonn. xxiv. 3 ) 1. ‘framing’, contrivance Ado IV. i. 191 “toil in of villanies.”

frank.text: adj. (1 is obs.; 2 now somewhat archaic) 1. unrestrained All'sW. II. iii. 61 “thy election.”

franked.text: shut up in a sty R3 I. iii. 314 , &c.

fraught.text: laden, loaded, fig. stored, filled Gent. III. ii. 70 “full with serviceable vows,” Mer.V. II. viii. 30 “A vessel . . . richly ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 527 “so with curious business,” H5 II. ii. 139 , Troil. Prol. 4, Lr. I. iv. 243 .

free.text: adj. (the foll. are the chief obs. senses) 1. of noble or honourable character, generous, magnanimous Tw.N. I. v. 281 , H8 III. i. 59 “Like and honest men,” Troil. I. iii. 235 , IV. v. 138 , Oth. II. iii. 328 “of so , so kind . . . a disposition,” III. iii. 199 “your free and noble nature.”

frequent.text: adj. (twice only in S.) 1. addicted “to” Wint. IV. i. [ ii. ] 36

fresh.text: adj. (1 cf. ‘freshman’ at a university) 1. raw, inexperienced John III. iv. 145 .

fret.text: to adorn (a ceiling) with carved or embossed work in decorative patterns Cym. II. iv. 88 “The roof o' the chamber With golden cherubins is fretted” ; fig. Ham. II. ii. 320 [ 313 ]; to chequer Cæs. II. i. 104 “yon grey lines That fret the clouds.”

friending.text: friendliness Ham. I. v. 185 “his love and ”

fro.text: =from Rom. IV. i. 75 , Cym. V. v. 262 .

from.text: prep. (the chief obs. uses are) 1. among, from among All'sW. II. i. 130 “entreating your royal thoughts A modest one,” Tim. I. ii. 96 “why have you that charitable title from thousands?.”

front.text: sb. (1 the usual S. sense) 1. forehead, (hence) face John II. i. 356 “these royal f-'s,” R3 I. i. 9 “smooth'd his wrinkled ,” Mac. IV. iii. 231 ; transf. 1H4 III. i. 14 “ of heaven” (cf. Lr. II. ii. 114 “flickering Phœbus' ” ), H5 I. Chor. 21 ; phr. Oth. I. iii. 80 “head and of my offending,” III. i. 52 “To take the saf'st occasion by the front.”

frustrate.text: frustrated Ant. V. i. 2 * ; vain Tp. III. iii. 10 “Our frustrate search.”

fumiter.text: the plant Fumaria Lr. IV. iv. 3 (Qq “femiter,” Ff incorrectly “Fenitar”); also fumitory (mod. edd.) H5 V. ii. 45 (most old edd. “femetary”).

furlong.text: “thousand f-s” opposed to “an acre” Tp. I. i. 70 , Wint. I. ii. 95 .

gage.text: vb. (3 a sense peculiar to S.) 1. to pledge, stake, risk Ham. I. i. 91 “a moiety competent Was g-d by our king,” Lucr. 144 “one for all, or all for one we gage.”

gall.text: vb. (orig. sense ‘make sore by chafing’ and fig. ‘harass, annoy’ occur; 2 is only S.) 1. to graze with a weapon, to wound, hurt Shr. V. ii. 60 , John IV. iii. 94 , H8 III. ii. 208 , Tit. IV. iii. 70 , Ham. IV. vii. 147 .

gallant.text: adj. (orig.=‘showy in appearance, smart’) 1. loosely used as a gen. epithet of praise=excellent, splendid, fine AYL. I. iii. 120 “A curtle-axe,” Wint. I. i. 42 “a child,” Cæs. IV. ii. 24 “ show” ; of a ship =noble, stately Tp. V. i. 237 .

galled.text: sore from chafing Ham. III. ii. 256 “the jade” ; fretted with salt water H5 III. i. 12 “a rock,” Lucr. 1440 “the shore” ; with tears R3 IV. iv. 53 , Ham. I. ii. 155 “her galled eyes.”

gaping.text: “ pig” * , pig's head served on the table with its mouth wide open Mer.V. IV. i. 47 , 54

geck.text: fool Tw.N. V. i. 355 , Cym. V. iv. 67 . ∥ Survives in midl. dial.; used by George Eliot in ‘Adam Bede’ ix.

general.text: 1. all, all collectively, whole 1H4 III. ii. 178 “Our forces,” 1H6 IV. iv. 3 “all our force,” Troil. V. ii. 129 “the sex” (=all womenkind), Lr. I. iv. 65 , Oth. III. iii. 346 “the general camp.”

gentle.text: adj. (the senses ‘well born’, ‘kind’, ‘not violent, mild’ are well represented in S.) 1. used in polite address or as a complimentary epithet Gent. I. ii. 14 “What think'st thou of the Proteus?,” II. i. 118 “I thank you, servant,” III. i. 14 “your daughter,” Cæs. III. ii. 78 “You gentle Romans.”

german.text: adj. and sb. (“cousin-german” = first cousin Troil. IV. v. 120 ) 1. closely related, akin Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 805 (Ff “Iermain(e),” Tim. IV. iii. 345 (Ff “Germa(i)ne”).

gest.text: pl. deeds Ant. IV. viii. 2 (old edd. “guests”).

ghost.text: sb. (the mod. use is the prevailing one) 1. incorporeal being, spirit Sonn. lxxxvi. 9 .

gig.text: (?) to walk wantonly Ham. III. i. 152 (so Q 1604; F “gidge,” Q 1676 “jig”).

gimmaled.text: made with gimmals or joints, consisting of two similar parts hinged together H5 IV. ii. 49 “the bit” (Ff “Iymold,” mod. edd. “gimmal”).

gird.text: sharp or biting remark Shr. V. ii. 58 ; so gird vb. intr. 2H4 I. ii. 6 , trans. Cor. I. i. 262 .

glad.text: gladness Per. II. Gower 38 . ∥ An archaism; not in current use after 1450

glance.text: 1. (of a weapon) to glide off an object struck Wiv. V. v. 261 [ 249 ] “your arrow hath g-d”; fig. Shr. V. ii. 61 “the jest did away from me,” Lr. V. iii. 150 ; “ on,” to strike obliquely upon and turn aside Per. III. iii. 7 .

gleek.text: gibe, jest 1H6 III. ii. 123 , Rom. IV. v. 115 ; so gleek vb. MND. III. i. 154 , H5 V. i. 78 .

gloze.text: vb. (orig.=to make glosses upon) 1. to interpret (a thing) to be (so and so) H5 I. ii. 40 “Which Salique land the French unjustly To be the realm of France.”

gnaw.text: pa. pple. “gnawn” Wiv. II. ii. 311 “my reputation gnawn at.”

gossip.text: 1. a child's godfather or godmother, sponsor (always with ref. to their relation to the parents) Gent. III. i. 270 “'tis not a maid, for she hath had g-s” (i.e. for a child of hers), Wint. II. iii. 41 “About some g-s for your highness,” H8 V. v. 13 “My noble g-s” (=sponsors to Princess Elizabeth).

goujere.text: incorrect spelling of GOOD YEAR in mod. edd.

grace.text: sb. (1 “do grace” occurs also in the sense ‘do a kindness, confer a favour’ cf. 3; 5 is only S. and is an extension of the religious sense ‘favour of God’) 1. “do” (a person or thing) “,” reflect credit on, set in a good light, embellish 1H4 II. i. 79 “to do the profession some ,” V. iv. 161 “if a lie may do thee ,” Ham. I. i. 131 , Sonn. xxviii. 10 , cxxxii. 11 “mourning doth thee ;—in of,” in honour of MND. IV. i. 140 .

graff.text: to insert a graft in (a stock) AYL. III. ii. 126 “ it with a medlar,” 2H4 V. iii. 3 “pippin of my own g-ing,” 2H6 III. ii. 214 “stock Was graft with crab-tree slip,” R3 III. vii. 126 .

graft.text: vb. (‘graft’ as a sb. does not occur) 1. to fix, implant, or attach, as one does a graft or scion All'sW. I. ii. 54 , Wint. I. ii. 246 “A servant g-ed in my serious trust,” R2 III. iv. 101 “the plants thou g-'st,” 1H4 III. ii. 15 “Such . . . rude society, As thou art . . . grafted to,” Mac. IV. iii. 51 .

grained.text: ingrained Ham. III. iv. 90 “such black and spots” ; furrowed, lined Err. V. i. 313 “this face of mine.”

grasp.text: vb. (2 not pre-S.) 1. to clutch 2H6 III. ii. 172 “g-'d And tugg'd for life.”

grate.text: grating 1H6 I. iv. 10 , 60 ; barred place of confinement Wiv. II. ii. 9 “looked through the , like a geminy of baboons.”

gratulate.text: to greet, salute R3 IV. i. 10 “To the gentle princes,” Tim. I. ii. 133 ; to express joy at Tit. I. i. 221 “gratulate his safe return.”

graze.text: to abrade in passing Oth. IV. i. 279 “neither nor pierce” ; to ricochet H5 IV. iii. 105 (F2 “grasing,” F1 Qq “crasing”).

green.text: adj. (“a eye” is regarded as a point of beauty MND. V. i. 343 , Rom. III. v. 222 ） 1. said of the sea, and hence of Neptune, Tp. V. i. 43 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 28, Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 58

grey.text: hoary, ancient 1H4 II. iv. 506 [ 499 ] “that iniquity.” ∥ In its application to the colour of eyes “grey” is supposed by some, e.g. Malone, to mean what we now call ‘blue’.

gripe.text: vb. (commonly said of grief in the 16th cent.) 1. to clutch or grasp “at” Per. I. i. 49 .

gross.text: adj. (the senses ‘glaring, flagrant’ and ‘coarse’ are common) 1. big, bulky Wiv. III. iii. 42 “this watery pumpion,” Lr. IV. vi. 14 “The crows . . . Show scarce so as beetles” : with quibble in Ado V. i. 168 “a great one,” 1H4 II. iv. 254 “[lies] as a mountain.”

ground.text: sb. (2 is freq.; many quibbles occur between literal and figurative meanings) 1. the bottom of the sea or other water 1H4 I. iii. 204 “Where fathom-line could never touch the ” ; the bottom where the water becomes too shallow for a vessel to float 2H4 IV. i. 17 “touch And dash themselves to pieces,” IV. iv. 40 “on ” (=aground).

grudge.text: “ one thought,” have one envious thought 1H6 III. i. 175 .

grudging.text: =GRUDGE sb. Ado III. iv. 89 “he eats his meat without ” ; so grudging ppl. adj., unwilling, reluctant 1H6 IV. i. 141 “their stomachs.”

guard.forms: guard sb. (other S. uses than those below are
