guard.text: ‘protection, defence,’ ‘posture of defence,’ ‘watch,’ ‘protector, defender’) 1. keeping, guardianship, custody Err. V. i. 149 “He broke from those that had the of him,” Mer.V. I. iii. 176 “in the fearful Of an unthrifty knave,” Cor. I. x. 25 (‘under the protection of my brother’), Lr. V. iii. 1 , 48 , Ant. V. ii. 67 “I'll take her to my ”

gull.text: unfledged bird 1H4 V. i. 60 “that ungentle , the cuckoo's bird,” Tim. II. i. 31 “a naked ” ∥ Now used in Worcestershire and Warwickshire dial. for a gosling.

gust.text: taste, liking, relish Tw.N. I. iii. 34 “the he-hath in quarrelling,” Tim. III. v. 55 * “sin's extremest ,” Sonn. cxiv. 11 .

gyve.text: to fetter, shackle Oth. II. i. 171 (Ff1 3 4 “giue,” Qq “catch”).

hack.text: of uncertain meaning in Wiv. II. i. 52 , IV. i. 69 ; the context suggests some indelicate ref. (cf. HACKNEY).

hand.forms: hand sb. (the foll. obs. uses of phrases are found) 1. with preps.
hand.text: “at ,” (i) at the beginning, at the start Cæs. IV. ii. 23 “like horses hot at ” ; (ii) by hand John V. ii. 75 “a lion foster'd up at ;—at” or “in any , of all h-s,” in any case LLL. IV. iii. 219 “Therefore, of all h-s must we be forsworn,” Shr. I. ii. 150 “see that at any ,” 229, All'sW. III. vi. 44 “in any ;—by this , by” one's own or another's “,” used freq. in asseverations Tp. III. ii. 57 “by this , I will supplant some of your teeth,” AYL. III. ii. 420 “by the white of Rosalind,” All'sW. III. vi. 75 , 2H6 V. iii. 29 “by my , lords, 'twas a glorious day,” Troil. IV. i. 22 “By Venus' I swear,” Cor. IV. v. 156 , Ven. 80 ; also “for my ” Shr. I. i. 193 ; “in” one's “,” led or held by one John II. i. 236 , R3 IV. i. 2 , H8 V. iii. 22 , Cor. V. iii. 23 , Tit. V. iii. 138 ; “brief in ,” shortly to be dispatched John IV. iii. 158 ; “in with,” occupied or engaged with Ven. 912 “In with all things, nought at all effecting;—of” one's “h-s,” in respect of one's actions or valour in fight Wiv. I. iv. 27 , Wint. V. ii. 186 [ 178 ] “a tall fellow of thy h-s,” &c., 2H4 II. ii. 74 ; “out of ,” (i) at once 1H6 III. ii. 102 , 3H6 IV. vii. 63 , Tit. V. ii. 77 ; (ii) done with 2H4 III. i. 107 “were these inward wars once out of ;—unto thy ,” ready for thee Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 29

hang.text: (pa. t. and pa. pple. “hung,” except in the sense ‘put to death by hanging’, in which “hanged” is usual; in MND. V. i. 367 Qq “hanged,” Ff “hung”; in AYL. III. ii. 183 , Cym. II. iv. 68 , Pilgr. xiv. 3 [ 183 ] “hanged” is used for “hung):—hang off,” leave go MND. III. ii. 260 ; “hang up,” hang on a gibbet LLL. IV. iii. 54 “love's Tyburn, that h-s up simplicity,” Rom. III. iii. 56 .

hanging.text: gloomy Meas. IV. ii. 35 “a hanging look.”

hangings.text: fruit on a tree Cym. III. iii. 63 “my mellow hangings.”

happy.text: adj. 1. propitious, favourable; phr. “in time” Shr. Ind. i. 90 , All'sW. V. i. 6 , Cæs. II. ii. 60 , Ham. V. ii. 214 , Oth. III. i. 32 ; “in a hour” Ado IV. i. 288 ; “in very season” 2H4 IV. ii. 79 ; all meaning ‘at an appropriate moment, in time’; also Rom. III. v. 112 “in happy time” =a propos.

harbour.text: to lodge; trans. Err. I. i. 136 “any place that h-s men,” Tw.N. II. iii. 106 “she h-s you as her kinsman,” John II. i. 262 ; intr. Gent. III. i. 140 , R2 I. i. 195 , 3H6 IV. vii. 79 .

hard.text: adj. (the ordinary lit. and fig. meanings occur) 1. hardened, obdurate Tim. IV. iii. 270 , Mac. III. iv. 143 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 111 “when we in our viciousness grow hard.”

harlock.text: see HARDOCK. ∥ Actually recorded once, from Drayton's Dowsabel.

harsh.text: （‘rough to the ear’ and ‘rude, roughly offensive’ are the commoner S. meanings) 1. unpleasantly rough (i) to the touch Troil. I. i. 60 , (ii) to the taste (fig.) Oth. V. ii. 114 .

hatch.text: (2 chiefly “under” or “beneath the h-es,” which is now associated with the mod. sense of ‘grated framework covering the hatchway’) 1. half-door, gate or wicket with an open space above Err. III. i. 33 , John I. i. 171 “In at the window, or else o'er the ” (=born irregularly), V. ii. 138 “take” (=jump over) “the hatch,” Lr. III. vi. 76 .

hatched.text: closed with a hatch Per. IV. ii. 37 .

haught.text: haughty R2 IV. i. 254 “thou insulting man,” 2H6 I. iii. 71 (F1 “haughtie”), R3 II. iii. 28 “ and proud.”

haunt.text: trans. to frequent the company of, accompany or follow persistently Err. III. ii. 83 , MND. II. ii. 85 “do not me thus,” 1H4 II. iv. 498 , Troil. IV. i. 10 “how Diomed . . . Did you in the field” ; intr. to resort habitually, remain continually Mac. I. vi. 9 , Oth. I. i. 96 “to about my doors,” Compl. 130 “following where he haunted.”

having.text: possession, property, wealth, estate Wiv. III. ii. 76 “The gentleman is of no ,” AYL. III. ii. 401 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 743, H8 II. iii. 23 “Our content Is our best ,” Cym. I. ii. 20 ; also pl. H8 III. ii. 160 ; in Oth. IV. iii. 94 “our ” * = our allowance of expense (J.); fig. endowments, ‘gifts’, accomplishments Troil. III. iii. 97 , Compl. 235 .

hawk.text: in Ham. II. ii. 406 [ 397 ] commonly taken to be the bird (cf. HANDSAW), but perhaps a variant of ‘hack’, which was applied to various tools of the mattock, hoe, and pickaxe type.

hawking.text: ‘hawk-like, keen’ (Schmidt) All'sW. I. i. 106 “his hawking eye.”

hay.text: country dance having a winding or serpentine movement LLL. V. i. 166 .

hazard.text: (2 the prevailing sense; 4 cf. ‘Pelouse . . . the lower hazard in a tennis-court’ Cotgr.) 1. game at dice at which the chances are complicated by a number of arbitrary rules H5 III. vii. 98 ; hence fig. “come” or “go to ,” to run extreme risks Mer.V. II. ix. 18 , H5 III. vii. 98 .

head.text: sb. (the chief idiomatic, technical, and special uses are the foll.) 1. put for ‘ears’ LLL. IV. iii. 336 “When the suspicious of theft is stopp'd,” Troil. IV. v. 5 , Per. II. iii. 97 “Loud music is too harsh for ladies' heads” ; for ‘mouth’ Cym. V. v. 158 “Those” [viands] “which I heav'd to head”; = the mod. ‘face’ in the phr. “to” (one's) “head” Meas. IV. iii. 151 , Ado. V. i. 62 , MND. I. i. 106 .

heap.text: sb. (3 a late ex. of this sense; cf. Coverdale, Ezekiel xxxviii. 22 ‘vpon him and all his heape’) 1. phr. “on heaps, on a heap,” in a fallen or prostrate mass, prostrate, in ruins H5 V. ii. 39 “all her husbandry doth lie on h-s,” Tit. II. iii. 223 “Lord Bassianus lies . . . All on a ,” Tim. IV. iii. 101 “laid proud Athens on a heap.”

heat.text: heated John IV. i. 61 “Theiron . . . red-hot” ; ? in Tw.N. I. i. 26 * “till seven years ” (?=heated for seven years by the sun's rays).

heave.text: pa. t. and pa. pple always “heaved”; the meaning ‘utter’ (a groan, word) is not pre-S., AYL. II. i. 36 “h-'d forth such groans,” Lr. IV. iii. 27 “heav'd the name of ‘father’ Pantingly forth.”

hebenon.text: (?) yew, which was notorious for its poisonous properties Ham. I. v. 62 “juice of cursed ” ∥ So ‘iouyce of Hebon’, Marlowe ‘Jew of Malta’ III.

heel.text: in phr. referring to (1) flight or speed Err. I. ii. 94 “I'll take my h-s,” Mer.V. II. ii. 32 “my h-s are at your commandment,” AYL. III. ii. 295 “You have a nimble wit: I think 'twas made of Atalanta's h-s,” 1H4 II. iv. 52 “show it a fair pair of h-s,” Mac. I. ii. 30 “to trust their h-s” ; (2) punishment in the stocks All'sW. IV. iii. 119 “his h-s have deserved it,” 2H4 I. ii. 142 “To punish you by the h-s;—out at h-s,” in unfortunate or decayed circumstances, in trouble or distress Wiv. I. iii. 32 , Lr. II. ii. 164 .

helm.text: to steer, fig. Meas. III. ii. 155 .

help.forms: help vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. “helped,” but more often “holp”)
help.text: to relieve, cure, remedy Tp. II. ii. 102 “I will his ague,” Gent. IV. ii. 48 “To him of his blindness,” Rom. I. ii. 49 “Turn giddy, and be holp by backward turning,” Lr. IV. iv. 10 , Lucr. 1822 “Do wounds help wounds?.”

hent.text: in Ham. III. iii. 88 * “Up, sword, and know thou a more horrid hent” it is doubtful whether we have the sense of ‘clutch, grasp’ or of ‘intention, design’, or whether “hent” is for HINT in its S. sense.

herald.text: sb. (in old edd. also “herauld, -ault, har(r)old”) 1. officer having the duty of (i) making proclamations 2H6 IV. ii. 190 , (ii) bearing messages between princes and hostile forces John. II. i. 325 , H5 III. v. 36 , Troil. I. iii. 218 , (iii) conveying challenges H8 I. i. 34 , Lr. V. i. 48 , (iv) arranging public processions, funerals, &c. 1H6 I. i. 45 , Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 145 “the most noble corse that ever Did follow to his urn,” (v) regulating the use of armorial bearings Shr. II. i. 223 “A , Kate? O! put me in thy books,” Lucr. 206 “Some loathsome dash the herald will contrive.”

hewgh.text: imitation of a whistling sound Lr. IV. vi. 94 (Qq “hagh”).

high.text: All'sW. II. i. 12 * “higher Italy,” (?) the Italian nobility; Tim. IV. iii. 246 “at high wish,” at the height of one's desires; Cæs. II. i. 110 “the high east,” the exact east.

hind.text: 2 (2 occurs more frequently than 1) 1. servant Wiv. III. v. 101 , AYL. I. i. 20 .

hinge.text: to bend Tim. IV. iii. 212 “ thy knee.”

hip.text: “on” or “upon the hip,” at a disadvantage Mer.V. I. iii. 47 , IV. i. 335 , Oth. II. i. 317 .

history.text: sb. (in Per. V. i. 119 almost=life-story) 1. narrative, tale, story Tw.N. II. iv. 111 , 3H6 V. vi. 28 “that tragic ,” R3 III. v. 27 “The of all her secret thoughts,” Ham. III. ii. 314 , Oth. I. iii. 139 “in my travel's history,” Cym. III. v. 99 .

hive.text: sb. (the ordinary sense occurs 5 times) 1. hived swarm 2H6 III. ii. 125 “an angry of bees.”

hoar.text: to become mouldy Rom. II. iv. 147 “When it hoars ere it be spent” ; to smite with ‘hoar leprosy’ (S.) Tim. IV. iii. 156 .

hoise.text: （“hoist” is also used by S.) 1. to hoist (sail) R3 IV. iv. 528 .

hold.text: vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. usually “held”; pa. pple. once “holden” 2H6 II. iv. 71 , once HILD, q.v.) A.. Transitive meanings:— 1. to endure, bear Cor. III. ii. 80 “the ripest mulberry That will not the handling,” Tim. I. ii. 161 , Ham. V. i. 181 “many pocky corses . . . that will scarce the laying in.”

holla.text: =stop! cease! AYL. III. ii. 259 “Cry ‘holla!’ to thy tongue,” Oth. I. ii. 56 “Holla! stand there!,” Ven 284; used to excite attention LLL. V. ii. 898 “Holla! approach,” Shr. IV. i. 12 “Holla, ho! Curtis,” Ham. I. i. 18 “Holla! Bernardo!” ; used to express surprise Tit. II. i. 25 “Holla, what storm is this?” (Qq F1 “Hollo”), Lr. V. iii. 72 “Holla, holla!.”

hollow.text: insincerely, falsely Tw.N. III. iv. 103 ; so hollowly Tp. III. i. 70 , Meas. II. iii. 23 , hollowness insincerity Lr. I. ii. 126 . ∥ The corresponding meaning of the adj. is common.

hood.text: to blindfold (a hawk) when it is not pursuing game; always fig. H5 III. vii. 126 “'tis a h-ed valour; and when it appears, it will bate,” Rom. III. ii. 14 (see BATE vb. 1 ).

hoop.text: vb. 2 (mod. edd. mostly “whoop”) 1. to shout with astonishment AYL. III. ii. 204 “and yet again wonderful! and after that, out of all h-ing,” H5 II. ii. 108 “admiration did not at them.”

hope.text: 1. “out of ,” (i) without hope Tp. III. iii. 11 , Shr. V. i. 147 ; (ii) not merely hoping MND. III. ii. 279 ; (iii) past hope Ven. 567 “Things out of ” ; (iv) in hopes H8 Prol. 8, Cor. IV. v. 85 .

house.text: “keep (the) ,” stay indoors, remain at home Meas. III. ii. 77 , Cym. III. iii. 1 “A goodly day not to keep ” ; so Tim. III. iii. 42 “Who cannot keep his wealth must keep his ” (=stay at home and look after it); cf. AYL. IV. iii. 83 “the doth keep itself,” Cym. III. vi. 36 “Poor , that keep'st thyself!” (i.e. that is empty).

housekeeping.text: hospitality LLL. II. i. 104 , Shr. II. i. 350 [ 358 ], 2H6 I. i. 192 .

howbeit.text: nevertheless H5 I. ii. 91 , Cor. I. ix. 70 ;—conj. although Oth. II. i. 300 .

humour.text: vb. (not pre-S.; used nonsensically in Wiv. I. iii. 61 , II. i. 132 ; cf. note on prec. sb.) 1. to comply with the humour of, indulge; also, to influence (a person) by observing his humours or inclinations Err. IV. iv. 83 , Ado II. i. 399 , LLL. IV. ii. 52 , 2H4 V. i. 79 , Cæs. I. ii. 320 .

hundredth.text: Wiv. II. i. 63 “the Hundredth Psalm” † (old edd. “the hundred Psalms”).

hurricano.text: waterspout Troil. V. ii. 169 “the dreadful spout Which shipmen do the call,” Lr. III. ii. 2 “You cataracts and h-es.” ∥ In this sense otherwise only in Drayton (? copying S.) ‘downe the shower impetuously doth fall, Like that which men the Hurricano call’, Moon-Calfe, 1627

hurry.text: is used trans. and intr.; in John V. i. 35 * trans. or intr. according as “up and down” is taken as adv. or as prep.; Per. IV. i. 20 “Hurrying me from my friends” (Qq1 2 3 “whirring”).

husband.text: sb. (cf. the senses of HUSBANDRY) 1. one who manages a household 2H4 V. iii. 11 (Ff3 4 “husbandman”).

idle.text: 1. ineffective, worthless, vain, trifling LLL. V. ii. 873 “your scorns,” MND. III. ii. 168 “waste more breath,” Tw.N. III. iii. 46 “ markets” (= for articles of fancy or luxury), Tim. I. ii. 162 “an banquet,” IV. iii. 27 “I am no votarist,” Oth. I. ii. 95 “Mine's not an idle cause.”

ill.text: sb. (is used only in the foll. senses) 1. wrong-doing, wickedness, sin Tp. I. ii. 353 “capable of all ill,” R2 I. i. 86 “So much as of a thought of ill in him,” Oth. IV. iii. 106 “The ills we do,” Lucr. 91 “Whose inward ill no outward harm express'”

illustrate.text: illustrious LLL. IV. i. 65 , V. i. 132 .

image.text: (2 and 4 were 16-17th cent. senses) 1. appearance semblance, likeness Wint. V. i. 127 “Your father's is so hit in you,” John IV. ii. 71 “The of a wicked heinous fault,” Ham. V. ii. 77 “by the image of my cause I see The portraiture of his.”

immure.text: spelt “emure” in LLL. III. i. 131 , IV. iii. 328 (Qq F1).

imp.text: properly a term of falconry, to engraft feathers in the wing of a bird so as to make good losses and deficiencies and thus restore or improve the powers of flight R2 II. i. 292 “Imp out our drooping country's broken wing.”

impeach.text: to call in question, discredit, disparage MND. II. i. 214 “You do your modesty,” Mer.V. III. ii. 279 , III. iii. 29 , R2 I. i. 189 .

impone.text: (?) intended to suggest an affected pronunciation of ‘impawn’ = to stake, wager Ham. V. ii. 155 (Qq “impawned, impaund”), 171

importing.text: significant, meaning All'sW. V. iii. 136 “her business looks in her With an visage.”

impose.text: vb. (2 not post-S.) 1. to lay (an imputation) “upon” H5 IV. i. 159 .

imposthume.text: purulent swelling, abscess Troil. V. i. 24 , Ham. IV. iv. 27 , Ven. 743 .

impress.text: enforced levy Troil. II. i. 107 , Ham. I. i. 75 , Ant. III. vii. 36 .

incaged.text: caged, confined R2 II. i. 102 , 3H6 IV. vi. 12 , Ven. 582 .

inch.text: “the furthest inch,” the most distant part Ado II. i. 277 ; “the very extremest inch,” the very utmost 2H4 IV. iii. 39 ; “at an inch,” in immediate readiness 2H6 I. iv. 45 ; “even to his inches,” from top to toe Troil. IV. v. 111 . ∥ S. is the earliest authority for “inches”=stature Ant. I. iii. 40 , and the fig. phr. “by inches” Cor. V. iv. 43 .

inclining.text: party, following (cf. prec.) Oth. I. ii. 82 .

incorporate.text: 1. united in one body, closely united or combined, intimately bound up (with) MND. III. ii. 208 , Cor. I. i. 136 “my friends,” Tit. I. i. 462 “I am in Rome,” Cæs. I. iii. 135 “one To our attempts,” Ven. 540 .

increase.text: to cause to thrive Cor. IV. v. 236 * .

indifferent.text: tolerably, fairly Shr. I. ii. 184 , Tw.N. I. iii. 145 , H5 IV. vii. 35 , Ham. III. i. 126 .

infect.text: to affect “with” some feeling Wint. I. ii. 262 “a fear Which oft i-s the wisest,” John IV. iii. 69 “Never to be i-ed with delight,” Cor. V. v. [ vi. ] 72 “infected with my country's love.”

inly.text: inward(ly) Tp. V. i. 200 “I have wept,” Gent. II. vii. 18 “the inly touch of love.”

inquire.text: in old edd. “enquire, enquier”; 3 syll. in Shr. I. ii. 169 “I pro'mis'd to' enqui're ca'refully'.”

insanie.text: madness LLL. V. i. 28 “it insinuateth me of ” (old edd. “infamie”). ∥ The word is otherwise known only from one other author.

insisture.text: (a) steady continuance in their path, (b) persistency, (c) regularity Troil. I. iii. 87 .

instant.text: 1. now present, existing, happening All'sW. IV. iii. 128 , H8 I. i. 225 “this cloud,” Troil. III. iii. 153 “Take the way,” Cor. V. i. 37 “the army we can make.”

irrecoverable.text: not to be recovered or redeemed 2H4 II. iv. 360 .

issue.text: sb. (the usual S. meanings are ‘offspring, progeny’ and ‘event, result, consequence’; 1 is not pre-S.; 2 is peculiar to S.) 1. outcome, product (“of” a practice or condition) All'sW. II. i. 109 , John III. iv. 21 “the of your peace,” Troil. II. ii. 89 , Lr. I. i. 18 .

jade.text: 1. ‘sorry,’ ill-conditioned horse Meas. II. i. 276 [ 269 ] “let carman whip his jade,” H5 IV. ii. 46 , Ham. III. ii. 256 “let the galled jade wince” ; vicious horse (allusively) Ado I. i. 151 “You always end with a jade's trick,” Shr. I. ii. 252 “give him head: I know he'll prove a jade,” All'sW. IV. v. 64 , Troil. II. i. 21 .

jar.text: vb. (2 cf. JAR sb. 2) 1. to make a musical discord, be out of tune Gent. IV. ii. 68 , Shr. III. i. 40 “the treble jars” ; in fig. context Shr. V. ii. 1 “our jarring notes agree,” All'sW. I. i. 188 “His jarring concord,” 2H6 II. i. 57 “When such strings jar,” Lr. IV. vii. 16 “The untun'd and jarring senses.”

jaunce.text: =JAUNT sb. Rom. II. v. 26 (Qq23 “iaunce,” Ff Qq4 5 “iaunt, jaunt”). ∥ Perhaps only a misprint for “iaunte”; recorded otherwise only as in mod. Sussex dial.

jaunt.text: running up and down or to and fro, ‘trotting’ or trudging about Rom. II. v. 26 ; so jaunt vb. Rom. II. v. 53 ; cf. JAUNCE sb. and vb.

jest.text: sb. (the meaning ‘object of ridicule’ Wiv. III. iii. 161 is not pre-S.) 1. merriment, jocosity Ham. V. i. 203 .

jet.text: to encroach “upon” Err. II. ii. 28 “Your sauciness will jet† upon my love” (F1 “iest”), R3 II. iv. 51 “tyranny begins to jet” (Ff “Iutt, jut) Upon the . . . throne,” Tit. II. i. 64 “to jet” (Qq “iet,” Ff “set) upon a prince's right.”

jig.text: sb. (3 cf. Cotgr. s.v. ‘Farce,’ ‘the Iyg at the end of an Enterlude, wherein some pretie knauerie is acted’） 1. lively, rapid kind of dance Ado II. i. 79 “hot and hasty, like a Scotch jig,” Tw.N. I. iii. 140 “My very walk should be a jig” ; music for such a dance, rapid, lively dance-tune LLL. IV. iii. 168 “to tune a jig.”

jigging.text: Cæs. IV. iii. 136 “these fools,” ‘these foolish writers of doggerel’ (Wright); cf. JIG sb. 2, 3

joy.text: 1. to gladden, delight R3 I. ii. 220 “it joys me,” Cym. V. v. 425 “Joy'd are we,” Per. I. ii. 9 .

jump.text: vb. (unexplained in [ Wint IV. iii. iv. ] 195) 1. to agree, tally, coincide Mer.V. II. ix. 32 “ with common spirits,” Shr. I. i. 194 “meet and in one,” Tw.N. V. i. 262 “cohere and ,” 1H4 I. ii. 78 “it j-s with my humour,” R3 III. i. 11 .

just.text: in replies and expressions of assent= exactly so, just so, right! Meas. III. i. 66 , V. i. 196 [ 202 ], Ado II. i. 29 , AYL. III. ii. 282 “Rosalind is your love's name?—Yes, just,” All'sW. II. iii. 21 , H5 III. vii. 163 , Tit. IV. ii. 24 “O! 'tis a verse in Horace . . . —Ay just, a verse in Horace.”

jutty.text: to project beyond, overhang (S.) H5 III. i. 13 “O'erhang and jutty his confounded base.”

keep.text: vb. (3 freq. in literary use c. 1580-1630) 1. refl. to restrain oneself Gent. IV. iv. 12 .

ken.text: sb. (1 Bourne, 1574, says that a ken is 6 or 9 leagues; Leland, 1538, has ‘a Kenning, that is to say about a xx miles,’ Botoner, 15th cent., ‘quilibet kennyng continet 21 miliaria’) 1. the distance that bounds the range of ordinary vision, esp. at sea; about 20 miles 2H4 IV. i. 151 “within a ken our army lies,” Cym. III. vi. 6 “Thou wast with in a ken.”

kennel.text: street gutter Shr. IV. iii. 98 , 2H6 IV. i. 71 .

kind.text: sb. (the foll. and the sense ‘sort, species’ are all the S. uses; 1 was common down to about 1600; 3 common in the 17th cent., freq. in S.) 1. natural disposition or character, nature AYL. IV. iii. 60 “thy youth and kind” (=thy youthful nature), Lucr. 1147 “to change their k-s;—of its own kind,” of itself, naturally Tp. II. i. 170 ; “do his kind,” act according to its nature Ant. V. ii. 263 .

kindle.text: to incite (cf. ENKINDLE) AYL. I. i. 182 .

kindly.text: adj. ( AYL. II. iii. 53 * (a) natural, proper, (b) agreeable, pleasant; 2H4 IV. v. 82 k. * tears (a) natural, not forced, (b) naturally shed for a father; cf. sense 2) 1. innate, inherent Tim. II. ii. 227 “ warmth.”

knee.text: part of the body used in kneeling or curtseying; hence, kneeliing, prostration, curtsey R2 II. iii. 83 , 1H4 IV. iii. 68 “with cap and knee,” Cor. V. iii. 57 “Your knees to me!,” Tim. III. vi. 108 “Cap and knee slaves,” IV. iii. 36 “give them title, knee, and approbation,” Oth. II. i. 84 .

knit.text: to tie in or with a knot John IV. i. 42 “I my handkercher about your brows” ; usu. transf. or fig. to bind, pin, or unite firmly or closely MND. I. i. 172 “that which knitteth souls” ; also knit up (in various senses) Tp. III. iii. 89 “all up In their distractions,” MND. V. i. 194 “Thy stones with lime and hair up,” Rom. IV. ii. 25 “I'll have this knot up.”

knock.text: the foll. uses are not recorded before S.:—to drive by striking Tp. III. ii. 71 “ a nail into his head;— off” Cym. V. iv. 198 ; “ out” 1H6 III. i. 83 ; “ it” (=strike up) H8 I. iv. 108 “Let the music knock it.”

knot.text: sb. (said fig. of the marriage tie, e.g. R3 IV. iii. 42 ; 2 survives in midl. and south-west dial.) 1. folded arms Tp. I. ii. 224 , Tit. III. ii. 4 .

know.text: “have known (together),” have been acquainted (S.) Ant. II. vi. 83 , Cym. I. iv. 38 ; “more known,” better acquainted Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 66; “be not you known on't,” have no knowledge of it Oth. III. iii. 320 (Ff “acknown(e)”; know for, be aware of 2H4 I. ii. 5 ; know of, ascertain from Meas. I. iv. 8 , MND. I. i. 68 , Lr. V. i. 1 , Oth. V. i. 117 .

knowing.text: (2 is peculiar to S.) 1. knowledge Tim. III. ii. 75 “in My ,” Ham. V. ii. 44 (Qq) “on the view and of these contents,” Cym. I. iv. 31 “gentlemen of your ,” II. iii. 102 .

label.text: slip of paper Cym. V. v. 431 ; slip of paper or parchment for appending a seal to a document (fig.) Rom. IV. i. 57 . ∥ The sense ‘codicil’ is represented in S. in the vb.

labour.text: vb. (the ordinary uses are freq.) 1. to endeavour to bring about, work for or with a view to Ado V. i. 296 , Shr. I. i. 119 “to and effect one thing,” R3 I. iv. 256 “he would my delivery.”

labouring.text: heaving, palpitating 2H6 III. ii. 163 “the heart” ; rolling or pitching heavily Oth. II. i. 190 “the labouring bark.”

lace.text: to trim with ornamental (gold or silver) braid Ado III. iv. 20 “l-d with silver” ; fig. to streak or stripe “with” golden (or other) colour Rom. III. v. 8 “envious streaks Do the severing clouds,” Mac. II. iii. 119 “His silver skin l-'d with his golden blood,” Cym. II. ii. 22 “white and azure l-'d with blue of heaven's own tinct” ; to trick out, adorn Sonn. lxvii. 4 “That sin . . . should . . . itself with his society.”

lading.text: cargo Mer.V. III. i. 3 , Tit. I. i. 72 .

lag.text: lowest class Tim. III. vi. 91 (old edd. “leg(ge,” conj. “tag”†). ∥ ‘Lag’ is not found elsewhere with this meaning.

lakin.text: “by'r ”=BY'R LADY Tp. III. iii. 1 , MND. III. i. 14 .

lamb.forms: lamb and lambkin are used as terms of endearment
lamb.text: Troil. IV. iv. 23 , Rom. I. iii. 3 ; 2H4 V. iii. 119 .

languishing.text: pl. lingering disease All'sW. I. iii. 237 ; so the ppl. adj.=lingering Cym. I. v. 9 .

lapse.text: vb. (not pre-S.; 2 there was a 17th cent. sense ‘to let slip’ of which this may be an early instance with inverted construction) 1. to fall into sin (by lying) Cor. V. ii. 19 , Cym. III. vi. 12 .

larum.text: 1. call to arms, battle cry Shr. I. ii. 210 “in a pitched battle heard Loud larums,” Cor. I. iv. 9 .

lasting.text: contextually=everlasting (freq.) Tp. V. i. 208 “set it down With gold on lasting pillars.”

late.text: recently, of late, lately Tp. V. i. 113 “to abuse me, As I have been,” MND. V. i. 53 “ deceas'd,” Tw.N. V. i. 225 “but so ago,” R3 III. i. 99 “Too he died that might have kept that title,” Ant. IV. i. 13 “those that serv'd Mark Antony but ” ; with ppl. adjs. 1H4 II. iii. 64 “Like bubbles in a -disturbed stream,” 1H6 III. ii. 82 “this -betray'd town,” Tit. I. i. 184 “our -deceased emperor's sons,” Ven. 818 “Gazing upon a -embarked friend,” Lucr. 1740 “a late-sack'd island.”

lavolt.forms: lavolt Troil. IV. iv. 86 , lavolta H5 III. v. 33

law.text: sb. (special uses are the foll.) 1. what the law awards 2H6 I. iii. 214 .

lay.text: vb. (4 only once in S., but common in literature from the 14th cent. and app. not regarded as a solecism in the 17th and 18th) 1. to bury Tw.N. II. iv. 52 “in sad cypress let me be laid,” H8 IV. ii. 22 “to lay his weary bones among ye,” Cym. IV. ii. 233 “where shall's lay him?.”

leading.text: command H5 IV. iii. 130 , R3 V. iii. 298 ; direction Lucr. 436 , Cor. IV. v. 143 “The of thine own revenges” ; generalship 1H4 IV. iii. 17 “men of such great leading.”

lean.text: poor, meagre, mean Err. III. ii. 93 “I have but lean luck,” Tw.N. III. iv. 380 “my lean and low ability,” Ant. II. ii. 19 “A leaner action” ; unfertile, barren 1H4 II. ii. 120 , 2H4 IV. iii. 129 ; scantily furnished 1H4 I. ii. 82 “no lean wardrobe.”

leap.text: 1. to be eager “to” do a thing Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 51 “Will leap to be his friend,” Per. V. iii. 45 .

learning.text: what is learnt:—(1) lesson, instruction Cym. I. i. 43 , Sonn. lxxvii. 4 “of this book this mayst thou taste” ; (2) information Ant. II. ii. 51 “I . . . have my from some true reports” ; (3) acquirement (S.) Ham. V. ii. 35 “I . . . labour'd much How to forget that learning.”

leave.text: sb. (1 also in phr. “by , under of, by your , with your leave, have leave.”) 1. permission Gent. II. iv. 25 “Give him ” (=make allowances for him), Err. I. i. 35 “I'll utter what my sorrow gives me ” (=allows), 3H6 III. ii. 34 “you will have leave” (=you will be free to do as you please), Ven. 568 “love, whose exceeds commission.”

leer.text: complexion, countenance AYL. IV. i. 69 “a Rosalind of a better leer than you,” Tit. IV. ii. 120 “Here's a young lad fram'd of another leer.”

leg.text: obeisance made by drawing back one leg and bending the other All'sW. II. ii. 11 , 1H4 II. iv. 432 “here is my leg,” Cor. II. i. 78 “caps and legs,” Tim. I. ii. 241 .

lege.forms: lege [aphetic form of ‘allege’ in use 14th-16th cent.]
lege.text: to bring forward Shr. I. ii. 28 .

legend.text: misused for ‘legion’ Wiv. I. iii. 57 . (Ff Q3 “a legend,” Q1 “legians,” Q2 “legions”).

length.text: sb. (1 rare outside S.; 5 common Eliz.) 1. “of ,” long R2 IV. i. 11 “Is not my arm of ,” Troil. I. iii. 136 “To end a tale of length.”

let.text: vb. (the other vb. “let” ‘to hinder’ occurs) 1. to allow to remain Wint. I. ii. 41 .

level.text: vb. (2 is transf. from the sense of ‘aim’, which is the most freq. S. sense, lit. and fig.) 1. “level with,” be on a par with Oth. I. iii. 240 .

libel.text: to make libellous statements Tit. IV. iv. 17 .

licence.text: leave, permission Meas. II. iv. 146 , H5 IV. vii. 75 , 2H6 IV. iii. 8 , Ham. IV. iv. 2 .

liegeman.text: vassal, subject Wint. II. iii. 173 , 1H4 II. iv. 377 “that . . . swore the devil his true ,” Ham. I. i. 15 .

light.text: adj. (quibbles are frequent) 1. unimportant, slight, trivial Tp. I. ii. 449 “Make the prize ,” MND. III. ii. 133 “as as tales,” H5 II. ii. 89 “for a few crowns;—hold, set ,” account of small value R2 I. iii. 293 , Oth. II. iii. 176 .

like.text: adv. (the use in “like as”=even as, e.g. Sonn. lx. 1 , gives rise by ellipsis to “like” conj., as in Per. I. i. 163 , where Ff read “as”) 1. equally, similarly, alike Tp. III. iii. 66 “my fellowministers Are invulnerable,” Err. I. i. 82 , H5 II. ii. 183 , Cym. III. iii. 41 “Like war-like as the wolf,” Sonn. cxxxii. 12 “suit thy pity like in every part.”

limit.text: 1. prescribed time or period Meas. III. i. 223 “the . . . of the solemnity,” R2 I. iii. 151 “The dateless of thy dear exile,” R3 III. iii. 7 “the of your lives is out;” period of rest after child-bearing Wint. III. ii. 107 “before I have got strength of limit.”

line.text: (?) lime-tree Tp. IV. i. 193 * , 237 * . ∥ This form, a 16th-17th cent. variant of ‘lind’=linden, is older than ‘lime’ (first in the 17th cent.). Cf. LINE-GROVE.

ling.text: heather Tp. I. i. 71 “ling†, heath, broom†, furze” (F1 “Long heath, Browne firrs”).

lip.text: “falling a lip of contempt,” expressing contempt by a movement of the lip Wint. I. ii. 373 ; “make a lip at,” make a contemptuous face at Cor. II. i. 129 .

liquor.text: to dress with oil or grease Wiv. IV. v. 101 “liquor fishermen's boots,” 1H4 II. i. 94 .

liquorish.text: pleasant, sweet Tim. IV. iii. 195 “ draughts” (Ff1 2 “Licourish,” Ff3 4 “Liquorish”).

list.text: spec. catalogue of the soldiers of a force Ham. I. i. 98 , I. ii. 32 “the levies, The lists,” Lr. V. iii. 112 “within the lists of the army,” Ant. III. vi. 76 (cf. line 67 “levying The kings o' the earth for war”); also gen. catalogue H8 IV. i. 14 “the list Of those that claim their offices this day.”

listen.text: to endeavour to hear of 2H4 I. i. 29 “to after news,” 2H6 I. iii. 152 “ after Humphrey.”

lively.text: ‘to the life’ Gent. IV. iv. 176 “Which I so acted,” Tim. V. i. 87 “Thou counterfeit'st most ”

livery.text: legal delivery of property into one's possession; only in “sue” one's “,” to institute a suit as heir to obtain possession of lands which are in the hands of the court of wards R2 II. i. 205 , II. iii. 129 , 1H4 IV. iii. 62 .

living.text: 1. during one's life or lifetime, while one is or was alive Gent. III. i. 170 “death rather than torment,” R2 V. i. 39 “my last leave,” H8 IV. ii. 70 “my actions,” Sonn. lxvii. 6 “his hue” ; so “ death” R3 I. ii. 153 , Lucr. 726 .

lo.text: with 2nd personal pron. (cf. O. Fr. ‘es vos’) Wint. I. ii. 106 “lo you now,” Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 87 “Lo thee!.”

lob.text: to hang heavily, droop H5 IV. ii. 47 .

loffe.text: rare form of ‘laugh’ in old edd. of MND. II. i. 55 (rhyming with “coffe”).

long.text: phr. “before” or “ere it be long,” before long, shortly Meas. IV. ii. 79 , 1H6 III. ii. 75 , 3H6 III. iii. 232 ; “think ,” grow weary or impatient Rom. IV. v. 41 , Lucr. 1359 “ she thinks till he return again” :— adv. after a long time Shr. V. ii. 1 “At last, though ”

longing.text: prompted by strong desire Gent. II. vii. 85 “my journey,” Pilgr. vi. 4 [ 74 ] “A tarriance.”

look.text: vb. (obs. and idiomatic uses are) 1. to take care, see Tp. IV. i. 51 “ thou be true,” R3 III. iv. 77 “ that it be done,” Oth. IV. iii. 9 “look it be done.”

loop.text: (app.) part of a hinge Oth. III. iii. 366 “no hinge nor To hang a doubt on.” ∥ A north-country sense.

loose.text: adj. (1 cf. ‘Mosquettiers . . . are not be imployed as loose shot in skirmishes’, Sir J. Smyth, 1590) 1. “loose shot,” marksmen not attached to a company H8 V. iv. 60 .

lording.text: 1. lord Sonn. Music 1 [ Pilgr. 211 ]; pl.=Sirs! 2H6 I. i. 146 .

losing.text: resulting in loss Mer.V. IV. i. 62 “A suit,” 2H4 I. i. 101 “a office,” Cæs. V. v. 36 “this day.”

lovely.text: amorous, loving Shr. III. ii. 126 “a kiss,” Pilgr. iv. 3 [ 44 ] “many a lovely look.”

loving.text: of love AYL. V. iv. 198 “thy voyage,” Lucr. 480 “my tale” ; H5 v. Chor. 29 “by a lower but likelihood” (‘one which the love of the people leads them to dwell on’, Wright). ∥ The usu. sense is ‘affectionate’, ‘friendly’.

low.text: adj. (see also LOWER) 1. short, not tall Ado I. i. 179 , MND. III. ii. 295 “so dwarfish and so low,” AYL. IV. iii. 89 .

lower.text: “ chair,” (?) easy chair Meas. II. i. 137 ; “the” or “this world” (not pre-S.), the earth Tp. III. iii. 54 , R2 III. ii. 38 .

lure.text: apparatus used by falconers to recall their hawks, ‘being made of feathers and leather in such wise that in the motion it looks not vnlike a fowle’ (Latham, 1615) Shr. IV. i. 195 “she never looks upon her ,” Ven. 1027 “As falcon to the lure.”

lym.text: rare form of ‘lyam’ in the sense of ‘lyamhound’= bloodhound, proposed by Hanmer in Lr. III. vi. 72 (Qq “him,” Ff “Hym”).

mad.text: to make mad, madden (freq.); to be mad 2H6 III. ii. 117 “madding Dido.”

mailed.text: wrapped up, enveloped 2H6 II. iv. 31 “Mail'd up in shame, with papers on my back.”

maim.text: mutilation or mutilating wound, (hence fig.) grave defect or disablement R2 I. iii. 156 , 1H4 IV. i. 42 “Your father's sickness is a to us,” 2H6 II. iii. 41 , Cor. IV. v. 92 .

making.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. form, shape, build, make Err. IV. ii. 22 , MND. II. i. 32 .

mammock.text: to break into fragments Cor. I. iii. 71 “O! I warrant, how he mammocked it.”

man.text: “Since I was man,” since I was born Lr. III. ii. 45 ; “I write man,” I am entitled by my years to call myself a man All'sW. II. iii. 207 ; 2H6 IV. ii. 94 “I was never mine own man since” =what I used to be; Tp. V. i. 213 “no man was his own” =in his senses.

manage.text: sb. (1 used both lit. and fig.) 1. training of a horse in its paces R2 III. iii. 179 “the of unruly jades,” 1H4 II. iii. 54 “terms of ,” H8 V. iii. 24 “spur 'em, Till they obey the ,” Per. IV. vi. 70 , Compl. 112 .

manly.text: gallantly, bravely (S.) Mac. IV. iii. 234 “This time” (Rowe “tune”†） “goes manly.”

manner.text: “taken with the ,” taken with the thing stolen in one's possession, (hence) taken in the very act LLL. I. i. 203 , 1H4 II. iv. 350 ; Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 755 “if you had not taken yourself with the ” (=kept what you were going to give us). ∥ A term of Anglo-French law, orig. ‘mainoure’ (= Fr. ‘manœuvre’, lit. hand-work), which acquired the concrete sense of ‘thing stolen’.

mannerly.text: decently, becomingly Ado II. i. 80 , “ modest,” Mer.V. II. ix. 100 , Cym. III. vi. 91 .

mansionry.text: (?) abode Mac. I. vi. 5 (Ff “mansonry,” ? misprint for “masonry”†).

mantle.text: vegetable coating on the surface of stagnant water (S.) Lr. III. iv. 137 “the green of the standing pool” ; cf. Tp. IV. i. 182 “the filthymantled pool.”

manure.text: to till, cultivate Oth. I. iii. 329 .

many.text: “ a day,” a long time ago H8 V. ii. 20 (contrast “for this a day”=all this long time Ham. III. i. 91 ); “ a ” = many and many a John I. i. 183 ; followed by a possessive pron. Tim. III. vi. 11 “ my near occasions” (= many urgent affairs of mine), Ant. I. ii. 195 “ our contriving friends” ; used once in the possessive form Sonn. xciii. 7 “In many's looks.”

mare.text: “The man shall have his again,” all will come right in the end MND. III. ii. 463 ; “ride the wild mare,” play at see-saw 2H4 II. iv. 268 ; “Whose mare is dead?” What is amiss? 2H4 II. i. 48 .

marish.text: marsh, swamp 1H6 I. i. 50 “a of salt tears” (old edd. “nourish”).

mark.forms: mark 1 (1 freq. in the literal sense) 1. target, butt
mark.text: fig. phr. “beyond the of,” beyond the reach of Cor. II. ii. 94 “he fought Beyond the of others,” Ant. III. vi. 87 “Beyond the of thought.”

marry.text: orig. the name of the Virgin Mary used as an oath or invocation:=‘indeed, to be sure’ Err. II. ii. 105 “, and did, sir,” All'sW. II. iii. 64 , R3 I. iii. 261 , III. iv. 34 ; esp. (1) in answering a question, when it often implies surprise that it should have been asked = ‘why’ or ‘why, to be sure’ Tp. III. ii. 47 “Wilt thou be pleas'd? . . . —, will I,” Gent. II. i. 66 “How painted?—, sir, so painted,” R3 I. iii. 98 “What may she not? She may,—ay, , may she,” Cæs. I. ii. 228 “Was the crown offer'd him thrice?—Ay, , was't” ; (2) with asseverative words or invocations Tw.N. IV. ii. 111 “God be wi' you . . . , amen,” R2 IV. i. 114 “, God forbid!,” Rom. IV. v. 8 “God forgive me, , and amen!” ; (3) “marry come up!” (not pre-S.), used to express indignant or amused surprise or contempt Rom. II. v. 64 , Per. IV. vi. 164 ; “marry-trap” * (S.), ? be off with you Wiv. I. i. 172 .

marshal.text: sb. (scanned as 2 or as 3 syll.) 1. high officer of state in England, now called ‘earl marshal’ 1H4 IV. iv. 2 “the lord ,” H8 IV. i. 19 “earl marshal.”

mart.text: sb. (not pre-S. in the sense ‘market-place or hall’ Err. I. ii. 74 , &c., Mer.V. III. i. 51 ) 1. meeting of people for buying and selling, time of holding a market Err. I. i. 17 “Syracusian m-s and fairs,” Per. IV. ii. 5 “this mart.”

marvel.text: 1. astonishment, wonder Wint. V. i. 188 , iii. 100 , Cym. III. i. 10 .

marvellous.text: wonderfully; only with adjs. and advs. (freq.) MND. IV. i. 26 “ hairy about the face.”

master.text: vb. (neither sense is pre-S.) 1. to rule as a master, be the master of Cym. IV. ii. 383 , 395

match.text: vb. (sense 7 is peculiar to S.) 1. to ally oneself in marriage Ado II. i. 69 “to in my kindred,” Tw.N. I. iii. 118 , 2H6 I. i. 132 , 3H6 III. iii. 210 .

mate.text: to stupefy, confound Err. V. i. 282 “I think you are all m-d or stark mad,” 2H6 III. i. 265 , Mac. V. i. 85 “My mind she has m-d, and amaz'd my sight.”

maugre.text: in spite of Tw.N. III. i. 165 , Lr. V. iii. 133 .

mean.text: sb. (used in sing. and pl. with the sense ‘instrument, agency, method, &c. employed for doing something’ the pl. sometimes taking sing. concord; the meaning ‘pecuniary resources,’ e.g. Meas. II. ii. 24 , is not pre-S.) 1. middle position, medium Mer.V. I. ii. 48 “seated in the ,” Ant. II. vii. 22 “the height, the lowness, or the ” ; moderation 1H6 I. ii. 121 “since he keeps no ”

meaning.text: intention, purpose Shr. III. ii. 127 “He hath some meaning in his mad attire,” R2 II. iii. 74 , R3 III. v. 54 “Something against our ,” Lr. I. ii. 196 “if there be any good toward you,” V. iii. 4 “with best meaning.”

meanly.text: poorly, badly LLL. V. ii. 329 “he can sing A mean most ” ; basely, lowlily R3 IV. iii. 37 , Cym. III. iii. 82 .

measure.text: sb. (the sense ‘quantity (of drink),’ arising out of that of ‘unit of capacity’, develops into ‘carouse, toast’ in Mac. III. iv. 11 , Oth. II. iii. 32 ) 1. distance of a fencer from his opponent, fig.=reach Gent. V. iv. 127 “Come not with in the of my wrath.”

medicine.text: applied, as commonly from 1400 to S.'s time, to drugs, &c., used for other than remedial purposes; e.g. the philosopher's stone or elixir All'sW. V. iii. 102 “multiplying ,” Ant. I. v. 36 “that good ” ; poison Lr. V. iii. 97 , Oth. IV. i. 46 “Work on, My , work!” ; a philtre 1H4 II. ii. 20 , 22 , Oth. I. iii. 61 .

melting.text: yielding or softening to emotion, tender (hence of eyes, &c.) tearful 2H4 IV. iv. 32 “ charity,” 3H6 I. iv. 174 “thy tears,” II. ii. 41 “thy heart,” Cæs. II. i. 122 “The spirits of women,” Oth. V. ii. 348 “unused to the mood,” Ven. 315 “his melting buttock.”

memorial.text: of remembrance Troil. V. ii. 77 “memorial . . . kisses.”

merchandise.text: construed as a pl. Ant. II. v. 104 ; “make ,” trade, traffic Mer.V. III. i. 137 “make what merchandise I will.”

mere.text: absolute, sheer, perfect, downright Wiv. IV. v. 64 “cozenage, cozenage,” LLL. I. ii. 36 “the contrary,” H8 III. ii. 330 “the undoing Of all the kingdom,” Mac. IV. iii. 152 “The despair of surgery,” Oth. II. ii. 3 , Cym. IV. ii. 92 “to thy confusion.” ∥ A common sense for more than two centuries, surviving late in the 18th; but less freq. in S. than the ordinary mod. use (which is not pre-Eliz.).

meteor.text: luminous body or appearance of any kind in the sky R2 II. iv. 9 “And m-s fright the fixed stars of heaven,” Rom. III. v. 13 “some that the sun exhales” ; fig. Err. IV. ii. 6 “his heart's m-s tilting in his face.”

mickle.text: great Err. III. i. 45 , H5 II. i. 70 “An oath of might,” Rom. II. iii. 15 . ∥ In S.'s time its use in literature was archaistic; in colloquial use it was northern and north-midl. dial.

mind.text: sb. (1, 2 now obs. exc. in phrases) 1. judgement, opinion; phr. “in my , to my ,” as I think Mer.V. IV. i. 408 , Ham. I. iv. 14 .

mine.text: subterranean cavity Oth. IV. ii. 78 “The bawdy wind . . . Is hush'd within the hollow mine of earth.” ∥ Cf. ‘When a wherilewind . . . tosseth . . . His fixt root from his hollow mines’ (Chapman).

minister.text: 1. one employed by another to carry something into effect, agent Tp. I. ii. 131 “The m-s for the purpose,” All'sW. II. i. 140 , Wint. III. ii. 161 “I chose Camillo for the minister to poison My friend,” 2H6 III. i. 355 “a of my intent,” Ham. III. iv. 175 “their” [i.e. heaven's] “scourge and minister.”

mire.text: (2 not pre-S.) 1. to bespatter, defile Ado IV. i. 135 “m-'d with infamy.”

misdoubt.text: vb. (in common dial. use) 1. to have doubts as to All'sW. III. vii. 1 , Ant. III. vii. 62 ; absol. All'sW. I. iii. 132 .

misgraffed.text: fig. badly matched MND. I. i. 137 .

misprision.text: mistake, misunderstanding Ado IV. i. 187 , 1H4 I. iii. 27 , Sonn. lxxxvii. 11 .

miss.text: sb. (1 ‘feel the miss of’ is now the usual expression in midland dialects) 1. disadvantage caused by the loss “of” (a person) 1H4 V. iv. 105 “I should have a heavy miss of thee.”

missing.text: absence Cym. V. v. 276 “Upon my lady's ”

mist.text: to bedim Lr. V. iii. 264 “ or stain the stone.”

mistaking.text: mistake, error Tp. I. ii. 248 , Meas. III. ii. 154 , Shr. IV. v. 49 . ∥ A freq. sense about 1580-1650

mistrust.text: to suspect the existence of or anticipate the occurrence of Ado II. i. 191 “an accident of hourly proof, Which I m-ed not,” Wint. II. i. 47 “All's true that is m-ed,” 3H6 V. vi. 38 “Which now no parcel of my fear,” R3 II. iii. 42 “ Ensuing danger” ; with clause Lucr. 1516 .

misuse.text: vb. (‘use wrongly’ is the most freq. sense) 1. to abuse, revile Ado II. i. 248 , AYL. IV. i. 213 [ 205 ], Shr. II. i. 160 .

moan.text: lamentation, grief Ado V. iii. 16 “assist our ,” 1H6 II. iii. 44 “thy mirth shall turn to ,” Cym. IV. ii. 273 “Thou hast finished joy and moan” ; also phr. “make moan.” ∥ The mod. sense is post-S.

mock.text: vb. (3 is peculiar to S.) 1. to defy, set at nought Mer.V. II. i. 30 “mock the lion when he roars for prey,” Tw.N. III. iv. 228 “mocks reproof,” Mac. II. ii. 7 , Ant. III. xi. [ xiii. ] 184

mongrel.text: abusive epithets for persons Troil. V. iv. 14 , Lr. II. ii. 24 .

mood.text: 1 (1 current from the 12th cent. to 1600) 1. anger, displeasure Gent. IV. i. 51 “Who, in my , I stabb'd,” All'sW. V. ii. 5 “muddied in Fortune's ,” H5 IV. vii. 38 , Rom. III. i. 13 , Oth. II. iii. 276 ; (?) angry cast of countenance Sonn. xciii. 8 “m-s and frowns.”

moral.text: adj. (3 cf. MORAL sb. 1) 1. enunciating moral precepts, moralizing Ado V. i. 30 , Lr. IV. ii. 58 “a fool” ; so Ado I. iii. 13 “to apply a moral medicine to a mortifying mischief.”

morning.text: used as adj. connoting vaguely the attributes possessed in the morning, or the fact that morning is the time referred to MND. IV. i. 100 “I do hear the lark,” AYL. II. vii. 146 “the . . . schoolboy with his . . . shining face,” Ham. I. ii. 218 “the morning cock crew loud.”

morris.text: “nine men's ,” game played on a board between two players, each with nine pebbles, disks, pegs, or ‘pins’ MND. II. i. 98 .

motion.text: sb. (5, 6 still prevalent uses in 18th cent.) 1. power of movement Meas. III. i. 118 “This sensible warm ” (i.e. in the body), Rom. III. ii. 59 .

mould.text: sb. 2 (2 cf. Fr. ‘moule’; 3 in poetical use since the Eliz. period) 1. model, pattern Ham. III. i. 162 .

mount.text: 1. to cause to rise H8 I. i. 144 “The fire that m-s the liquor till it run o'er” ; to erect, set up Tp. II. ii. 11 “like hedge-hogs, which . . . Their pricks,” 2H6 I. iv. 40 “castles m-ed” ; to excite to a higher degree All'sW. I. i. 239 “which m-s my love so high.”

mounting.text: phr. of Eliz. writers, used quibblingly in LLL. IV. i. 4 .

mouse.text: playful term of endearment to a woman LLL. V. ii. 19 , Tw.N. I. v. 68 , Ham. III. iv. 183 .

mouth.text: 1. phr.:—“a sweet mouth,” (?) a taste for sweet things Gent. III. i. 333 ; “in the mouth(s of,” spoken of by Mer.V. I. iii. 61 “Your worship was the last man in our m-s,” John IV. ii. 187 , 1H6 III. i. 196 , Oth. II. iii. 195 “m-s of wisest censure” (Q1 “men”), Sonn. lxxxi. 14 .

mow.text: (derisive) grimace Tp. IV. i. 47 “with mop and ,” Ham. II. ii. 390 [ 381 ], Cym. I. vi. 41 “Contemn with m-s the other” ; also as vb. Tp. II. ii. 9 “apes that mow and chatter,” Lr. IV. i. 63 “mopping and m-ing.”

mural.text: wall MND. V. i. 210 “Now is the down” (Ff “morall”; ? read ‘wall’).

muse.text: 2) this sense occurs in Sternhold & Hopkins, Psalm ii, ‘Why did the Jewish people muse?’) 1. to wonder, marvel All'sW. II. v. 71 , John III. i. 317 , R3 I. iii. 305 “I why she's at liberty,” Cor. III. ii. 7 , Mac. III. iv. 85 “Do not at me,” Ven. 866 ; also trans. to marvel at Tp. III. iii. 36 “I cannot too much muse Such shapes” . . .

mutiny.text: discord, contention LLL. I. i. 168 , 1H6 IV. i. 131 , H8 III. ii. 121 “There is a in 's mind,” Rom. I. v. 84 , Lucr. 1153 “So with herself is she in ”

mystery.text: 2 (late Latin ‘misterium’=‘ministerium’) 1. craft, trade, profession Meas. IV. ii. 30 , &c., Tim. IV. i. 18 , iii. 461 “thrive in our mystery,” Oth. IV. ii. 29 .

nag.text: applied to a wanton woman 2H4 II. iv. 204 , Ant. III. viii. 20 [ x. 10 ] “Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt.” ∥ Cf. HACKNEY, JADE.

native.text: adj. (the gen. mod. sense ‘belonging to a certain country, or to one's birthplace’ is freq.) 1. natural LLL. IV. iii. 263 “ blood,” John III. iv. 83 “ beauty,” Rom. IV. i. 97 , Ham. III. i. 84 “the hue of resolution” ; with “to” Oth. II. i. 219 “a nobility . . . more than is native to them.”

natural.text: adj. (various ordinary uses occur) 1. that is so by birth 3H6 I. i. 82 “Whom should he follow but his king?,” Lr. IV. vi. 196 “The fool of fortune” (= born to be the sport of fortune).

near.text: nearer R2 III. ii. 64 “Nor near nor further off . . . Than this weak arm,” Mac. II. iii. 147 “the near in blood, The nearer bloody;—ne'er the ,” no nearer the object in view R2 V. i. 88 .

neat.text: adj. (1 applied in both laudatory and depreciatory sense) 1. elegant Gent. I. ii. 10 “a knight . . . neat and fine,” Wint. I. ii. 124 “not neat, but cleanly,” 1H4 I. iii. 33 , Lr. II. ii. 46 “you neat slave.”

need.text: “it needs,” it is necessary, there is necessity Err. V. i. 393 “It shall not need,” 3H6 I. iv. 125 , Mac. V. ii. 29 ; “what need(s . . .?,” what necessity is there for . . .? Err. III. i. 60 “What needs all that?,” Tim. I. ii. 251 “what need these feasts?,” Ant. II. vii. 132 “What needs more words?,” Lucr. 31 “What needeth then apology be made?.”

neighbour.text: “the to,” privy to R3 IV. ii. 43 ; in attrib. use freq.=neighbouring.

new.text: 1. newly, freshly, recently, lately John III. i. 233 “even before this truce, but new before,” Tim. I. ii. 81 “they were bleeding new,” Sonn. lvi. 10 “two contracted new.”

nick.text: sb. (1 developed from the sense of ‘notch used as a means of keeping a score’) 1. “out of all nick,” lit. beyond all reckoning, i.e. exceedingly Gent. IV. ii. 77 .

nightly.text: 1. belonging to the night, used by night, active at night Gent. II. iv. 133 “ tears,” MND. V. i. 379 “ revels,” Tit. II. iii. 97 “the owl,” Lucr. 680 “ linen,” 1080

nod.text: to beckon (a person) Ant. III. vi. 66 .

noise.text: sb. (2 Chaucer applies ‘make noyse’ to the nightingale) 1. rumour, report Troil. I. ii. 12 “The goes,” Lr. III. vi. 120 , Ant. I. ii. 150 “the least noise of this.”

nourish.text: to support, maintain 2H6 III. i. 348 “Whiles I in Ireland nourish a mighty band.”

number.text: the multitude, the populace Cor. III. i. 71 “us, the honour'd number.”

nuzzle.text: to train “up” Per. I. iv. 42 “to up their babes” (old edd. “nouzle, nouzell,” mod. edd. “nousle†”).

object.text: often somewhat specific=one that excites love or pity or their opposites MND. IV. i. 176 “The and the pleasure of mine eye, Is only Helena,” H8 I. i. 127 (see ABJECT), Troil. IV. v. 106 , Tim. IV. iii. 123 “Swear against objects” (i.e. be not moved to pity), Ven. 255 “her object will away.”

obscure.text: adj. (stressed like ENTIRE) 1. dark, dim Mer.V. II. vii. 51 “the o'bscure grave,” Ven. 237 “brakes obscu're and rough” ; loving the darkness Mac. II. iii. 65 “The o'bscure bird.”

obstruct.text: impediment, bar Ant. III. vi. 61 “Being an 'tween his lust and him” (Ff “abstract”). ∥ A word not otherwise known.

illade.text: amorous glance, ogle Wiv. I. iii. 66 , Lr. IV. v. 25 .

off.text: adv. (idiomatic uses with vbs. will be found under these vbs.; 3 not pre-S., still in dial. use) 1. beside the mark Cor. II. ii. 65 “that's off.”

oft.text: frequent Sonn. xiv. 8 “By oft predict” ; so often AYL. IV. i. 20 “by often rumination.”

old.text: adj. (4 remains in midland dial.) 1. belonging to or characteristic of advanced age Tp. I. ii. 369 “old cramps,” Lr. I. i. 190 “his old course” ; Sonn. ii. 11 “my old excuse.”

on.text: prep. (2 orig. often an actual difference of idiom, but from Eliz. times resulting from confusion of OF and ON, both of which were reduced to o') 1. =from Lr. V. iii. 167 * “what art thou That hast this fortune on me?”; often taken=against (cf. UPON).

opposite.text: hostile, antagonistic, adverse 2H6 III. ii. 251 , R3 IV. iv. 216 “at their births good stars were ,” Tim. I. i. 285 “ to humanity,” Lr. II. i. 51 , Oth. I. ii. 67 “ to marriage” ; const. “with” Tw.N. II. v. 164 “Be opposite with a kinsman,” R3 II. ii. 94 .

or.text: conj. 2 (“or . . . or”=either . . . or, is very freq.) 1. “or . . . or” introduces alternative questions Mer.V. III. ii. 64 “Tell me where is fancy bred, Or in the heart or in the head?,” Cym. IV. ii. 356 “How! a page! Or dead or sleeping on him?” ; so “Or whether . . . Or whether” Sonn. cxiv. 1 , 3

order.text: sb. (1 a common 16th-17th cent. sense) 1. suitable measures for the accomplishment of a purpose Meas. II. ii. 25 “There shall be for't” ; esp. in phr. “take ,” take measures or steps, make necessary arrangements All'sW. IV. ii. 55 “I'll take my mother shall not hear,” R2 V. i. 53 “there is ta'en for you,” 1H6 III. ii. 126 “Now will we take some order in the town,” Oth. V. ii. 72 .

orphan.text: (?) = UNFATHERED, q.v. Wiv. V. v. 45 “You heirs of fixed destiny” (addressed to fairies).

other.text: adj., and sb. or pron. (“other” as a pl. is freq.) 1. each preceding (one) Meas. IV. iv. 2 “Every letter he hath writ has disvouched other,” R2 I. i. 22 “Each day still better other's happiness!,” Cæs. I. ii. 229 “every time gentler than other.”

out.text: expressing abhorrence, reproach, or indignation Gent. II. vii. 54 “Out, out, Lucetta! that will be ill-favour'd,” MND. III. ii. 65 “Out, dog! out, cur!,” R3 I. iii. 118 “Out, devil!,” Lr. IV. vi. 250 “Out, dunghill!” ; so “out upon” (freq.) Wiv. I. iv. 174 “Out upon't! what have I forgot?” ; also with words of lamentation (“alack, alas”) Wiv. I. iv. 37 , Oth. V. ii. 117 , Sonn. xxxiii. 11 .

outward.text: externally Meas. III. i. 87 “This sainted deputy,” Ado I. ii. 9 , Ham. II. ii. 401 [ 392 ] (Ff).

own.text: Tp. V. i. 213 “When no man was his own” = master of his senses.

pace.text: to train (a horse) in its paces (e.g. to amble) H8 V. iii. 22 , Ant. II. ii. 68 ; fig. Meas. IV. iii. 141 “pace your wisdom In that good path that I would wish it go,” Per. IV. vi. 68 “she's not paced yet.”

pack.text: confederacy, conspiring gang Wiv. IV. ii. 126 “a knot, a ging, a ,” Err. IV. iv. 104 , R3 III. iii. 4 , Lr. V. iii. 18 . ∥ Apparently a blending of “pack” =bundle, used fig., and the Eliz. “pack”=plot, conspiracy, intrigue.

paction.text: compact H5 V. ii. 393 (Ff1 2 “pation,” Ff3 4 “passion,” not in Q).

pageant.text: sb. (orig.=scene or act in a mediæval mystery play) 1. theatrical representation; hence, show, spectacle, sight Tp. IV. i. 155 “this insubstantial ,” Gent. IV. iv. 166 “When all our p-s of delight were play'd,” MND. III. ii. 114 “their fond ” (=the foolish spectacle they present), H8 IV. i. 11 “shows, P-s,” Troil. III. iii. 276 “the of Ajax” ; occas. false show Oth. I. iii. 18 “a pageant To keep us in false gaze.”

pain.text: sb. (1 chiefly in phr. “on pain of,” also “in pain of” 2H6 III. ii. 257 ; 2 the pl. in this sense is freq.; “for thy pains” Wiv. III. iv. 104 has not its mod. ironical sense) 1. punishment, penalty Meas. II. iv. 86 “his offence is so, as it appears Accountant to the law upon that pain.”

pajock.text: of unknown meaning, app. intended as an obscure substitute for ‘ass’ Ham. III. ii. 300 . ∥ Commonly taken to be a form of ‘peacock’; perhaps identical with ‘patchocke’, Spenser's name for the degenerate English in Ireland.

palate.text: vb. (not pre-S.) 1. to enjoy the taste of, relish Troil. IV. i. 59 , Ant. V. ii. 7 “never palates more the dung (dug†).”

pale.text: paleness, pallor Ven. 589 “a sudden pale . . . Usurps her cheeks” ; also probably in Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 4 (see PALE sb. 1 3).

pall.text: to cover as with a pall Mac. I. v. 52 .

pang.text: to cause pangs H8 II. iii. 15 .

paper.text: note fastened on the back of a criminal undergoing punishment, specifying his offence LLL. IV. iii. 48 , 2H6 II. iv. 31 .

parcel.text: sb. (1 cf. phr. ‘part and parcel of . . .’) 1. part, portion Wiv. I. i. 237 “that the lips is of the mouth,” Err. V. i. 106 “a branch and of my oath,” 1H4 II. iv. 115 , H8 III. ii. 126 , Cor. I. ii. 32 “Some p-s of their power,” Oth. I. iii. 154 “by parcels.”

pardon.text: leave, permission Ado II. i. 356 , LLL. IV. ii. 104 “Under ,” Ham. IV. vii. 46 “first asking your thereunto,” Ant. III. vi. 60 “I begg'd His for return.”

parlous.text: [contracted from ‘perilous’] 1. perilous, dangerous AYL. III. ii. 46 “in a state.”

part.text: sb. (6 “on the part of” occurs also in mod. sense) 1. “the better ,” the greater part Mer.V. I. i. 16 , AYL. III. i. 2 , 2H4 I. ii. 180 ; “a little ,” a little Tim. III. ii. 53 ; “no part,” not at all All'sW. II. i. 135 .

participate.text: to share in common with others Tw.N. V. i. 248 * .

particular.text: 1. detail All'sW. IV. iii. 207 “let me answer to the of the inter'gatories,” 1H4 II. iv. 419 , 2H4 IV. iv. 90 “With every course in his ,” Cor. II. iii. 48 * “by p-s” (=one by one, in detail), Ham. II. ii. 248 “question more in particular.”

pash.text: to strike violently, smash Troil. II. iii. 217 “I'll pash him o'er the face” (Q “push”), V. v. 10 “the pashed corses of the kings.” ∥ Only in this play; common in Warwickshire in this sense.

pass.text: vb. (13 common 16th-17th cent.) 1. to die, ‘pass away’ 2H6 III. iii. 25 “let him peaceably,” Lr. IV. vi. 48 , V. iii. 315 .

passing.text: adj. surpassing, extreme Gent. I. ii. 17 “a shame,” II. i. 83 , 3H6 V. i. 106 “O traitor” ;—adv. pre-eminently, exceedingly (freq.)

passion.text: sb. (applied widely to all kinds of feeling by which the mind is powerfully moved, e.g. mirth John III. iii. 47 , H5 II. ii. 132 ; 2 is a special application; cf. the vb.) 1. painful affection or disorder of the body Err. V. i. 47 , 1H4 III. i. 35 , Mac. III. iv. 57 .

passionate.text: adj. (1 cf. PASSION sb. 2, and vb.) 1. grieved, sorrowful Gent. I. ii. 121 , LLL. III. i. 1 , John II. i. 544 “She is sad and passionate.”

patched.text: app. motley fool MND. IV. i. 216 ; cf. AYL. II. vii. 13 and Tp. III. ii. 73 .

pattern.text: sb. (1 16th-17th cent., not pre-S.) 1. precedent, instance appealed to John III. iv. 16 “find some pattern of our shame,” Tit. V. iii. 44 .

paunch.text: to stab in the belly Tp. III. ii. 101 .

pause.text: hesitation, suspense Mer.V. II. ix. 53 , Troil IV. iv. 35 , Ham. IV. iii. 9 ; “give” (one) “pause,” cause one to hesitate, ‘pull up’ Ham. III. i. 68 ; “in pause,” hesitating Ham. III. iii. 42 “I stand in where I shall first begin.”

pawn.text: sb. (1, 2 only S.; in 2 there may be a ref. to the pawn in chess) 1. gage of battle R2 I. i. 74 “to take up mine honour's ,” V. i. 55 .

peace.text: 1. “the ,” the king's peace, the general peace and order of the realm as provided for by law Wiv. II. iii. 47 , “I am of the ” (=an officer of the public peace), 55 “sworn of the peace” (=made a justice of the peace), 2H4 III. ii. 100 .

peascod.text: season for peas 2H4 II. iv. 420 [ 413 ]. ∥ In old edd. also “pescod,” showing the shortened vowel, a pronunciation which has survived locally in the northern and east-Anglian area.

pelting.text: paltry, petty Meas. II. ii. 112 , MND. II. i. 91 “every river” (Ff “petty”), R2 II. i. 60 “ farm,” Troil. IV. v. 266 , Lr. II. iii. 18 .

perfect.text: adj. (7 is peculiar to S.; the senses ‘entire, pure’ and ‘mere, sheer’ are not pre-S.) 1. full, mature Lr. I. ii. 79 “sons at perfect age.”

perjure.text: one guilty of perjury LLL. IV. iii. 48 “like a perjure, wearing papers” (cf. PERJUR'D).

pheere.text: Malone's reading in Per. I. Gower 21 (old edd. “Peer(e),” mod. edd. “fere”†).

phraseless.text: which there is no word to describe Compl. 225 “that phraseless hand.”

physic.text: the healing art LLL. II. i. 186 , Per. III. ii. 32 ; transf. Rom. II. iii. 52 “thy help and holy ” ; the medical faculty, physicians Cym. IV. ii. 268 “The sceptre, learning, physic.”

piece.text: 1 cask of liquor; in fig. context Troil. IV. i. 62 “a flat tamed piece.” 2 applied to a woman or girl H8 V. v. 27 “such a mighty as this,” Tit. I. i. 309 , Per. IV. ii. 48 “I have gone through for this piece.”

pilcher.text: scabbard Rom. III. i. 86 . ∥ App. transf. and contemptuous use of a word meaning ‘outer garment of skin or leather’.

pinch.text: vb. (1 used by Chapman and Dryden) 1. to bite 3H6 II. i. 16 “a bear . . . having pinch'd a few.”

pipe.text: “put up” one's “p-s,” put one's instruments away, cease playing Rom. IV. v. 96 , Oth. III. i. 20 . ∥ This phr. was used fig. in the 16th cent. for ‘desist from action’.

pitch.text: height (fig.) Tw.N. I. i. 12 “Of what validity and soe'er,” R3 III. vii. 187 , Ham. III. i. 86 “of great pitch and moment” (Ff “pith”).

planched.text: boarded Meas. IV. i. 32 “a planched gate.”

plant.text: to set up, establish LLL. I. i. 163 “A man in all the world's new fashion p-ed,” R2 IV. i. 127 , V. i. 63 “To unrightful kings,” 1H6 II. v. 80 “to the rightful heir.”

plantage.text: plants Troil. III. ii. 184 “As true as steel, as to the moon” (‘plants were supposed to improve as the moon increases’, Nares).

plate.text: to clothe in armour R2 I. iii. 28 , Lr. IV. vi. 170 (fig.), Ant. I. i. 4 “plated Mars.”

pleasing.text: willing (scil. to listen) Lucr. 1126 * “Relish your nimble notes to pleasing ears.”

plenty.text: abundant, plentiful Tp. IV. i. 110 “foison ,” 1H4 II. iv. 269 (Q1 “plentiful”).

pocket.text: (1) to put away out of sight, (hence) conceal or leave unheeded Tp. II. i. 71 , Ant. II. ii. 77 ; (2) to submit to, ‘swallow’ John III. i. 200 “I must pocket up these wrongs,” 1H4 III. iii. 182 .

point.text: aphetic form of APPOINT Shr. III. i. 19 “tied to . . . p-ed times,” &c., Lucr. 879 , Sonn. xiv. 6 “P-ing to each” [minute] “his thunder, rain, and wind.”

poise.text: sb. (1 the literal sense does not occur) 1. weight (fig.) Meas. II. iv. 69 , 3H6 II. v. 13 “the equal of this fell war” (=equipoise, balance), Lr. II. i. 122 “Occasions . . . of some poise” (Qq2 3 Ff “prize”), Oth. III. iii. 82 .

poison.text: =EMPOISON LLL. IV. iii. 305 (“prisons”†), 1H6 V. iv. 121 “my p-'d voice,” Rom. III. ii. 46 , Oth. V. ii. 363 “the object poisons sight.”

poring.text: looking closely as if short-sighted, peering H5 IV. Chor. 2 “the poring dark.”

port.text: 2 (both senses are freq. 16th-17th cent.) 1. bearing, carriage, demeanour H5 I. Chor. 6 “Assume the port of Mars,” 2H6 IV. i. 19 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 52 “with our sprightly port.”

portage.text: port-holes (fig.) H5 III. i. 10 “Let it pry through the portage of the head.”

posset.text: drink composed of hot milk curdled with ale, wine, &c., formerly used as a delicacy and as a remedy Wiv. I. iv. 8 , Mac. II. ii. 7 .

post.text: 1. courier Mer.V. V. i. 46 “there's a come . . . with his horn full of good news,” 2H4 Ind. 37 “The p-s come tiring on,” Mac. I. iii. 98 “As thick as hail Came post with post.”

potting.text: tippling Oth. II. iii. 80 “potent in potting.”

pound.text: pound-weight Cor. III. i. 312 “Tie leaden pounds to's heels.”

prank.text: malicious or mischievous deed or trick Err. II. ii. 212 , 1H6 III. i. 15 , Ham. III. iv. 2 “Tell him his p-s have been too broad to bear with,” Oth. II. i. 142 “foul pranks.”

precipit.text: precipice H8 V. i. 140 (F1 “Precepit,” mod. edd. “precipice”†).

pregnant.text: clear, obvious Meas. II. i. 23 , Wint. V. ii. 34 “Most true, if ever truth were by circumstance,” Oth. II. i. 241 , Ant. II. i. 45 , Cym. IV. ii. 325 . ∥ Old Fr. ‘preignant’, from ‘preindre’ to press; hence=pressing, cogent.

prenominate.text: to name beforehand Troil. IV. v. 249 ; also ppl. adj. aforesaid Ham. II. i. 43 “the prenominate crimes.”

presage.text: sb. (the stress varies; the vb. is always “presa'ge” and is used in senses corresponding to those of the noun) 1. omen, portent John I. i. 28 “sullen pre'sage of your own decay,” III. iv. 158 “Abortives, pre'sages, and tongues of heaven,” Ven. 457 “This ill presa'ge.”

press.text: vb. (in 3H6 III. i. 19 F1 has “prease”) 1. “ to death,” (properly) subject to the ancient torture called the ‘peine forte et dure’ Meas. V. i. 524 “p-ing to death, whipping, and hanging” ; also in fig. use Ado III. i. 76 “she would . . . me to death with wit,” R2 III. iv. 72 , Troil. III. ii. 217 .

pribbles.text: petty disputing, vain chatter Wiv. I. i. 56 .

prick.text: vb. (1 metaphor from spurring) 1. to urge, incite Gent. III. i. 8 “My duty p-s me on to utter that,” Shr. III. ii. 75 “some odd humour p-s him to this fashion,” 1H4 V. i. 131 “honour p-s me on,” Oth. III. iii. 413 .

pricksong.text: descant or accompanying melody to a plainsong or simple theme ‘pricked’ or noted down Rom. II. iv. 22 .

prime.text: adj. (4 only S.) 1. first in time R3 IV. iii. 19 .

quail.text: to overpower Ant. V. ii. 85 “to and shake the orb” ; intr. MND. V. i. 294 “, crush, . . . and quell.”

quarrel.text: sb. (2 used also by Bacon) 1. “have a to,” have a difference with Ado II. i. 245 , Cor. IV. v. 133 .

quarter.text: 1. part of an army or camp 1H6 II. i. 63 “Had all your q-s been so safely kept,” 68 “Within her ”; soldiers' lodging All'sW. III. vi. 69 , Tim. V. iv. 60 .

quest.text: (2 occurs once; 3 only S.) 1. body of persons appointed to hold an inquiry R3 I. iv. 193 “What lawful have given their verdict up,” Ham. V. i. 23 “crowner's quest law,” Sonn. xlvi. 10 .

question.text: sb. (2 cf. QUESTION vb. 2) 1. phr. “in ,” (i) under judicial examination, on trial Ado III. iii. 190 “A commodity in ” (? quibble on the meaning ‘in demand’), Wint. V. i. 198 , 2H4 I. ii. 67 “He that was in for the robbery” ; (ii) under consideration, to be considered Meas. I. i. 46 “Though first in question,” H5 I. i. 5 , Cym. I. i. 34 “besides this gentleman in question. call in ,” (i) inquire into, examine, consider AYL. V. ii. 6 “Neither call the giddiness of it in ,” Troil. III. ii. 58 , Rom. I. i. 235 , Cæs. IV. iii. 164 “call in our necessities,” Ham. IV. v. 217 ; (ii) raise doubts concerning Tw.N. I. iv. 6 “you call in the continuance of his love,” Troil. IV. iv. 84 . The foll. are all used=without doubt, no doubt:— “no ” Meas. III. ii. 150 , 2H6 IV. ii. 64 , Oth. IV. iii. 64 ; “out of ” Ado II. i. 348 , H5 V. i. 48 ; “past ” Tw.N. I. iii. 106 ; “sans ” LLL. V. i. 93 ; “in contempt of ” Tw.N. II. v. 99 .

quire.text: to make music Mer.V. V. i. 62 , Cor. III. ii. 113 .

quit.text: vb. (the sense ‘leave’ also occurs; the older form “quite” occurs in R2 V. i. 43 Qq1-4, Rom. II. iv. 206 Ff, Per. III. ii. 18 Qq) 1. to set free Tw.N. V. i. 333 “Your master quits you.”

quittance.text: 1. discharge from debt Wiv. I. i. 10 , AYL. III. v. 133 .

race.forms: race vb. [variant of RASE, RAZE in common use circa 1400-1650]
race.text: to make away with Tit. I. i. 451 “to massacre them all, And their faction,” Cym. V. v. 70 “that [tribute] The Britons have r-'d out” ; mod. edd. “razed.”

rack.text: mass of cloud driven before the wind in the upper air Ham. II. ii. 514 [ 505 ] “as we often see, against some storm . . . the rack stand still,” Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 10 ∥ In Tp. IV. i. 156 “Leave not a rack behind,” prob. blended with ‘wrack’.

racking.text: driving 3H6 II. i. 27 “ clouds.” ∥ Cf. RACK sb.

rag.text: (1 in old cant=farthing) 1. ‘scrap’ (of money) Err. IV. iv. 88 .

rage.text: sb. (the sense of ‘violent anger, furious passion’ is the commonest) 1. madness, insanity Err. IV. iii. 88 , V. i. 48 , Lr. IV. vii. 78 “the great rage, You see, is kill'd in him.”

rake.text: very lean person Cor. I. i. 24 .

ramping.text: (2 cf. “rampant” 2H6 V. i. 203 ) 1. rearing on the hind legs and showing fierceness 1H4 III. i. 152 “A couching lion, and a cat” ; (hence) of fierce disposition 3H6 V.ii.13 “the lion.”

range.text: vb. (1, 2, 3, 5 not pre-S.) 1. lit. to stretch out in a line; hence, to have a clearly recognized position Cor. III. i. 205 .

rank.text: adj. (a common meaning is ‘gross, coarse’ in various applications) 1. coarsely luxuriant H5 V. ii. 45 , 50 “Wanting the scythe, all uncorrected, rank,” Ham. III. iv. 152 ; fig. AYL II. vii. 46 , Troil. I. iii. 318 “the seeded pride That hath to this maturity blown up In rank Achilles” ; (hence) high or excessive in amount AYL. IV. i. 87 , Ham. IV. iv. 22 “A ranker rate.”

ransom.text: sb. (the ordinary sense is freq.) 1. procuring of one's release from captivity 2H6 IV. i. 10 “Here shall they make their ransom.”

rash.text: adj. (1 and 2 are peculiar to S.) 1. operating quickly Wint. I. ii. 319 “with no rash potion, But with a lingering dram,” 2H4 IV. iv. 48 “rash gunpowder.”

rate.text: to drive away by chiding or scolding Shr. I. i. 164 “Affection is not r-d from the heart,” 1H4 IV. iii. 99 “Rated my uncle from the council-board.”

ravishing.text: ravenous Mac. II. i. 55 * “With Tarquin's ravishing strides”† (Pope; Ff “sides”).

raze.text: vb. 1 (see also RACE vb.) 1. to erase, blot out 2H6 I. i. 102 “Razing the characters of your renown,” Mac. V. iii. 42 “Raze out the written troubles of the brain,” Sonn. xxv. 11 “from the book of honour razed quite.”

reach.text: vb. (pa. t. and pple. “raught”) 1. to lay hold of with the hand 2H6 II. iii. 43 “This staff of honour raught,” Ant. IV. ix. 30 “The hand of death hath raught him.”

reaching.text: able to reach far 2H6 IV. vii. 85 .

rear.text: used in various senses of ‘raise’, e.g. Tp. II. i. 303 [ 295 ] “ my hand,” R2 IV. i. 145 “ this house against this house.”

reason.text: vb. (1 cf. REASON sb. 1) 1. to hold discussion, carry on conversation, discourse, talk LLL. I. i. 94 “How well he's read, to against reading!,” Mer.V. II. viii. 27 “I r-'d with a Frenchman yesterday, Who told me” . . ., H5 III. vii. 38 “my horse . . . 'Tis a subject for a sovereign to on,” R3 IV. iv. 536 “while we here,” Rom. III. i. 57 “Or coldly of your grievances.”

rebato.text: kind of stiff collar worn about 1590-1630 Ado III. iv. 6 .

receiving.text: reception Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 539 “you shall have such As shall become your highness”; understanding Tw.N. III. i. 133 “To one of your ” ∥ ‘Reception’ is not S.

reckoning.text: (3 Eliz. and Caroline sense) 1. way of looking at a thing Shr. IV. i. 87 “By this he is more shrew than she.”

recollected.text: (a) gathered with pains, not spontaneous, (b) picked, refined, studied, (c) recalled, repeated Tw.N. II. iv. 5 “recollected terms.”

record.text: sb. (chiefly “reco'rd”; also “re'cord”) 1. “in” or “upon ,” (properly) committed to writing as authentic evidence of a matter of legal importance; (hence) Meas. II. ii. 40 “whose fine stands in ,” Ado V. i. 252 , R2 IV. i. 230 .

recover.text: 1 (2 an Eliz. use) 1. to bring back to friendship, reconcile Oth. II. iii. 275 .

recoverable.text: capable of being retraced Tim. III. iv. 13 “a prodigal course Is like the sun's; but not, like his, recoverable.”

recure.text: to restore, make whole R3 III. vii. 129 , Sonn. xlv. 9 ; to remedy Ven. 465 .

refigure.text: to reproduce the form of (a person) Sonn. vi. 10 .

refuge.text: 1. resource Cor. V. iii. 11 “Their latest refuge Was to send him.”

refuse.text: 1. to decline to meet (an opponent) Ant. III. vii. 39 ; to decline to bear (a name) Rom. II. ii. 34 .

regard.text: sb. (exx. such as Tp. III. i. 40 , Gent. II. iv. 61 , by some referred to 6, probably have the sense ‘esteem, affection, kindly feeling’) 1. look, glance Tw.N. V. i. 222 “You throw a strange upon me,” Troil. III. iii. 257 “he . . . bites his lip with a politic regard.”

register.text: record Wiv. II. ii. 198 “turn another” eye] “into the of your own” [follies], Sonn. cxxiii. scil. 9 “Thy” [Time's] “r-s,” Compl. 52 ;—“in ,” on the list Ant. IV. ix. 21 .

regreet.text: greeting Mer.V. II. ix. 89 “From whom he bringeth sensible r-s,” John III. i. 241 “this seizure and this kind regreet.”

reguerdon.text: reward 1H6 III. i. 169 ; also as vb. 1H6 III. iv. 23 .

rein.text: chiefly in fig. phr. “give the ,” allow full scope LLL. V. ii. 660 ; “take the ,” go on without restraint Wint. II. iii. 51 ; in phr. with the vb. “bear,” expressing the holding of the head up high or haughtily Troil. I. iii. 189 “Ajax . . . bears his head In such a rein . . . As broad Achilles,” Lr. III. i. 27 “the hard rein which both of them have borne.”

relish.text: vb. 1 (the sense ‘enjoy’ is commonest) 1. to taste (a thing) AYL. III. ii. 248 “take a taste of my finding him, and it with good observance” ; fig. to appreciate Wint. II. i. 166 “if you . . . cannot . . . a (as†） truth like us” ; to feel Tp. V. i. 23 “One of their kind, that relish all as sharply.”

remain.text: vb. (1 not post-S.; 3 only S.) 1. to dwell Tp. I. ii. 420 , AYL. III. ii. 236 , Cym. IV. iii. 14 “for my mistress, I nothing know where she r-”

remedy.text: reparation, redress; esp. in phr. “there's no ”=there's no help for it Wiv. I. iii. 34 , John IV. i. 91 , Oth. I. i. 35 ; “no ” often=inevitably, without a doubt Wiv. II. ii. 128 “You must send her your page; no ,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 673, V. i. 77 , Troil. IV. iv. 55 , Cym. III. iv. 165 ; “what ?,” what help is there for it? what can be done? Wiv. V. v. 262 [ 250 ] “Well, what ? . . . What cannot be eschew'd must be embrac'd,” Tw.N. I. v. 55 , 1H6 V. iii. 131 .

remove.text: to depart, go away, move to another place AYL. III. iv. 57 “let us ,” All'sW. V. i. 23 , John V. ii. 33 , V. vii. 62 , 1H6 II. v. 104 “is removing hence” (=dying), Mac. V. iii. 2 “Till Birnam wood to Dunsinane,” Ham. I. v. 163 “once more , good friends,” Ven. 81 “From his soft bosom never to ”

renegue.text: intr. to deny Lr. II. ii. 83 “, affirm” (Ff2-4 “Renege,” Qq “Reneag”; F1 misprinted “Reuenge”); trans. to renounce Ant. I. i. 8 “r-s all temper” (Ff “rene(a)ges”).

renown.text: sb. (1, 2 not post-S.; 3 only S.) 1. report, rumour Tp. V. i. 193 “Of whom so often I have heard , But never saw before.”

renying.text: renunciation Sonn. Music iii. 7 [ Pilgr. 250 ] “Heart's renying.”

repair.text: to return LLL. V. ii. 293 , MND. IV. i. 73 “May all to Athens back again ,” Tim. III. iv. 70 “to some other hour.” ∥ The prevailing meaning is ‘go, betake oneself’.

repeal.text: vb. (1 see the prec. word) 1. to recall from exile R2 II. ii. 49 “The banish'd Bolingbroke r-s himself,” Cor. V. iv. 71 [ v. 5 ]; fig. All'sW. II. iii. 55 “whose banish'd sense Thou hast repeal'”

report.text: sb. (the sense ‘what is said about something’ is very freq. in various phrases: “give good ”= speak well (of a person) Wint. V. ii. 170 [ 162 ], “make r-s”=speak All'sW. IV. iii. 344 , “suffer the ” =be told Cym. I. iv. 63 ) 1. rumour, common talk AYL. I. i. 6 “ speaks goldenly of his profit,” 1H6 II. iii. 18 “I see is fabulous and false,” Ant. II. ii. 192 “if be square to her,” Per. I. i. 35 .

reproach.text: to bring disgrace upon Meas. V. i. 422 “reproach your life.”

reprobance.text: reprobation, rejection by God Oth. V. ii. 207 “fall to reprobance” (Qq “reprobation”).

requiring.text: demand, request Tp. II. ii. 195 [ 186 ], Meas. III. i. 254 , H5 II. iv. 101 “if fail, he will compel.”

resolve.text: vb. (cf. RESOLVED; 4 common 17th cent.) 1. to dissolve, melt Tim. IV. iii. 445 “r-s The moon into salt tears,” Compl. 296 “his passion . . . r-'d my reason into tears” ; also refl. and intr. John V. iv. 25 “as a form of wax R-th from his figure 'gainst the fire,” Ham. I. ii. 130 “Thaw and thyself into a dew.”

respect.text: sb. (the mod. sense of ‘deferential regard or esteem’ is one of the most freq.) 1. phr. “in of,” (i) in comparison with Ado III. iv. 19 , LLL. V. ii. 636 “Hector was but a Troyan in of this,” AYL. III. ii. 69 , Cæs. I. i. 10 ; (ii) in consideration of, on account of Gent. III. i. 330 “She is not to be kissed fasting, in of her breath,” 1H4 II. iii. 2 , Ham. V. ii. 121 ; (iii) in regard to MND. I. i. 137 “misgraffed in respect of years,” AYL. III. ii. 13 .

respecting.text: having regard to, considering 2H6 III. i. 24 , H8 II. iv. 178 ; in comparison with Wint. V. i. 35 .

rest.text: vb. 1 (the ordinary senses are freq.) 1. “ in,” to lie in the power of Meas. I. iii. 31 “It r-ed in your Grace T' unloose this tied-up justice,” 3H6 III. ii. 45 , Tit. II. iii. 41 ; “ on,” to depend or rely upon Tit. I. i. 267 , Ham. III. iii. 14 ; cf. John V. i. 13 .

resting.text: stationary Cæs. III. i. 61 “the northern star, Of whose true-fix'd and resting quality.”

retire.text: vb. (1 an Eliz. sense) 1. to return Troil. I. iii. 281 , Oth. III. iii. 456 “retiring ebb,” Ven. 906 “now she will no further, But back r-s,” Lucr. 962 .

return.text: vb. 1 1. refl. to turn away 1H6 III. iii. 56 “ thee therefore, with a flood of tears.”

revenge.text: vb. (in the trans. use the injury or the person injured is the object) 1. pass. “be r-d,” to take vengeance (freq.); const. “of” = on 2H4 II. iv. 165 (Q; Ff “on”); const. “on” = for Lucr. 1778 “to be revenged on her death.”

reverberate.text: reverberating, resounding Tw.N. I. v. 293 “ hills.” ∥ Ben Jonson has ‘a reuerberate glasse’.

revolt.text: sb. 1 (the gen. sense of ‘casting off of allegiance, obedience, or faithfulness’ is freq.; 2 only S.) 1. “give” (one) “the revolt,” to rebel against Mac. V. iv. 13 .

rhyme.text: spelling of RIME in some mod. edd.

right.text: 1. just or equitable treatment; phr. “do” (one) “,” to do him justice, give him satisfaction Ado I. i. 254 [ 246 ] “I will do myself the right to trust none,” V. i. 152 “Do me , or I will protest your cowardice,” Tit. I. i. 203 “Romans, do me right: Patricians, draw your swords” ; with ref. to pledging a person by drinking to him 2H4 V. iii. 74 “Why, now you have done me right.”

rival.text: partner, associate Ham. I. i. 13 “The rivals of my watch.”

roll.text: sb. (2 not pre-Eliz.) 1. list, register (fig.) 1H4 III. i. 43 “in the of common men,” Ant. V. ii. 180 “i' the roll of conquest.”

ronyon.text: abusive term for a woman Wiv. IV. ii. 199 “you baggage . . . you ” (Ff “Runnion”), Mac. I. iii. 6 “the rump-fed ronyon.”

room.text: （“give room,” and simply “room,”=make way) 1. place assigned to one Shr. III. ii. 253 “let Bianca take her sister's ,” John III. iv. 93 , R2 V. v. 108 “Go thou and fill another in hell,” 3H6 II. vi. 54 , III. ii. 132 , Sonn. lv. 10 .

root.text: the ‘bottom’ “of” the heart Gent. V. iv. 103 “How oft hast thou with perjury cleft the root!,” Troil. IV. iv. 54 “my heart will be blown up by the root,” Cor. II. i. 204 “at very root on's heart,” Ant. V. ii. 105 “smites My very heart at root.”

roping.text: hanging or flowing down like a rope or thread H5 III. v. 23 “ icicles,” IV. ii. 48 “The gum down-roping from their pale-dead eyes.”

rother.text: ox Tim. IV. iii. 12 “It is the pasture lards the rother's sides” (Ff “Brothers”).

round.text: 1. (of a sum of money) large, considerable Mer.V. I. iii. 104 , H8 V. iv. 86 “round fines.”

rouse.text: sb. (prob. arose from phr. ‘drink carouse’, apprehended as ‘drink a rouse’) 1. full draught of liquor, bumper Ham. I. ii. 127 “the king's ,” I. iv. 8 “takes his ,” Oth. II. iii. 68 “they have given me a already—Good faith, a little one.”

royal.text: adj. (the senses of ‘belonging to, originating from, connected with, proceeding from a king or sovereign’, ‘of the rank of a sovereign’ are freq.; sometimes applied to dukes) 1. of or consisting of a sovereign or sovereigns John II. i. 347 “add a number to the dead,” H5 V. ii. 27 “this . . . interview” ; also H8 I. iv. 86 “My choice” (=choice of a king), Mac. I. iii. 56 “ hope” (=prospect of kingship).

rub.text: in bowls, to encounter an obstacle (allusively) LLL. IV. i. 143 “challenge her to bowl.—I fear too much rubbing,” Troil. III. ii. 50 “ on, and kiss the mistress.”

ruffle.text: vb. (1 a S. use) 1. to stir “up” to indignation Cæs. III. ii. 232 “ up your spirits.”

runagate.text: (later form of ‘renegade’) 1. deserter Cym. I. vi. 137 “that runagate to your bed.”

rush.text: sb. (1 the custom of ‘marrying’ with a rushring was formerly prevalent) 1. used for making a finger-ring All'sW. II. ii. 25 .

sack.text: general name for a class of white wines formerly imported from Spain and the Canaries Tw.N. II. iii. 209 “I'll go burn some sack,” 1H4 II. iv. 524 [ 516 ] “If sack and sugar be a fault, God help the wicked!.” ∥ See also SHERRIS,

safe.text: adj. (1 not post-S.; 2 not pre-S.) 1. (mentally or morally) sound or sane Meas. I. i. 71 “the man of discretion,” Cor. II. iii. 226 “on a safer judgement,” Cæs. I. i. 14 “with a safe conscience,” Lr. IV. vi. 82 “The safer sense,” Oth. IV. i. 280 “Are his wits safe?,” Cym. IV. ii. 131 “in all safe reason.”

sag.text: to droop, decline Mac. V. iii. 10 .

sail.text: collective sing.=ships, vessels John III. iv. 2 “A whole armado of convicted sail,” Oth. I. iii. 37 ; also pl. Ant. II. vi. 24 “Thou canst not fear us, Pompey, with thy sails,” III. vii. 49 .

sallet.text: a prevalent Eliz. form of ‘salad’ 2H6 IV. x. 9 ; used as a type of (1) a mixture All'sW. IV. v. 18 “she was the sweet-marjoram of the ” ; (2) something tasty Ham. II. ii. 471 [ 462 ] “no s-s in the lines to make the matter savoury.”

salt.text: lecherous, wanton Meas. V. i. 402 “Whose imagination,” Tim. IV. iii. 85 “thy hours,” Oth. II. i. 246 “his and most hidden loose affection,” III. iii. 405 , Ant. II. i. 21 . ∥ Orig. ‘to go assaut’=to be in heat.

save.text: prep. and conj. (“ for”=‘but for’ not pre-S.) 1. followed by a pronoun in the nominative Tw.N. III. i. 174 “save I alone,” Cæs. III. ii. 67 , V. v. 69 “save only he” ; in the accusative Tim. IV. iii. 509 “all, save thee, I fell with curses.”

saving.text: prep. (2 see REVERENCE) 1. except John I. I. John I. I. 201

savour.text: sb. (2 rare) 1. smell, perfume Tp. II. ii. 55 “the of tar,” Shr. Ind. ii. 73 “I smell sweet s-s,” John IV. iii. 112 “The uncleanly savours of a slaughter-house.”

say.text: vb. 1 (3 cf. the vulgar ‘Now you're talking’) 1. “I have said,” (i) I have finished speaking, I have spoken my mind John II. i. 235 “When I have said, make answer to us both,” Ant. III. ii. 34 ; (ii) I have spoken decisively H8 V. i. 86 “I have said. Begone” ; (iii) It is as I have said, That is so Mac. IV. iii. 213 “My wife kill'd too?—I have said,” Ant. I. ii. 60 ;— “You have said,” What you say is true Gent. II. iv. 29 , Tw.N. III. i. 12 , Oth. IV. ii. 204 , Ant. II. vi. 110 ;— “Say you?,” What is that you say? Meas. V. i. 270 , Ham. IV. v. 28 , Oth. III. iv. 82 , Cym. II. i. 28 (after an aside), IV. ii. 379 ;—“How say you by . . .?,” What do say about (see BY 1) Mer.V. I. ii. 57 , Oth. I. iii. 17 .

scald.text: vb. (1 cf. SCALDING) 1. intr. to get burning hot with the sun 2H4 IV. v. 30 “Like a rich armour worn in heat of day, That scalds with safety” [i.e. to the wearer].

scale.text: “equal ,” just balance Ham. I. ii. 13 “In equal weighing delight and dole.” ∥ The pl. takes sing. concord in Rom. I. ii. 101 “that crystal s-s” (fig. ‘eyes’).

scamble.text: to struggle indecorously or rapaciously to obtain something, scramble John IV. iii. 146 “To tug and scamble,” H5 V. ii. 217 .

scambling.text: contentious, rapacious Ado V. i. 94 , H5 I. i. 4 .

scandal.text: disgraceful imputation Ham. II. i. 29 “You must not put another on him, That he is open to incontinency.”
