scant.text: 1. to put (a person) off “with” a scanty supply, to stint Troil. IV. iv. 47 “He . . . s-s us with a single famish'd kiss.”

scape.text: sb. (some mod. edd. “'scape”) 1. escape Shr. V. ii. 3 “To smile at s-s and perils overblown,” Oth. I. iii. 136 “hair-breadth scapes.”

scarf.text: 1. to blindfold Mac. III. ii. 47 “Come, seeling night, up the tender eye of pitiful day.”

scathe.text: harm 2H6 II. iv. 62 ; phr. “do ” John II. i. 75 , R3 I. iii. 317 , Tit. V. i. 7 .

school.text: sb. 1 (2 a sense once currentin certain phrases, e.g. ‘men of school’, ‘degree of school’, ‘art of school’) 1. “set to ,” to send to be taught, give instruction to 3H6 III. ii. 193 “And set the murd'rous Machiavel to ,” Lr. II. iv. 68 “We'll set thee to to an ant,” Lucr. 1820 “Now set thy long-experienc'd wit to school.”

scold.text: to quarrel noisily, brawl, rail (“against”), wrangle (“with”) Ado II. i. 251 , Tim. IV. iii. 157 , with phr. denoting the result H8 V. i. 175 “-it out of him.”

scolding.text: = CHIDING ppl. adj. Cæs. I. iii. 5 “ winds.”

sconce.text: jocular term for the head Err. I. ii. 79 , Cor. III. ii. 99 “my unbarbed ,” Ham. V. i. 108 “knock him about the sconce.”

score.text: 1. notch cut in a stick or tally used in keeping accounts 2H6 IV. vii. 39 .

scorn.text: 1. derisive utterance or gesture, taunt, insult LLL. V. ii. 873 “if sickly ears . . . Will hear your idle s-s,” 1H6 II. iv. 77 , Ham. III. i. 70 “bear the whips and s-s of time,” Oth. IV. i. 83 “the gibes, and notable scorns.”

scot.text: used fig. to express paying a person out thoroughly 1H4 V. iv. 115 “or that hot termagant Scot had paid me scot and lot too.”

scotch.text: to cut, score, gash Cor. IV. v. 198 “he s-ed him and notched him like a carbonado.” ∥ See also SCORCH.

scout.text: to keep a look-out Tw.N. III. iv. 196 .

seal.text: 1. something which authenticates, attests or confirms a covenant or undertaking, final addition which completes and secures Meas. IV. i. 7 “my kisses . . . S-s of love,” MND. III. ii. 144 , H5 IV. i. 174 , Troil. IV. iv. 122 ; pl. Ham. III. ii. 424 [ 417 ] “To give them seals” (=to confirm them by making words into deeds).

sear.text: 1. to dry up, cause to wither, blight Cym. I. i. 116 .

search.text: vb. (1 now only used with ‘out’) 1. to seek for Cym. V. v. 11 “He hath been search'd among the dead and living.”

season.text: sb. (the sense of ‘time’ is freq.) 1. “of (the) ,” in season Wiv. III. iii. 169 “buck; and of the too,” Meas. II. ii. 85 “kill the fowl of ;—of ,” befitting the time of year, seasonable All'sW. V. iii. 32 “a day of ;—to ,” when opportunity presents itself Err. IV. ii. 58 ;—“of such a ,” of such an age Cym. III. iv. 175 .

seat.text: sb. (the sense of ‘throne’ is freq. in the historical plays, e.g. R2 III. ii. 119 ) 1. estate Mer.V. I. i. 172 , 1H4 V. i. 45 , H5 III. v. 47 , Cym. V. iv. 60 .

second.text: 1. supporter Tp. III. iii. 103 , Cor. I. iv. 43 , viii. 16 , Lr. IV. vi. 199 “No s-s? All myself?,” Cym. V. iii. 90 ; (of a thing) Ham. IV. vii. 153 .

secret.text: adj. ( Lr. III. i. 32 “have feet In” = have landed secretly at) 1. belonging peculiarly to oneself, private Tw.N. I. iv. 14 “my soul,” R3 III. v. 27 “her thoughts,” Ham. II. ii. 243 “the secret parts.”

see.forms: see vb. (in sense 3 also with various constr.
see.text: —object and adj. 1H6 II. v. 121 , 2H6 II. iii. 54 , object and pple. Mer.V. II. ii. 126 , 170 , clause Gent. I. ii. 44 , MND. III. ii. 98 ) 1. “see away,” spend in seeing H8 Prol. 12

seeming.text: vbl. sb. (1 the commonest use) 1. outward form, appearance, or show Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 75 “these keep and savour all the winter long,” H8 II. iv. 106 “in full ” (=to all appearance), Troil. I. iii. 157 , Ham. III. ii. 92 , Cym. V. v. 65 “thought her like her seeming.”

seldom.text: “ but” = it is seldom that . . . not, usually Per. IV. ii. 133 ; “ when” = seldom that Meas. IV. ii. 89 , 2H4 IV. iv. 79 .

sequent.text: 1. consequent Meas. V. i. 374 , Lr. I. ii. 118 ; “ to,” consequent upon All'sW. II. ii. 60 , Ham. V. ii. 54 .

sequester.text: to separate AYL. II. i. 33 “a poor s-'d stag,” Troil. III. iii. 8 , Tit. II. iii. 75 .

sere.text: part of a gun-lock which keeps the hammer at full or half cock; only in fig. phr. “tickle o' the ,” ready to ‘go off’ at any time, yielding easily to any impulse Ham. II. ii. 347 [ 337 ].

serpigo.text: skin eruption Meas. III. i. 31 , Troil. II. iii. 82 .

serving.text: “in their ,” using them Cym. III. iv. 173 .

set.text: vb. (used in many connexions where ‘place’ or ‘put’ is now idiomatic) 1. pass. to sit Gent. II. i. 95 “I stand affected to her. —I would you were set,” H8 III. i. 73 “I was set at work,” Cor. IV. v. 204 , Ven. 18 “being set” ; also refl. LLL. IV. iii. 4 “set thee down” ; mixed constr. 3H6 IV. iii. 2 “The King . . . is set him down.”

setting.text: set expression Tp. II. i. 237 [ 229 ] “The setting of thine eye.”

sewer.text: servant who carried in and arranged dishes for a banquet Mac. I. vii. stage dir.

shade.text: sb. (1 only in rhyme; 3 cf. SHADOW 6) 1. (a person's) shadow Sonn. liii. 3 .

shadow.text: sb. (in 2H4 III. ii. 147 =mere name without a man to correspond to it) 1. shade Tp. IV. i. 67 “groves, Whose the dismissed bachelor loves,” R2 III. iv. 25 , Lr. V. ii. 1 “take the of this tree For your good host” ; shady place AYL. IV. i. 229 “I'll go find a ” ; obscurity, darkness Meas. III. i. 258 ; pl. Sonn. xliii. 5 .

shape.text: vb. (rare in material sense) 1. to conform, adjust, proportion (one thing “to” another) LLL. V. ii. 65 “make him . . . his service wholly to my hests,” Tw.N. I. ii. 59 “ thou thy silence to my wit,” Lucr. 1458 “shapes her sorrows to the beldam's woes” ; also intr. to suit, agree Cym. V. v. 347 .

sharp.text: 1. hungry, famished (also used as epithet of “hunger” itself=keen) Shr. IV. i. 193 “My falcon now is and passing empty,” All'sW. III. ii. 121 “ constraint of hunger,” Ven. 55 “an empty eagle, by fast,” Lucr. 422 “Sharp hunger.”

sheathing.text: having a sheath made Shr. IV. i. 138 “Walter's dagger was not come from sheathing.”

shelving.text: projecting Gent. III. i. 115 “Her chamber is . . . built so shelving.”

shent.text: blamed, reproved, rebuked, rated Wiv. I. iv. 38 , Tw.N. IV. ii. 115 “I am for speaking to you,” Cor. V. ii. 104 , Ham. III. ii. 423 [ 416 ]. ∥ Introduced as a pa. t. by Theobald in Troil. II. iii. 87 for Ff “sent.”

shift.text: vb. (freq. in the sense of ‘change’, trans. and intr.) 1. to exchange Ant. V. ii. 151 “mine will now be yours; And, should we shift estates, yours would be mine.”

shore.text: H5 IV. i. 285 “the high of this world,” the exalted places of the earth; Ant. IV. xiii. [ xv. ] 11 “the varying of the world,” (?) the earth with its continual variations.

short.text: adj. (1 see also COME “short”) 1. inadequate LLL. IV. iii. 241 “praise too doth blot,” Tim. I. i. 97 “five talents is his debt, His means most ”

show.text: vb. (1 very freq.; by ellipsis app.=seem to do in Sonn. xciv. 2 ） 1. to have (a certain) appearance, appear, seem AYL. I. iii. 84 “thou wilt more bright and seem more virtuous When she is gone,” H5 IV. i. 108 “the element shows to him as it doth to me,” Cor. IV. v. 68 “Thou show'st a noble vessel,” Mac. I. iii. 54 “Are ye fantastical, or that indeed Which outwardly ye show?,” Lr. I. iv. 267 “this our court . . . Shows like a riotous inn,” Ant. IV. viii. 7 “you have shown all Hectors,” Sonn. cv. 2 “Let not . . . my beloved as an idol show.”

shrew.text: = the much commoner “beshrew” Wint. I. ii. 281 “ my heart,” Cym. II. iii. 147 “shrew me.”

shrill.text: to utter loudly Troil. V. iii. 84 “Andromache shrills her dolours forth.”

shroud.text: to shelter, conceal LLL. IV. iii. 137 , 3H6 III. i. 1 , IV. iii. 39 ; intr. to take shelter Tp. II. ii. 43 “I will here shroud.”

side.text: vb. (2 perhaps aphetic form of ‘decide’, still in use in northern dial.) 1. to take sides with Cor. I. i. 199 [they] “side factions.”

sign.text: vb. (2 cf. note on SIGN sb.) 1. to mark H8 II. iv. 106 “You your place and calling . . . With meekness,” Cæs. III. i. 206 “S-'d in thy spoil” (=bearing the bloody tokens of thy slaughter); to mark out John IV. ii. 222 “s-'d to do a deed of shame” (? if not aphetic form of ‘assigned’).

silence.text: euphemistically for ‘to keep under restraint’ 2H4 V. ii. 97 , H8 I. i. 97 ; cf. “put to silence,” Cæs. I. ii. 291 .

simple.text: adj. (the chief meanings are ‘humble, unpretentious’, ‘artless, unaffected’, ‘ordinary, undistinguished’, ‘plain, homely’, ‘insignificant, feeble’, ‘plain, mere’, ‘of weak intellect’, ‘foolish, silly’) 1. of poor or humble condition Shr. Ind. i. 135 “this peasant,” Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 774, Ant. V. ii. 340 “A countryman” [cf. line 232 “a rural fellow”]; phr. “simple though I stand here” Wiv. I. i. 226 .

sinew.text: 1. pl. nerves Lr. III. vi. 107 , Ven. 903 .

tag.text: rabble Cor. III. i. 247 ; so tag-rag “people” Cæs. I. ii. 259 .

taint.text: vb. (not pre-Eliz. in these senses) 1. to affect or imbue slightly with an undesirable quality 1H6 V. iii. 182 “Never yet taint” [pa. pple.] “with love,” 3H6 III. i. 40 “Nero will be tainted with remorse” ; also intr. to become so affected Mac. V. iii. 3 “I cannot taint with fear.”

taintingly.text: (F1) Cor. I. i. 116 , app. misprint for “tantingly” (Ff2 3), “tauntingly” (F4), which last is the reading of mod. edd.

taking.text: vbl. sb. (1 cf. TAKE 2) 1. blasting, malignant influence Lr. III. iv. 60 .

talent.text: common old form of ‘talon’; hence the pun in LLL. IV. ii. 65 “If a talent be a claw, look how he claws him with a talent.”

tang.text: ‘something that leaves a sting or pain behind it’ (J.) Tp. II. ii. 53 * “she had a tongue with a ” ∥ Perhaps ‘tang’=tongue of a snake (supposed to sting), sting of an insect, is here associated with ‘tang’=sharp ringing sound.

tardy.text: “ta'en ,” taken unawares, surprised R3 IV. i. 51 ; “come off,” fallen short, inadequately done Ham. III. ii. 29 .

task.text: “at ” (S.), blamed Lr. I. iv. 368 “at task for want of wisdom” (Qq “attask'd”).

taste.text: vb. (2 the commonest sense) 1. to put to the proof, try, test Tw.N. III. iv. 270 “ their valour,” 1H4 IV. i. 119 “let me my horse,” Troil. III. ii. 97 “Praise us as we are t-d” (= prove to be); used affectedly Tw.N. III. i. 88 “ your legs, sir” ; also intr. const. “of” with same meaning 2H4 IV. i. 192 “every idle . . . reason Shall to the king of this action.”

tattering.text: in rags John V. v. 7 (old edd. “tott'ring”).

tax.text: vb. (2 the prevailing sense) 1. to censure, blame, accuse Ado I. i. 46 “you tax Signior Benedick too much,” Ham. I. iv. 18 “traduc'd and t-'d of other nations” ; with “of” for the more freq. “with” All'sW. V. iii. 122 “Shall tax my fears of little vanity.”

temper.text: vb. (used twice of tempering swords Tp. III. iii. 62 , Ven. 111 “Strong-t-'d steel” ; cf. MISTEMPERED 2; 4 cf. the Warwickshire expression of ‘humouring’ butter, e.g. before a fire) 1. to compound (a poison) Ado II. ii. 22 , Rom. III. v. 98 , Ham. V. ii. 342 , Cym. V. v. 251 .

temporary.text: (?) devoted to secular affairs Meas. V. i. 145 .

tender.text: (1) offer, (2) thing offered LLL. II. i. 170 “such welcome . . . As honour . . . may Make of,” John V. vii. 106 “the like of our love,” Rom. III. iv. 12 “I will make a desperate Of my child's love,” Ham. I. iii. 99 , 106 “you have ta'en these t-s for true pay,” Sonn. lxxxiii. 4 .

tending.text: attendance Mac. I. v. 38 “Give him tending.”

tent.text: to apply a tent to (a wound); only fig. to probe Ham. II. ii. 634 [ 626 ] “I'll tent him to the quick,” Cym. III. iv. 118 ; to cure Cor. I. ix. 31 “tent themselves with death,” III. i. 235 “a sore .. You cannot tent.”

tetter.text: skin eruption Troil. V. i. 27 , Ham. I. v. 71 .

than.text: 1 (commonly spelt “then” in old edd.) 1. =as LLL. III. i. 188 [ 180 ] “Than whom no mortal so magnificent.”

thankings.text: thanks Meas. V. i. 4 “Many and hearty thankings,” Cym. V. v. 408 ,

that.text: chiefly used to introduce characterizing clauses, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 6 “I have suffer'd With those that I saw suffer,” Err. I. ii. 36 “like a drop of water That in the ocean seeks another drop” ; but freely employed also in descriptive clauses, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 160 “Some food . . . and some fresh water that A noble Neapolitan, Gonzalo, . . . did give us” ; correlated with “so” and “such” it forms constructions now obs. Tp. V. i. 270 “a witch . . . so strong That could control the moon,” Cæs. I. iii. 116 “such a man That is no fleering tell-tale,” Cym. III. iv. 80 “a prohibition so divine That cravens my weak hand.”

then.text: old form of THAN 1 , as prob. in John IV. ii. 42 “more” [reason], “more strong, than” (F1 “then) lesser is my fear” (=‘more strong in proportion as my fear is less’, Aldis Wright); conj. “when†, the†.”

think.text: “it t-s,” it seems (impers., as in ‘methinks’) R3 III. i. 63 “Where it t-s† best unto your royal self” (Ff “think'st,” Qq12 “seems”), Ham. V. ii. 63 “Does it not, thinks't thee,” . . . (F1 “thinkst,” Qq “think(e)”; with the Ff readings cf. “methink'st” in All'sW. II. iii. 269 . ∥ In Compl. 91 “thinks” app.=methinks.

thorough.text: through R2 V. vi. 43 “With Cain go wander thorough† shades of night” (Q1 “through,” Ff “through the”), 2H6 IV. i. 87 , Cæs. V. i. 110 “to be led. . . the streets of Rome,” Per. IV. iii. 35 “It pierc'd me ,” Lucr. 1851 “To show her bleeding body thorough Rome.”

throw.text: cast of the dice LLL. V. ii. 545 , Mer.V. II. i. 33 ; fig. venture Tw.N. V. i. 45 “at this ” ; of a bowl Cor. V. ii. 21 “Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground, I have tumbled past the ” (i.e. gone beyond the mark).

thwart.text: crosswise, the wrong way Troil. I. iii. 15 * “every action . . . trial did draw Bias and thwart” (taken by some as a vb.).

tickle.text: easily shifted, unstable, insecure Meas. I. ii. 183 “thy head stands so on thy shoulders,” 2H6 I. i. 217 “the state of Normandy Stands on a point,” Ham. II. ii. 346 [ 337 ] (see SERE). ∥ Cf. Tickyll nat stedy, ‘inconstant’ (Palsgr.).

tickled.text: app. error for TICKLE adj. Ham. II. ii. 346 [ 337 ].

tidy.text: (?) in seasonable or prime condition, fit for killing; or delicate, tender (ironically) 2H4 II. iv. 249 “Thou whoreson little tidy Bartholomew boar-pig.” ∥ Cf. Tidie, fatte, or tender, ‘Cereus’ (Rider's Dict., 1589 ).

timely.text: early, speedy Err. I. i. 138 “my death” ; opportune, welcome Mac. III. iii. 7 “To gain the inn” (or?=to reach the inn betimes).

tiny.text: always joined with “little,” Tw.N. V. i. 401 , 2H4 V. i. 29 , Lr. III. ii. 74 .

tire.text: vb. (cf. ‘Tiring [in Falconry], giving a Hawk a Leg or Wing of a Pullet to Pluck at’, Bailey) 1. to prey or feed ravenously “upon” 3H6 I. i. 269 “Will . . . like an empty eagle on the flesh of me,” Ven. 56 ; fig. Tim. III. vi. 5 “Upon that were my thoughts tiring” (=busily engaged), Cym. III. iv. 97 “her That now thou tir'st on.”

tithe.text: tenth All'sW. I. iii. 90 “One good woman in ten . . . we'd find no fault with the tithe-woman if I were the parson” (quibblingly,=tenth woman and woman paying tithe), Troil. II. ii. 19 “Every tithe soul.”

tithing.text: district, being orig. the tenth part of a hundred Lr. III. iv. 138 “whipped from to ” (i.e. as a vagabond).

tod.text: 28lb. weight of wool; as vb. to yield this quantity Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 33, 34 “Every 'leven wether t-s; every tod yields pound and odd shilling.”

toge.text: Roman toga Gor. II. iii. 122 “in this wolvish toge” (F1 “tongue,” Ff2-4 “gowne”).

toil.text: to put to exertion, tax the strength of MND. V. i. 74 “t-'d their . . . memories,” R2 IV. i. 96 “toil'd with works of war,” 2H6 I. i. 84 , Ham. I. i. 72 .

token.text: mark on the body of disease or infection, esp. of the plague LLL. V. ii. 424 “the Lord's t-s” (=plague-spots), Troil. II. iii. 189 (see DEATHTOKEN), Lucr. 1748 “Corrupted blood some watery token shows.” ∥ Cf. ‘Tokens’, the plague (Dict. of Canting Crew).

toll.text: vb. 1 (each sense only once) 1. to take toll, levy a tax John III. i. 154 .

top.text: sb. (3 Lodge has ‘in top of all thy pride’) 1. head All'sW. I. ii. 43 , Lr. II. iv. 165 “fail On her ungrateful top,” Cym. IV. ii. 354 .

touch.text: sb. (the physical sense of ‘act of touching, contact’ is the most freq.; cf. also the application to unlawful commerce in Meas. III. ii. 25 , V. i. 141 , Sonn. cxli. 6 ） 1. fingering or playing of a musical instrument Gent. III. ii. 79 “Orpheus' lute . . . Whose golden ” . . .; phr. “know no ,” have no skill in playing R2 I. iii. 165 , Ham. III. ii. 378 [ 371 ]; transf. in pl. notes, strains Mer.V. V. i. 57 “the touches of sweet harmony,” 67

toward.text: prep. (freq.=simple ‘to’, e.g. Mac. I. iii. 152 ） 1. with a view to, tending to, aiming at Shr. II. i. 99 , Tim. II. ii. 202 “to use them a supply of money,” Cæs. I. ii. 85 , Mac. I. iv. 27 .

towards.text: prep. (the uses correspond precisely with those of TOWARD prep., except that “towards” is used also in relation to time R3 III. v. 100 ） 1. =TOWARD 1, R2 II. i. 161 , 235 , Mac. V. iv. 22 .

tower.text: (of a falcon) to rise in circles of flight till she reaches her ‘place’ 2H6 II. i. 10 “My Lord Protector's hawks do so well,” Mac. II. iv. 12 “A falcon, t-ing in her pride of place” ; (hence) to soar, lit. and fig. John II. i. 350 , V. ii. 149 .

toy.text: sb. (not in the sense of ‘plaything’) 1. trifle, trifling ornament Tw.N. III. iii. 44 , Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 328 “Any toys for your head.”

trace.text: vb. (reading of Ff Qq2 3 in Oth. II. i. 315 , but difficult to explain; see TRASH vb.) 1. to follow 1H4 III. i. 48 “ me in the tedious ways of art,” H8 III. ii. 45 , Mac. IV. i. 153 “his babes, and all . . . souls That him in his line,” Ham. V. ii. 126 .

tract.text: （“trace, track,” and “tract” were largely interchangeable in the Eliz. period; cf. Cotgr., ‘Trac’, a tracke, tract, or trace) 1. track of a path Tim. I. i. 51 “Leaving no behind.”

train.text: to lure, allure, entice Err. III. ii. 45 “ me not . . . with thy note, To drown me,” John III. iv. 175 , 1H4 V. ii. 21 “train him on,” Tit. V. i. 104 .

trash.text: to check (a dog) that is too fast by attaching a weight to its neck Shr. Ind. i. 17 “Trash† Merriman, the poor cur is emboss'd” (old edd. “Brach”); fig. Tp. I. ii. 81 “who t'advance, and who To for over-topping,” Oth. II. i. 315 “this poor trash of Venice, whom I † For his quick hunting” (Ff Qq2 3 “trace,” Q1 “crush”). ∥ The meaning ‘lop’ assigned by some to Tp. I. ii. 81 is not supported elsewhere.

traverse.text: to march, esp. backwards and forwards Wiv. II. iii. 25 “To see thee fight . . . to see thee ,” 2H4 III. ii. 294 “Hold, Wart, ” ; transf. Oth. I. iii. 378 (spoken by Iago, the ancient') “Traverse; go.” ∥ The full phr. was ‘traverse one's ground’.

treasure.text: treasury Sonn. cxxxvi. 5 “Will will fulfil the treasure of thy love.”

trembling.text: tremor denoting possession by a devil Tp. II. ii. 86 .

trench.text: 1. to cut Gent. III. ii. 7 “a figure T-ed in ice,” Mac. III. iv. 27 “t-ed gashes,” Ven. 1052 “the wide wound that the boar had trench'”

trenchering.text: trenchers collectively Tp. II. ii. 196 “Nor scrape trenchering (trencher†).”

trick.text: sb. (‘device, artifice’, ‘deception’, ‘freakish practice or act’, ‘prank, joke’ are freq. senses) 1. custom, habit, way Meas. III. ii. 56 “Which is the way? Is it sad, and few words, or how? The of it?,” V. i. 506 “I spoke it but according to the ,” All'sW. III. ii. 9 , 1H4 V. ii. 11 , 2H4 I. ii. 244 , Ham. IV. vii. 188 .

trifle.text: vb. (2 occurs only once) 1. to spend to no purpose Mer.V. IV. i. 299 “We time,” H8 V. iii. 178 “we trifle time away.”

trigon.text: triangle; in astrology, conjunction of three planets in a certain sign 2H4 II. iv. 288 “the fiery ” (=the three superior planets meeting in Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius).

trim.text: sb. (2 Bailey defines ‘Trim of a Ship’, as ‘her best Posture, Proportion of Ballast, hanging of her Masts, &c. which conduce most to her good sailing’) 1. fine attire, apparel, trappings 1H4 IV. i. 113 “sacrifices in their trim” (i.e. decorated), Cor. I. ix. 62 “My noble steed . . . With all his belonging,” Ant. IV. iv. 22 “their riveted ,” Cym. III. iv. 167 “dainty t-s” ; fig. H5 IV. iii. 115 “our hearts are in the trim.”

triumph.text: sb. (mod. senses also occur) 1. public festivity or rejoicing, festive show or entertainment Gent. V. iv. 161 , MND. I. i. 19 “with , and with revelling,” 1H4 III. iii. 47 “a perpetual , an everlasting bonfire-light,” 3H6 V. vii. 43 , Per. V. i. 17 ; spec. tournament R2 V. ii. 52 “justs and t-s,” 1H6 V. v. 31 “at a having vow'd To try his strength,” Per. II. ii. 1 ; so “triumph day” R2 V. ii. 66 .

troth.text: (pronounced “trot” by Dr. Caius, Wiv. IV. v. 90 ) 1. truth MND. II. ii. 36 , Cor. IV. v. 198 , Cym. V. v. 275 “I'll speak troth.”

truant.text: “ with,” be unfaithful to Err. III. ii. 17 .

trust.text: 1. to believe, be sure of Shr. IV. ii. 67 “If he be credu-” “lous and trust my tale,” Wint. II. iii. 49 “ it, He shall not rule me,” Mac. I. iii. 120 “That, t-ed home, Might yet enkindle you unto the crown.”

try.text: vb. (3 cf. ‘a Ship is said to try, when she has no more Sails abroad but her Main or Missen Sail only, [and] is let alone to lie in the Sea’, Bailey) 1. to refine (gold) Mer.V. II. vii. 53 “tried gold” ; fig. ix. 63 , 64

tug.text: to buffet Mac. III. i. 112 “tugg'd with fortune.”

turn.text: vb. (5 cf. TURNING and TRIPLE-TURNED) 1. to shape on a lathe 1H4 III. i. 130 “I had rather hear a brazen canstick turn'”

twelfe.text: old form of “twelfth”† (which is not found in old edd.) Tw.N. II. iii. 93 , and in the title of the play itself.

twiggen.text: cased in wicker work Oth. II. iii. 153 * “I'll beat the knave into a bottle” (Qq “wicker bottle”).

twist.text: to draw out (a thread) John IV. iii. 128 “the smallest thread That ever spider t-ed from her womb” ; fig. Ado I. i. 321 [ 313 ] “to so fine a story.”

uncleanly.text: improper, indelicate AYL. III. ii. 52 , John IV. i. 7 “Uncleanly scruples,” Oth. III. iii. 139 .

underborne.text: with a lining or undergarment of Ado III. iv. 21 “underborne with a bluish tinsel.”

undeserving.text: ‘want of merit, unworthiness’ (Schmidt) LLL. V. ii. 367 “My lady . . . gives undeserving praise.”

unfolding.text: the star that by its rising tells the shepherd the time to release the sheep from the fold Meas. IV. ii. 219 .

unhatched.text: fig. not brought to maturity Ham. I. iii. 65 “each u-'d . . . comrade” (Qq “new hatcht”), Oth. III. iv. 140 “some u-'d practice Made demonstrable.”

unkind.text: (prob.) unnatural AYL. II. vii. 175 , 1H6 IV. i. 193 , Tit. I. i. 86 “ and careless of thine own,” Lr. III. iv. 70 “his unkind daughters,” Ven. 204 (? with play on the sense ‘unfeeling, cruel’).

unpeeled.text: stripped LLL. II. i. 88 “his house” (Q1; the rest “unpeopled”).

unperfect.text: not knowing one's part Sonn. xxiii. 1 “an actor.” ∥ Cf. “perfectness” LLL. V. ii. 174 .

unproper.text: not belonging exclusively to an individual, common Oth. IV. i. 69 “lie in those beds Which they dare swear peculiar.” ∥ There is prob. no allusion to a sense ‘indecent’, since corresponding uses of the words ‘proper’ and ‘improper’ are post-S.

unsanctified.text: wicked Mac. IV. ii. 79 , Lr. IV. vi. 282 .

unsisting.text: (?) misprint in Ff1 2 3 for “insisting” (F4) =persistent Meas. IV. ii. 92 (many conj., e.g. “unresisting†, unassisting†”).

untempering.text: not having a softening influence H5 V. ii. 239 “the poor and effect of my visage.”

unthrift.text: prodigal, (hence) good-for-nothing; adj. Mer.V. V. i. 16 “an love,” Tim. IV. iii. 311 “What man didst thou ever know that was beloved after his means?” ;—sb. R2 II. iii. 122 “upstart u-s,” Sonn. ix. 9 , xiii. 13 . ∥ Marked as an ‘old word’ by Bailey.

untrue.text: untruth Sonn. cxiii. 14 * “maketh mine ” (=is the cause of my not seeing things truly); Capell, Malone “makes mine eye† untrue.”

untrussing.text: untying the points (see POINT sb. 5) Meas. III. ii. 194 .

unwrung.text: not wrenched or galled, as by a bad saddle Ham. III. ii. 257 “our withers are unwrung.”

upon.text: prep. (follows its noun in All'sW. III. iv. 6 “the cold ground upon,” R2 II. iii. 138 ; 6 developed from the use with words like ‘attack’; for idiomatic uses with vbs. and adjs. see the latter) 1. on the side or party of John II. i. 237 “whose protection Is most divinely vow'd upon the right Of him it holds,” Mac. III. vi. 30 “upon his aid To wake Northumberland.”

upspring.text: the wildest dance at the old German merrymakings Ham. I. iv. 9 “Keeps wassail, and the swaggering upspring reels.”

upstaring.text: standing on end Tp. I. ii. 213 “With hair ” ∥ Spenser has ‘upstaring crests’ and ‘upstart haire’.

upward.text: top Lr. V. iii. 138 “from the extremest upward of thy head To the” . . .

use.text: sb. (obsolete or archaic uses) 1. habitual practice, custom Meas. I. iv. 62 “use and liberty” (=licentious practice), Mer.V. IV. i. 269 “it is still her” (viz. Fortune's) “use To let the wretched man outlive his wealth,” All'sW. V. i. 24 “with more haste Than is his use,” Tim. I. i. 292 “a return exceeding All use of quittance,” Oth. IV. i. 285 “Is it his use?” ; pl. usages, ways Ham. I. ii. 134 “all the uses of this world,” Oth. IV. iii. 107 (Q1 “vsage”).

usuring.text: usurious, grasping, stingy Tim. III. v. 112 , IV. iii. 518 “a usuring kindness.”

utis.text: [variant form of ‘utas’=octave of a festival, i.e. the eighth day after the feast-day, or the period of eight days beginning with it]: in transf. sense, merrymaking 2H4 II. iv. 22 “old utis” (=rare fun).

vail.text: vb. [aphetic form of ‘avail, avale’, Fr. ‘avaler’] 1. to let fall, lower LLL. V. ii. 298 “angels v-ing clouds” (=letting fall the clouds that hide them), Mer.V. I. i. 28 “Vailing her high-top,” 1H6 V. iii. 25 “ her lofty-plumed crest,” Ham. I. ii. 70 “thy vailed lids,” Per. II. iii. 42 .

vailful.text: advantageous Meas. IV. vi. 4 “to purpose” (Ff “vail(e full,” Malone “veil full”†).

value.text: vb. (1 freq. in the gen. sense) 1. to rate, estimate; 1H4 III. ii. 177 “Our business v-d,” taking into consideration how long our business will take us; V. ii. 59 “valu'd with you,” compared with you in respect of worth.

vary.text: to express in different terms H5 III. vii. 35 “vary deserved praise on my palfrey.”

vent.text: sb. 1 [? orig. a variant of ‘fent’=slit] 1. opening, aperture 2H4 Ind. 2 “The of hearing” (=the ear), Troil. V. iii. 82 “how thy wounds do bleed at many v-s,” Lucr. 310 “little v-s and crannies,” 1040

very.text: （“same ”=very same John IV. i. 125 , R3 III. ii. 49 ) 1. veritable, real, true, that is indeed so Ado IV. i. 188 “Two of them have the very bent of honour,” Ham. II. ii. 49 “The very cause of Hamlet's lunacy” ; esp. in “very friend” Gent. III. ii. 41 , Mer.V. III. ii. 224 , Rom. III. i. 116 ;— Cym. IV. ii. 107 “very Cloten” (=Cloten himself).

vice.text: sb. 1 (2 cf. Cotgr., ‘Badiner’, to play the foole, or Vice) 1. sinful act, offence, transgression Meas. II. iv. 117 “You . . . rather prov'd the sliding of your brother A merriment than a vice,” Oth. IV. i. 179 “how he laughed at his vice,” IV. iii. 71 “'tis a great price For a small vice.”

vinewed'st.text: most mouldy Troil. II. i. 15 “thou leaven” (Ff “whinid'st,” Q “vnsalted”).

virgin.text: of a virgin Mer.V. III. ii. 56 “The virgin tribute” (viz. Hesione) “paid by howling Troy To the sea-monster”; of virginity MND. I. i. 80 “my virgin patent” (=my privilege of virginity).

voice.text: sb. (the usual medium of expressing one's meaning, intention, or opinion; hence the foll. senses) 1. what one says, speech, words Wiv. I. iii. 49 , I. iv. 163 “let me have thy in my behalf” (=speak for me), H5 V. ii. 93 “Haply a woman's may do some good,” Ham. I. ii. 45 “lose your voice” (=speak in vain).

void.text: vb. [aphetic form of AVOID, q.v.] 1. to emit Mer.V. I. iii. 118 “ your rheum,” H5 III. v. 52 ; “void up,” vomit Tim. I. ii. 145 .

vouch.text: to bear witness Oth. I. iii. 263 “ with me, heaven.” ∥ The common senses are (1) warrant, answer for, (2) assert, maintain, where mod.idiom prefers ‘vouch for’ (which is not S.).

vulgar.text: adj. (the sense ‘low, mean’ occurs) 1. of the common people, plebeian 2H4 I. iii. 90 “the heart,” Cor. I. i. 221 “Five tribunes to defend their wisdoms,” II. i. 234 “ station” (=among the crowd), IV. vii. 21 .

wake.text: feast of the dedication (or title) of a church and the merrymaking connected with it LLL. V. ii. 319 “At w-s and wassails,” Wint. IV. ii. [ iii. ] 110, Lr. III. vi. 77 “wakes and fairs.”

walk.text: sb. (obsolete senses) 1. pl. (a person's) way or course MND. III. i. 172 “Hop in his walks, and gambol in his eyes,” V. i. 31 “in your royal walks,” Tit. II. iv. 8 “let's leave her to her silent walks,” Sonn. lxxxix. 9 “I will . . . Be absent from thy walks.”

wandering.text: “ knight,” knight errant MND. I. ii. 48 ; “ star,” planet Ham. V. i. 278 .

wanton.text: adj. (‘lascivious’ the most freq. sense) 1. unrestrained, sportive, frolicsome LLL. IV. iii. 104 “the air,” V. ii. 769 “All as a child,” Mer.V. V. i. 71 “a wild and herd,” H8 III. ii. 360 “little boys,” Ham. II. i. 22 “wanton, wild, and usual slips.”

ward.text: sb. (4 the commonest sense in S.) 1. guard, protection LLL. III. i. 139 .

ware.text: aware (“of”) AYL. II. iv. 57 “Thou speakest wiser than thou art ware of,” Rom. I. i. 130 , II. ii. 103 ; in AYL. II. iv. 59 the meaning ‘cautious’ is played upon.

warrant.text: vb. (2 cf. WARN 1) 1. to give (a person) security Meas. IV. ii. 179 “By the vow of mine order I you,” Err. IV. iv. 3 “I'll give thee . . . so much money, To thee, as I am rested for.”

wash.text: “wash” oneself “of,” get rid of Wiv. III. iii. 167 “I would I could wash myself of the buck!” (pun on BUCK-WASHING); “wash” one's “brain” (Eliz. phr.), drink copiously Ant. II. vii. 106 .

washing.text: =SWASHING (q.v.) Rom. I. i. 69 “thy blow.” ∥ Nashe uses this expression.

waste.text: sb. (in R2 II. i. 103 a ref. to the legal sense ‘destruction of houses, woods, lands, &c., done by the tenant to the prejudice of the heir’; 2 is also perhaps a legal metaphor) 1. wasting, squandering, devastation (often in phr. “make ”) Mer.V. I. i. 158 , H5 I. ii. 28 , III. iii. 18 , Lr. II. i. 102 “the waste and spoil of all revenues.”

watch.text: vb. (1 the commonest sense) 1. to be or lie awake, have no sleep, sit up at night LLL. III. i. 210 [ 202 ] “to sigh for her! to for her!,” Shr. IV. i. 208 , Lr. II. ii. 162 , Lucr. 1575 “they that see time how slow it creeps” ; to remain awake for a specified purpose John IV. i. 30 , Mac. V. i. 1 .

waterish.text: well-watered, abounding in rivers Lr. I. i. 261 “ Burgundy” (with play on the sense ‘poor, thin’ exemplified in Oth. III. iii. 15 “ diet” ).

wawl.text: to wail Lr. IV. vi. 185 (Ff “wawle,” Q1 “wayle,” Qq2 3 “waile”).

wax.text: vb. (pa. pple. “waxed, waxen”; 2 freq.) 1. to grow, increase LLL. V. ii. 10 (with quibble on “wax” sb.), Cor. II. ii. 104 “he waxed like a sea,” Tit. III. i. 96 “the waxing tide,” Ham. I. iii. 12 .

waxen.text: fig. uses:—easily impressed Tw.N. II. ii. 31 “women's hearts,” Lucr. 1240 “women” [have] “ minds”; easily effaced H5 I. ii. 233 * “a epitaph”; easily penetrable R2 I. iii. 75 “Mowbray's coat.”

we.text: used, like “I,” for the objective ‘us’ Cor. V. iii. 103 “to poor we,” Ham. I. iv. 54 “Making night hideous; and we fools of nature . . . to shake our disposition.”

wear.text: vb. (freq. used where ‘bear’ would now be idiomatic; Ado V. i. 82 “Win me and wear me,” a common Eliz. proverb; see also WORN) 1. to weary, ‘wear out’ AYL. II. iv. 38 “Wearing thy hearer” (Ff2-4 “Wearying”), All'sW. V. i. 4 “To wear your gentle limbs in my affairs.”

weed.text: to uproot (lit. and fig.) Gent. III. ii. 49 , Meas. III. ii. 292 [ 284 ] “To weed my vice and let his grow,” R2 II. iii. 167 “The caterpillars of the commonwealth, Which I have sworn to and pluck away,” Cor. IV. v. 108 , Oth. I. iii. 327 “set hyssop and up thyme.”

weet.text: to know Ant. I. i. 39 “I bind . . . the world to weet We stand up peerless.”

weigh.text: (rare in literal senses) 1. to consider, take into consideration Cæs. II. i. 108 “Weighing the youthful season of the year,” Sonn. cxx. 8 “To weigh how once I suffer'”

wheel.text: sb. (2 freq.; 3 in Warwickshire, a clock that goes fast is said to go on wheels) 1. spinning-wheel AYL. I. ii. 36 “mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel” (with ref. to sense 2), Ham. IV. v. 171 “how the wheel becomes it” (viz. as an accompaniment to the song).

which.text: 1. refers freq. to persons=who, whom, e.g. Tp. I. ii. 32 , 1H4 III. i. 46 , Mac. V. i. 65 , Lucr. 1392 ; “the which” is very common, e.g. Ado II. i. 30 , V. i. 159 , H5 IV. viii. 90 , Cæs. III. i. 295 , Ven. 683 .

whiffler.text: officer who clears the way for a procession H5 v. Chor. 12 “the deep-mouth'd sea, Which, like a mighty 'fore the king, Seems to prepare his way.”

while.text: “the while” in exclamations=(at) the present time Mer.V. II. i. 31 “alas the !,” John IV. ii. 100 “bad world the !,” R3 III. vi. 10 “Here's a good world the while!.”

whirligig.text: whipping-top; fig. Tw.N. V. i. 389 “thus the of time brings in his revenges” ; old edd. have only the old forms “whirl(e)gigg(”

whirling.text: impetuous, violent Ham. I. v. 133 “ words” (Q1 “wherling,” Q2 “whurling”; Ff “hurling”).

whissing.text: old form of ‘wheezing’ Troil. V. i. 24 (Q).

whistle.text: phr. 2H4 III. ii. 345 “tunes . . . that he heard the carmen ” (ref. to a popular Eliz. tune named ‘The Carman's Whistle’); Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 716 “let the law go whistle” (=go hang); whistle off, (in falconry) to send (a hawk) from the fist Oth. III. iii. 262 “if I do prove her haggard . . . I'd her off and let her down the wind” (i.e. so that she may not return) “To prey at fortune”; fig. Wint. IV. iii. [ iv. ] 247 “to whistle off these secrets.”

white.text: typical of cowardice Mer.V. III. ii. 86 “livers as milk” (cf. MILK-LIVER'D), 2H4 IV. iii. 113 , Mac. II. ii. 66 “I shame To wear a heart so ;— herring,” fresh herring or pickled herring (opposed to ‘red herring’) Lr. III. vi. 34 .

who.text: relative pron. (1 cf. prec.; see WHOM) 1. used for ‘whom’, e.g. Mer.V. I. ii. 25 (Qq “who,” Ff “whom”), R3 I. iii. 327 “who I, indeed, have cast in darkness” (F1 “who,” Qq “whom”), Oth. II. iii. 15 .

whom.text: 1. = which, e.g. 2H6 III. ii. 345 “the seal, Through whom a thousand sighs are breath'd for thee,” Troil. III. iii. 202 “a mystery—with whom” . . .

wide.text: indifferent to Wiv. III. i. 58 “so wide of his own respect.”

wild.text: inconsiderate, rash Wint. II. i. 181 , Cor. IV. i. 36 “a wild exposture to each chance” . . .

will.text: sb. (“good will” is freq. in the senses of ‘favourable regard, favour’, ‘acquiescence, consent’, and ‘willingness, readiness’) 1. phr. “by my will,” (i) of my own accord, voluntarily Ado III. iii. 67 “I would not hang a dog by my will,” Tw.N. III. iii. 1 ; (ii) with my consent 2H4 IV. i. 159 “by my will we shall admit no parley,” Troil. II. iii. 204 , Ven. 639 ;—“by” or “of” one's “(own) good will,” of one's own accord R2 IV. i. 177 “To do that office of thine own good will Which tired majesty did make thee offer,” Ven. 479 “she, by her good will, Will never rise, so he will kiss her still” ; so “on my free will” Ant. III. vi. 57 .

willing.text: as adv. willingly R2 III. iii. 206 “What you will have, I'll give, and too,” 2H6 V. i. 51 , Tim. III. vi. 33 “The swallow follows not summer more than we your lordship.”

wind.text: sb. (see also BREAK, DOOR) 1. phr. “down the wind,” (to fly) in the direction of the wind, as a hawk was made to do when dismissed Oth. III. iii. 262 ; “sits in the wind against,” is in opposition to Ant. III. viii. 46 [ x. 37 ]; “on the wind,” speedily and without impediment, as if on the ‘wings of the wind’ Ant, III. vi. 63 ; cf. Cym. III. iv. 38 ; “have i' the wind,” get scent of All'sW. III. vi. 123 ; “keeps the wind,” keep to windward of the game so as to force it into the toils 3H6 III. ii. 14 ; so “recover the wind of” Ham. III. ii. 369 [ 362 ] “why do you go about to recover the wind of me, as if you would drive me into a toil?;—have the wind of,” keep watch upon (as upon the game, when following it down the wind) Tit. IV. ii. 134 .

windgalls.text: disease attacking the fetlock in horses Shr. III. ii. 54 .

wink.text: vb. (1 the commonest S. sense) 1. to shut one's eyes, have the eyes closed; said also of the eyes themselves Tp. II. i. 224 [ 216 ] “Thou . . . wink'st Whiles thou art waking,” H5 II. i. 8 “I dare not fight; but I will and hold out mine iron,” Cym. V. iv. 193 “such as wink and will not use them” [viz. their eyes], Ven. 90 “He winks, and turns his lips another way,” Sonn. xliii. 1 ;—in some exx. =blink LLL. I. ii. 55 “ere you'll thrice wink,” R2 IV. i. 284 “the face That like the sun did make beholders wink,” Lucr. 375 “his eyes begun To wink, being blinded with a greater light.”

winking.text: with eyes shut H5 III. vii. 158 “that run into the mouth of a Russian bear” ; blind Cym. II. iv. 89 “ Cupids” ; (of flowers, &c.) closed John II. i. 215 “your gates,” Cym. II. iii. 26 “winking Mary-buds.”

wise.text: manner Per. V. ii. 11 (Gower) “in no wise” (=not at all), Pilgr. iii. 33 [ 277 ].

wish.text: to invite or commend (one) “to” another Shr. I. i. 112 “I will wish him to her father,” I. ii. 60 “shall I . . . wish thee to a shrewd ill-favour'd wife?.”

wist.text: knew 1H6 IV. i. 180 “An if I wist he did,—But let it rest” (old edd. “wish”; Theobald “I wis”†). ∥ See note S.V. WOT.

wit.text: sb. (the foll. senses are characteristic of the Eliz. period) 1. the mental powers or faculties, the mind; usu. pl. e.g. Gent. I. i. 44 “love Inhabits in the finest wits,” Cor. II. iii. 21 , &c.; “five wits,” common sense, imagination, fancy, estimation, memory Ado I. i. 67 , Rom. I. iv. 47 , Lr. III. iv. 57 , Sonn. cxli. 9 “my five wits nor my five senses” ; occas. sing. Gent. I. i. 47 “the young and tender wit,” 1H6 I. ii. 73 “My wit untrain'd in any kind of art.”

witness.text: to give or show evidence of Meas. IV. iii. 103 “letters . . . whose contents Shall to him I am near at home,” R2 II. iv. 22 “W-ing storms to come,” Sonn. xxvi. 4 “I send this written ambassage, To duty.”

woe.text: sorry Tp. V. i. 139 “I am woe for't,” 2H6 III. ii. 73 , Ant. IV. xii. [ xiv. ] 133 “woe are we,” Sonn. lxxi. 8 “If thinking on me then should make you woe.” ∥ ‘I am woe’ was developed from the old ‘Woe is me’; Chaucer blends the old and the new in ‘me is as wo For him as ever I was for any man’.

woman.text: sb. (1 contrast WIFE) 1. wife Wiv. II. ii. 309 “the hell of having a false ,” 1H4 II. iii. 44 .

womb.text: transf. applied to anything hollow or conceived as hollow (e.g. the earth, night) R2 II. i. 83 “a grave, Whose hollow womb” . . ., 1H4 III. i. 31 , H5 IV. Chor. 4 “the foul womb of night,” Rom. V. i. 65 “the fatal cannon's womb,” Compl. 1 “a hill Whose concave womb” . . .

wonder.text: to admire Sonn. cvi. 14 “we . . . Have eyes to , but lack tongues to praise” ; const. “at” LLL. V. ii. 267 “Are these the breed of wits so wonder'd at?.”

woollen.text: covered with woollen cloth Mer.V. IV. i. 56 “a bagpipe” (so Qq Ff1 2 3; Capell “wauling”†); coarsely clad, homely Cor. III. ii. 9 “woollen vassals” ;—sb. Ado II. i. 33 “lie in the ,” sleep between the blankets with no sheets.

word.text: sb. (4 is freq. in ordinary phrases) 1. “at a word,” to be brief, in short Wiv. I. i. 109 , Ado II. i. 120 , Cor. I. iii. 122 “go along with us.—No, at a , madam” ; so “with a word” 1H4 II. iv. 287 ; in phr. expressing prompt decision or action Wiv. I. iii. 14 “I am at a word; follow,” 2H4 III. ii. 322 “Go to; I have spoke at a word” (=you may depend upon me), Cæs. I. ii. 270 “if I would not have taken him at a word” ; cf. Cæs. I. ii. 104 “Upon the word . . . I plunged in.”

work.text: vb. (pa. t. and pa. pple. always “wrought”; 1 cf. WORKING vbl. sb. and ppl. adj.; 5 said esp. of seething waters in Eliz. period) 1. to act upon or affect, powerfully move Tp. IV. i. 144 “your father's in some passion That works him strongly,” V. i. 17 “your charm so strongly works them,” Mac. I. iii. 149 “my dull brain was wrought With things forgotten,” Oth. V. ii. 344 .

working.text: exciting the emotions, full of pathos H8 Prol. 3

worldlings.text: (?) men of this world, mortals AYL. II. i. 48 , 2H4 V. iii. 100 .

worship.text: honour, dignity Wint. I. ii. 314 “bench'd and rear'd to worship,” John IV. iii. 72 , 3H6 IV. iii. 16 “ and quietness” (=‘otium cum dignitate’), R3 I. i. 66 “that good man of ,” Cor. III. i. 141 (‘this divided authority of the senate and the people’), Lr. I. iv. 290 ; H8 I. i. 39 “belong to ” (=are of noble rank).

wort.text: infusion of malt before it is fermented, sweet unfermented beer LLL. V. ii. 234 .

worth.text: sb. (Malone explains “his ” in Cor. III. iii. 26 * ‘his full quota or proportion’) 1. wealth, riches MND. II. i. 219 “the rich of your virginity,” Tw.N. III. iii. 17 , Rom. II. vi. 32 “They are but beggars that can count their ,” Lr. IV. iv. 10 , Oth. I. ii. 28 “not . . . For the sea's worth.”

worthy.text: adj. (the senses ‘excellent’ and ‘deserving’ are the most freq., the latter with various constructions) 1. valuable Tp. I. ii. 247 “I have done thee service,” AYL. III. iii. 62 , Cæs. III. i. 116 “No worthier than the dust,” Sonn. xlviii. 6 .

wot.text: know(s) Wiv. II. ii. 91 “the picture . . . that you wot of,” Wint. III. ii. 77 “the gods themselves, Wotting no more than I,” H5 IV. i. 302 “The slave . . . little wots What watch the king keeps,” R3 II. iii. 18 “no, no, good friends, God wot,” III. ii. 89 “Wot you what, my lord?” (=let me tell you), Tit. II. i. 48 , Ant. I. v. 22 “wot'st thou whom thou mov'st?.” ∥ The present tense of WIT vb.; the past tense ‘wist’ occurs in the 1611 Bible (e.g. Luke ii. 49 ), but is not S.

wrack.text: sb. (always so spelt in old edd., not ‘wreck’) 1. destruction, ruin All'sW. III. v. 23 “the of maidenhood,” 2H6 I. ii. 105 “Hume's knavery will be the duchess' ,” Mac. I. iii. 114 “He labour'd in his country's wrack,” Ven. 558 “honour's wrack.”

wrath.text: sb. (1 freq.; 2 once) 1. warlike ardour=RAGE sb. 5 Tw.N. III. iv. 257 “your opposite hath in him what youth, strength, skill, and wrath can furnish withal,” 2H4 I. i. 109 , Cor. I. ix. 86 , Ham. II. ii. 492 [ 483 ].

wreak.text: vengeance, revenge Cor. IV. v. 91 “A heart of ,” Tit. IV. iii. 33 “Take ,” IV. iv. 11 “in his wreaks” (=vindictive acts).

wrest.text: key for tuning a harp; fig. Troil. III. iii. 23 “Antenor . . . is such a wrest in their affairs That their negotiations all must slack, Wanting his manage.”

wring.text: (see also WRINGING, WRUNG) 1. to wrench, wrest (lit. and fig.) Meas. V. i. 32 “ redress from you,” 3H6 III. i. 16 “thy sceptre wrung from thee,” Ham. I. ii. 58 “He hath . . . wrung from me my slow leave,” Oth. V. ii. 287 (Ff “Wrench”).

writ.text: sb. (2 “holy writ” is the usu. phrase) 1. that which is written, writing, document 2H6 I. iv. 60 “the devil's writ,” Tit. II. iii. 264 “this fatal writ,” Ham. II. ii. 430 [421 * ] “For the law of writ and the liberty” (?=‘for repeating correctly what is written, and for freedom of improvisation’, Clark and Wright; Q 1676 “wit”), V. ii. 51 [I] “folded the writ up”; ‘penned or premeditated oration’ (J.) Cæs. III. ii. 225 “I have neither writ, nor words, nor worth” (Ff2-4 “wit”).

writing.text: words of a song LLL. I. ii. 120 .

wroath.text: irregular spellings of ‘ruth’=calamity, ruin Mer.V. II. ix. 78 “Patiently to bear my ” ∥ ‘Roth’ is a 15th cent. form, and ‘routh’ occurs as late as the 17th cent.

wrong.text: (very freq. in the ordinary senses) 1. phr. “have wrong,” suffer injury, injustice, or loss 2H4 II. ii. 107 , V. i. 58 , 3H6 IV. i. 102 , Cæs. III. ii. 116 ; “do” oneself “wrong,” put oneself in the wrong, be mistaken Tp. I. ii. 440 , Wiv. III. iii. 220 , Meas. I. ii. 43 .

yean.text: form in mod. edd. of EAN.

yearn.text: to vex, grieve Wiv. III. v. 45 “it would your heart” ; impers. R2 V. v. 76 “it y-'d my heart” (Qq1-4 “ernd,” Ff1-3 Q5 “yern'd”), H5 IV. iii. 26 “It y-s me not.” ∥ Cf. EARN 2 .

yielding.text: compliance LLL. I. i. 118 , John II. i. 474 , Rom. II. ii. 105 , Lucr. 1658 .

yoke.text: to be joined or coupled 3H6 IV. i. 23 , IV. vi. 49 “We'll yoke together,” Cor. III. i. 56 .

young.text: 1. raw, inexperienced AYL. I. i. 58 “you are too young in this,” Mac. III. iv. 144 “We are yet but young in deed.”

younger.text: ago Per. I. iv. 39 “not yet two summers younger” † (=not two years ago; old edd. “yet”).

youngling.text: stripling, novice Shr. II. i. 331 [ 339 ], Tit. II. i. 73 , IV. ii. 94 .
